qs.q: Convert \(\frac{11}{4}\) radians to degrees. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
qs.s: Multiply \(\frac{11}{4}\) radians by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\) to get \(\frac{495^\circ}{\pi} \approx 157.6^\circ\).

qs.q: Convert \(19.5\) radians to degrees. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
qs.s: Multiply \(19.5\) by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\) to obtain \(\frac{3510^\circ}{\pi} \approx 1117.3^\circ\).

qs.q: Convert \(-14.25\) radians to degrees. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
qs.s: Multiply \(-14.25\) by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\) to get \(-\frac{2565^\circ}{\pi} \approx -816.5^\circ\).

qs.q: Convert \((6.35 - 1.8)\) radians to degrees. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
qs.s: First subtract to get \(6.35 - 1.8 = 4.55\) radians, then multiply by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\): \(4.55 \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{819^\circ}{\pi} \approx 260.7^\circ\).

qs.q: Convert from radians to degrees. Give the answer to 1 decimal place: \(-6.4\).
qs.s: Multiply the radian measure by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\) to obtain \(-6.4 \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = -\frac{1152^\circ}{\pi} \approx -366.7^\circ\).

qs.q: Convert from radians to degrees. Give the answer to 1 decimal place: \(5.7\).
qs.s: Multiply the radian measure by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\) to obtain \(5.7 \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{1026^\circ}{\pi} \approx 326.6^\circ\).

qs.q: Convert from radians to degrees. Give the answer to 1 decimal place: \(-8.1\).
qs.s: Multiply the radian measure by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\) to obtain \(-8.1 \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = -\frac{1458^\circ}{\pi} \approx -464.1^\circ\).

qs.q: Convert from radians to degrees. Give the answer to 1 decimal place: \(-14.5\).
qs.s: Multiply the radian measure by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\) to obtain \(-14.5 \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = -\frac{2610^\circ}{\pi} \approx -830.8^\circ\).

qs.q: Convert from radians to degrees. Give the answer to 1 decimal place: \(9.2\).
qs.s: Multiply the radian measure by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\) to obtain \(9.2 \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{1656^\circ}{\pi} \approx 527.1^\circ\).

qs.q: Convert from radians to degrees. Give the answer to 1 decimal place: \(-\frac{59}{8}\).
qs.s: Multiply by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\) to get \(-\frac{59}{8} \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = -\frac{2655^\circ}{2\pi} \approx -422.6^\circ\).

qs.q: Convert from radians to degrees. Give the answer to 1 decimal place: \(3.6 - 3\pi\).
qs.s: Multiply the entire expression by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\) to get \(\frac{3.6 \times 180^\circ}{\pi} - 3(180^\circ) = \frac{648^\circ}{\pi} - 540^\circ \approx -333.7^\circ\).

qs.q: Convert from radians to degrees. Give the answer to 1 decimal place: \(-148.5\).
qs.s: Multiply by the conversion factor \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\) to get \(-148.5 \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = -\frac{26730^\circ}{\pi} \approx -8508.4^\circ\).

exercises.name: Circle Arc Length, Radius, and Angle Calculations

qs.q: Find the radius of a circle if an arc of length \(8\) subtends a central angle of \(40^\circ\) on the circle.
qs.s: Convert the angle to radians: \(40^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{2\pi}{9}\text{ radians}\). Solving \(s = r\theta\) for \(r\) yields \(r = \frac{8}{2\pi/9} = \frac{36}{\pi}\).

qs.q: Along a circular path, an arc of length \(14\text{ m}\) subtends a central angle of \(120^\circ\). What is the radius of the circular path?
qs.s: Convert \(120^\circ\) to radians: \(120^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{2\pi}{3}\text{ radians}\). Using \(r = \frac{s}{\theta}\), we have \(r = \frac{14}{2\pi/3} = \frac{21}{\pi}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Find the radius of a circle if an arc of length \(5\) subtends a central angle of \(45^\circ\).
qs.s: Convert \(45^\circ\) to radians to get \(\theta = 45^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{\pi}{4}\text{ radians}\). Using \(r = \frac{s}{\theta}\), we find \(r = \frac{5}{\pi/4} = \frac{20}{\pi}\).

qs.q: An arc of length \(4\text{ cm}\) subtends a central angle of \(60^\circ\) on a circle. Find the radius of the circle.
qs.s: Convert the angle to radians: \(60^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{\pi}{3}\text{ radians}\). Then \(r = \frac{s}{\theta} = \frac{4}{\pi/3} = \frac{12}{\pi}\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A pendulum swings through a central angle of \(15^\circ\). If the tip of the pendulum travels an arc of length \(2\text{ cm}\), find the length of the pendulum.
qs.s: Convert \(15^\circ\) to radians: \(15^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{\pi}{12}\text{ radians}\). Since the pendulum length is the radius, \(r = \frac{s}{\theta} = \frac{2}{\pi/12} = \frac{24}{\pi}\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The tip of a clock's minute hand travels an arc length of \(16\pi\text{ cm}\) between 2:00 PM and 2:40 PM. Find the length of the minute hand.
qs.s: In 40 minutes, the minute hand covers \(\frac{40}{60} = \frac{2}{3}\) of a revolution, so \(\theta = \frac{2}{3}(2\pi) = \frac{4\pi}{3}\text{ radians}\). Using \(s = r\theta\), the length of the minute hand is \(r = \frac{16\pi}{4\pi/3} = 12\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: In a circle of radius \(r\), an arc subtended by a central angle of \(110^\circ\) is \(12\text{ cm}\) longer than an arc subtended by a central angle of \(30^\circ\). Find the radius \(r\).
qs.s: The difference between the angles is \(110^\circ - 30^\circ = 80^\circ\), which converts to \(80^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{4\pi}{9}\text{ radians}\). From \(\Delta s = r\Delta\theta\), we get \(12 = r\left(\frac{4\pi}{9}\right)\), so \(r = \frac{27}{\pi}\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A point on the rim of a flywheel travels an arc length of \(80\text{ m}\) as the wheel rotates through an angle of \(900^\circ\). Find the radius of the flywheel.
qs.s: Convert \(900^\circ\) to radians: \(900^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = 5\pi\text{ radians}\). Then using \(r = \frac{s}{\theta}\), the radius is \(r = \frac{80}{5\pi} = \frac{16}{\pi}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Two concentric circular arcs are subtended by the same central angle. The length of the inner arc is \(15\text{ cm}\) and the length of the outer arc is \(25\text{ cm}\). If the radius of the outer circle is \(4\text{ cm}\) greater than the radius of the inner circle, find the radius of the inner circle.
qs.s: Let \(r\) be the inner radius and \(r + 4\) be the outer radius. Since \(\theta\) is equal for both, \(\frac{r+4}{r} = \frac{25}{15} = \frac{5}{3}\), which simplifies to \(3(r+4) = 5r\) and gives \(r = 6\text{ cm}\).

exercises.name: Circle Arc Length, Radius, and Angle Calculations

qs.q: Find the arc length of a sector of a circle with radius 14 cm if the sector angle is 150°.
qs.s: Convert the angle to radians: \theta = 150^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{5\pi}{6}. Then, the arc length is s = r\theta = 14 \times \frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{35\pi}{3} \text{ cm}.

qs.q: Find the arc length of a sector of a circle with radius 16 cm if the sector angle is 135°.
qs.s: Convert the angle to radians: \theta = 135^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{3\pi}{4}. Then, the arc length is s = r\theta = 16 \times \frac{3\pi}{4} = 12\pi \text{ cm}.

qs.q: Find the arc length of a sector of a circle with radius 18 cm if the sector angle is 40°.
qs.s: Convert the angle to radians: \theta = 40^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{2\pi}{9}. Then, the arc length is s = r\theta = 18 \times \frac{2\pi}{9} = 4\pi \text{ cm}.

qs.q: Find the arc length of a sector of a circle with radius 21 cm if the sector angle is 80°.
qs.s: Convert the angle to radians: \theta = 80^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{4\pi}{9}. Then, the arc length is s = r\theta = 21 \times \frac{4\pi}{9} = \frac{28\pi}{3} \text{ cm}.

qs.q: Find the arc length of a sector of a circle with radius 12 cm if the sector angle is 75°.
qs.s: Convert the angle to radians: \theta = 75^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{5\pi}{12}. Then, the arc length is s = r\theta = 12 \times \frac{5\pi}{12} = 5\pi \text{ cm}.

qs.q: A wheel of radius 42 cm rotates through an angle of 570°. Find the total distance traveled by a point on the rim of the wheel.
qs.s: Convert the angle to radians: \theta = 570^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{19\pi}{6} \text{ radians}. The distance traveled is s = r\theta = 42 \times \frac{19\pi}{6} = 133\pi \text{ cm}.

qs.q: An arc of a circle with radius 24 cm has a length of 14\pi \text{ cm}. If the central angle remains the same but the radius is increased to 36 cm, what is the length of the new arc?
qs.s: The central angle is \theta = \frac{s}{r} = \frac{14\pi}{24} = \frac{7\pi}{12} \text{ radians}. With the new radius, the arc length is s = 36 \times \frac{7\pi}{12} = 21\pi \text{ cm}.

qs.q: Find the central angle in degrees of a circle with radius 28 cm that intercepts an arc of length \frac{49\pi}{3} \text{ cm}.
qs.s: Using \theta = \frac{s}{r}, the central angle is \theta = \frac{49\pi/3}{28} = \frac{7\pi}{12} \text{ radians}. Converting to degrees gives \frac{7\pi}{12} \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = 105^\circ.

qs.q: The minute hand of a clock is 15 cm long. Find the exact distance traveled by the tip of the minute hand in 52 minutes.
qs.s: In 52 minutes, the hand rotates \frac{52}{60} = \frac{13}{15} of a revolution, so \theta = \frac{13}{15}(2\pi) = \frac{26\pi}{15} \text{ radians}. The distance traveled is s = r\theta = 15 \times \frac{26\pi}{15} = 26\pi \text{ cm}.

qs.q: Two concentric circles have radii of 12 cm and 20 cm. A central angle of 135° intercepts an arc on each circle. Find the difference between the lengths of the two arcs.
qs.s: The angle in radians is 135^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{3\pi}{4}. The difference between the arc lengths is \Delta s = (r_2 - r_1)\theta = (20 - 12) \times \frac{3\pi}{4} = 6\pi \text{ cm}.

exercises.name: Circle Arc Length, Radius, and Angle Calculations

qs.q: A curved section along a circle of radius 9 mm has an arc length of 4 mm. Find the central angle in degrees.
qs.s: Using \(\theta = \frac{s}{r}\), we have \(\theta = \frac{4}{9}\text{ radians}\). In degrees, \(\theta = \frac{4}{9} \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{80^\circ}{\pi}\).

qs.q: Find the angle in degrees if an arc length of 3 cm has a radius of 4 cm.
qs.s: The central angle in radians is \(\theta = \frac{s}{r} = \frac{3}{4}\). Converting to degrees gives \(\theta = \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{135^\circ}{\pi}\).

qs.q: What is the degree measure of a central angle opposite an arc of 7 cm in a circle of radius 10 cm?
qs.s: The angle in radians is \(\theta = \frac{s}{r} = \frac{7}{10}\). Converting to degrees yields \(\theta = \frac{7}{10} \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{126^\circ}{\pi}\).

qs.q: In a circle with a radius of 5 cm, an arc has a length of 2 cm. Find the central angle in degrees.
qs.s: The angle in radians is \(\theta = \frac{s}{r} = \frac{2}{5}\). Converting to degrees gives \(\frac{2}{5} \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{72^\circ}{\pi}\).

qs.q: Find the degree measure of a central angle subtended by an arc of length 7 m in a circle of radius 12 m.
qs.s: The central angle in radians is \(\theta = \frac{7}{12}\). Multiply by \(\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\) to obtain \(\frac{7}{12} \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{105^\circ}{\pi}\).

qs.q: Find the central angle in degrees if an arc of length 0.75 m is intercepted by a radius of 45 cm.
qs.s: Convert 0.75 m to 75 cm so the units match. Then \(\theta = \frac{75}{45} = \frac{5}{3}\text{ radians}\), which in degrees is \(\frac{5}{3} \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{300^\circ}{\pi}\).

qs.q: On a circle of radius 36 cm, an arc length increases from 14 cm to 29 cm. Find the increase in the central angle in degrees.
qs.s: The change in arc length is \(\Delta s = 29 - 14 = 15\text{ cm}\), giving \(\Delta \theta = \frac{15}{36} = \frac{5}{12}\text{ radians}\). Converting to degrees gives \(\frac{5}{12} \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{75^\circ}{\pi}\).

qs.q: An object travels around a circular track of radius 25 m for a total distance of 65 m. Find the central angle swept out by the object, in degrees.
qs.s: The central angle in radians is \(\theta = \frac{s}{r} = \frac{65}{25} = \frac{13}{5}\). Converting to degrees gives \(\frac{13}{5} \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{468^\circ}{\pi}\).

qs.q: A circle has a diameter of 24 cm. Find the central angle in degrees subtended by an arc of length 22 cm.
qs.s: The radius is \(r = \frac{24}{2} = 12\text{ cm}\), so \(\theta = \frac{s}{r} = \frac{22}{12} = \frac{11}{6}\text{ radians}\). Converting to degrees gives \(\frac{11}{6} \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{330^\circ}{\pi}\).

qs.q: A sector of a circle has a perimeter of 40 cm and a radius of 15 cm. Find the central angle of the sector in degrees.
qs.s: The perimeter of the sector is \(P = 2r + s\), so \(s = 40 - 2(15) = 10\text{ cm}\). Then \(\theta = \frac{10}{15} = \frac{2}{3}\text{ radians}\), which converts to \(\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{120^\circ}{\pi}\).

qs.q: As the time changes from 5:05 to 5:25 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the minute hand.
qs.s: The elapsed time is 20 minutes, which represents \(\frac{20}{60} = \frac{1}{3}\) of a clockwise revolution. The change in radian measure is \(-\frac{1}{3}(2\pi) = -\frac{2\pi}{3}\).

qs.q: As the time changes from 4:00 to 4:15 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the minute hand.
qs.s: In 15 minutes, the minute hand rotates clockwise through \(\frac{15}{60} = \frac{1}{4}\) of a full revolution. The change in radian measure is \(-\frac{1}{4}(2\pi) = -\frac{\pi}{2}\).

qs.q: As the time changes from 1:10 to 1:55 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the minute hand.
qs.s: The elapsed time is 45 minutes, which corresponds to \(\frac{45}{60} = \frac{3}{4}\) of a clockwise revolution. The change in radian measure is \(-\frac{3}{4}(2\pi) = -\frac{3\pi}{2}\).

qs.q: As the time changes from 9:00 to 9:50 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the minute hand.
qs.s: In 50 minutes, the minute hand moves clockwise through \(\frac{50}{60} = \frac{5}{6}\) of a revolution. Thus, the change in radian measure is \(-\frac{5}{6}(2\pi) = -\frac{5\pi}{3}\).

qs.q: As the time changes from 7:00 to 7:40 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the minute hand.
qs.s: In 40 minutes, the minute hand completes \(\frac{40}{60} = \frac{2}{3}\) of a clockwise revolution. Therefore, the change in radian measure is \(-\frac{2}{3}(2\pi) = -\frac{4\pi}{3}\).

qs.q: As the time changes from 9:40 to 1:20 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the hour hand.
qs.s: From 9:40 to 1:20 is 3 hours and 40 minutes, which equals \(\frac{11}{3}\) hours. Since the hour hand rotates clockwise at \(\frac{2\pi}{12} = \frac{\pi}{6}\) radians per hour, the change is \(-\frac{11}{3}\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{11\pi}{18}\).

qs.q: As the time changes from 1:05:15 to 1:08:35 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the second hand.
qs.s: The elapsed time is 200 seconds, which corresponds to \(\frac{200}{60} = \frac{10}{3}\) clockwise revolutions of the second hand. The change in radian measure is \(-\frac{10}{3}(2\pi) = -\frac{20\pi}{3}\).

qs.q: As the time changes from 2:00 to 5:30 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the hour hand.
qs.s: The elapsed time is \(3.5 = \frac{7}{2}\) hours, and the hour hand completes one clockwise rotation of \(2\pi\) radians every 12 hours. The change in radian measure is \(-\frac{7/2}{12}(2\pi) = -\frac{7\pi}{12}\).

qs.q: As the time changes from 8:15 to 11:40 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the minute hand.
qs.s: From 8:15 to 11:40 is 3 hours and 25 minutes, or \(\frac{41}{12}\) hours. Since the minute hand makes one full clockwise revolution of \(2\pi\) radians each hour, the change is \(-\frac{41}{12}(2\pi) = -\frac{41\pi}{6}\).

qs.q: As the time changes from 1:00 to 3:30 on a dial-face clock, determine the sum of the changes in radian measure of the hour hand and the minute hand.
qs.s: In 2.5 hours, the minute hand completes \(\frac{5}{2}\) clockwise revolutions for a change of \(-5\pi\), and the hour hand completes \(\frac{2.5}{12} = \frac{5}{24}\) of a clockwise revolution for a change of \(-\frac{5\pi}{12}\). Their sum is \(-5\pi + \left(-\frac{5\pi}{12}\right) = -\frac{65\pi}{12}\).

qs.q: As the time changes from 7:00 to 7:15 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the hour hand.
qs.s: From 7:00 to 7:15 is 15 minutes, or \(\frac{1}{4}\) of an hour. The change in radian measure is \(\frac{1}{4} \times \left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{\pi}{24}\) radians.

qs.q: As the time changes from 3:00 to 3:40 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the hour hand.
qs.s: From 3:00 to 3:40 is 40 minutes, which equals \(\frac{2}{3}\) of an hour. Multiplying by \(-\frac{\pi}{6}\) radians per hour gives \(\frac{2}{3} \times \left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{\pi}{9}\) radians.

qs.q: As the time changes from 8:00 to 8:50 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the hour hand.
qs.s: From 8:00 to 8:50 is 50 minutes, or \(\frac{5}{6}\) of an hour. The change in radian measure is \(\frac{5}{6} \times \left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{5\pi}{36}\) radians.

qs.q: As the time changes from 1:00 to 1:20 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the hour hand.
qs.s: From 1:00 to 1:20 is 20 minutes, which is \(\frac{1}{3}\) of an hour. The hour hand moves clockwise at \(-\frac{\pi}{6}\) radians per hour, giving a change of \(\frac{1}{3} \times \left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{\pi}{18}\) radians.

qs.q: As the time changes from 4:00 to 4:45 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the hour hand.
qs.s: From 4:00 to 4:45 is 45 minutes, or \(\frac{3}{4}\) of an hour. Since the hour hand rotates clockwise at \(-\frac{\pi}{6}\) radians per hour, the change is \(\frac{3}{4} \times \left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{\pi}{8}\) radians.

qs.q: As the time changes from 9:40 to 2:25 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the hour hand.
qs.s: Across 12:00, the elapsed time from 9:40 to 2:25 is 4 hours and 45 minutes, or \(\frac{19}{4}\) hours. Multiplying by \(-\frac{\pi}{6}\) radians per hour gives \(\frac{19}{4} \times \left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{19\pi}{24}\) radians.

qs.q: As the time changes from 1:20 to 3:50 on a dial-face clock, determine the sum of the changes in radian measure of the hour hand and the minute hand.
qs.s: The elapsed time is 2.5 hours, so the hour hand's change is \(2.5 \times \left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{5\pi}{12}\) radians and the minute hand's change is \(2.5 \times (-2\pi) = -5\pi\) radians. Their sum is \(-\frac{5\pi}{12} + (-5\pi) = -\frac{65\pi}{12}\) radians.

qs.q: As the time changes from 2:10 to 7:50 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the hour hand.
qs.s: The elapsed time from 2:10 to 7:50 is 5 hours and 40 minutes, which equals \(5 + \frac{2}{3} = \frac{17}{3}\) hours. Multiplying by the hour hand's clockwise rate of \(-\frac{\pi}{6}\) radians per hour yields \(\frac{17}{3} \times \left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{17\pi}{18}\) radians.

qs.q: As the time changes from 3:15 to 7:50 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the minute hand.
qs.s: The elapsed time is 4 hours and 35 minutes, or \(4 + \frac{7}{12} = \frac{55}{12}\) hours. Since the minute hand rotates at \(-2\pi\) radians per hour, the change is \(\frac{55}{12} \times (-2\pi) = -\frac{55\pi}{6}\) radians.

qs.q: As the time changes from 12:04:10 to 12:07:45 on a dial-face clock, determine the change in radian measure of the second hand.
qs.s: The elapsed time is 3 minutes and 35 seconds, which is \(3 + \frac{7}{12} = \frac{43}{12}\) minutes. Since the second hand completes one full clockwise rotation (\(-2\pi\) radians) each minute, the change is \(\frac{43}{12} \times (-2\pi) = -\frac{43\pi}{6}\) radians.

qs.q: A passenger sits in a Ferris wheel carriage that is \(10\text{ m}\) from the central axle. How many meters does the passenger travel if the wheel makes \(7\) complete revolutions?
qs.s: The distance traveled in one revolution is \(C = 2\pi(10) = 20\pi\text{ m}\). In \(7\) revolutions, the passenger travels \(7 \times 20\pi = 140\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A toy train moves around a circular track of radius \(8\text{ m}\). How many meters does the train travel if it completes \(9\) full circuits?
qs.s: The circumference of the circular track is \(C = 2\pi(8) = 16\pi\text{ m}\). Over \(9\) circuits, the train travels \(9 \times 16\pi = 144\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A rider on a spinning swing ride travels along a circular path of radius \(7\text{ m}\). How many meters does the rider travel if the ride makes \(11\) complete revolutions?
qs.s: One complete revolution covers a distance of \(C = 2\pi(7) = 14\pi\text{ m}\). For \(11\) revolutions, the rider travels \(11 \times 14\pi = 154\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: An athlete runs along a circular track with a radius of \(25\text{ m}\). How many meters does the athlete run after completing \(6\) full laps?
qs.s: The circumference of the track is \(C = 2\pi(25) = 50\pi\text{ m}\). After \(6\) laps, the total distance run is \(6 \times 50\pi = 300\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A child is riding a carousel horse that is \(6\text{ m}\) from the center. How many meters does the child travel if the carousel completes \(8\) full revolutions before stopping?
qs.s: The distance traveled in one revolution is \(C = 2\pi(6) = 12\pi\text{ m}\). For \(8\) complete revolutions, the total distance traveled is \(8 \times 12\pi = 96\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A centrifuge arm of length \(1.2\text{ m}\) rotates at a rate of \(45\) revolutions per minute. How many meters does a sample at the end of the arm travel in \(20\) seconds?
qs.s: In \(20\) seconds (\(\frac{1}{3}\) minute), the arm makes \(45 \times \frac{1}{3} = 15\) revolutions. The total distance traveled is \(s = 15 \times 2\pi(1.2) = 36\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A robotic arm of length \(80\text{ cm}\) rotates about a pivot through a central angle of \(1350^\circ\). How many centimeters does the tip of the arm travel?
qs.s: Convert the angle to radians: \(\theta = 1350^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{15\pi}{2}\text{ rad}\). The arc length traveled is \(s = r\theta = 80 \times \frac{15\pi}{2} = 600\pi\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A giant observation wheel has a diameter of \(120\text{ m}\) and takes \(30\) minutes to complete one full revolution. How many meters does a passenger travel during an \(8\)-minute ride?
qs.s: In \(8\) minutes, the wheel completes \(\frac{8}{30} = \frac{4}{15}\) of a revolution. The distance traveled is \(\frac{4}{15} \times \pi(120) = 32\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A bicycle wheel has a diameter of \(70\text{ cm}\). How many centimeters does a point on the outer edge of the tire travel if the wheel makes \(12.5\) revolutions?
qs.s: The circumference of the wheel is \(C = \pi d = 70\pi\text{ cm}\). Multiplying by \(12.5\) revolutions gives a total distance of \(12.5 \times 70\pi = 875\pi\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: On a carousel, an outer horse is \(6\text{ m}\) from the center and an inner horse is \(4.5\text{ m}\) from the center. How many more meters does a rider on the outer horse travel than a rider on the inner horse during a ride of \(16\) complete revolutions?
qs.s: The difference in distance traveled per revolution is \(2\pi(6 - 4.5) = 3\pi\text{ m}\). Over \(16\) revolutions, the difference is \(16 \times 3\pi = 48\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A ceiling fan rotates at 16 rpm. How many seconds does it take for the fan to turn through \(144^\circ\)?
qs.s: At 16 rpm, the fan turns at \(\frac{16 \times 360^\circ}{60\text{ s}} = 96^\circ/\text{s}\). The time to turn through \(144^\circ\) is \(\frac{144^\circ}{96^\circ/\text{s}} = 1.5\text{ seconds}\).

qs.q: A Ferris wheel rotates at 3 rpm. How many seconds does it take for the Ferris wheel to turn through \(126^\circ\)?
qs.s: At 3 rpm, the wheel turns at \(\frac{3 \times 360^\circ}{60\text{ s}} = 18^\circ/\text{s}\). The time to turn through \(126^\circ\) is \(\frac{126^\circ}{18^\circ/\text{s}} = 7\text{ seconds}\).

qs.q: An observation wheel rotates at 5 rpm. How many seconds does it take for a cabin to turn through \(120^\circ\)?
qs.s: At 5 rpm, the wheel turns at \(\frac{5 \times 360^\circ}{60\text{ s}} = 30^\circ/\text{s}\). The time to turn through \(120^\circ\) is \(\frac{120^\circ}{30^\circ/\text{s}} = 4\text{ seconds}\).

qs.q: A bicycle wheel rotates at 20 rpm. How many seconds does it take for the wheel to turn through \(300^\circ\)?
qs.s: At 20 rpm, the wheel turns at \(\frac{20 \times 360^\circ}{60\text{ s}} = 120^\circ/\text{s}\). The time to turn through \(300^\circ\) is \(\frac{300^\circ}{120^\circ/\text{s}} = 2.5\text{ seconds}\).

qs.q: A wind turbine blade rotates at 8 rpm. How many seconds does it take for the blade to turn through \(240^\circ\)?
qs.s: At 8 rpm, the blade turns at \(\frac{8 \times 360^\circ}{60\text{ s}} = 48^\circ/\text{s}\). The time to turn through \(240^\circ\) is \(\frac{240^\circ}{48^\circ/\text{s}} = 5\text{ seconds}\).

qs.q: A radar antenna rotates at 15 rpm. Starting at an initial angle of \(40^\circ\) in standard position, it turns counterclockwise to a terminal angle of \(1840^\circ\). How many seconds does this rotation take?
qs.s: The net angle of rotation is \(1840^\circ - 40^\circ = 1800^\circ\). At 15 rpm, the antenna turns at \(\frac{15 \times 360^\circ}{60\text{ s}} = 90^\circ/\text{s}\), giving a time of \(\frac{1800^\circ}{90^\circ/\text{s}} = 20\text{ seconds}\).

qs.q: A high-speed centrifuge rotates at 240 rpm. How many seconds does it take for the centrifuge to turn through an angle of \(10{,}080^\circ\)?
qs.s: At 240 rpm, the rotational speed is \(\frac{240 \times 360^\circ}{60\text{ s}} = 1440^\circ/\text{s}\). The time required to turn through \(10{,}080^\circ\) is \(\frac{10{,}080^\circ}{1440^\circ/\text{s}} = 7\text{ seconds}\).

qs.q: An electric drill bit rotates at 120 rpm. How many seconds does it take to turn through 14 complete revolutions plus an additional \(144^\circ\)?
qs.s: The total rotation angle is \(14 \times 360^\circ + 144^\circ = 5184^\circ\). At 120 rpm, the speed is \(\frac{120 \times 360^\circ}{60\text{ s}} = 720^\circ/\text{s}\), so the time is \(\frac{5184^\circ}{720^\circ/\text{s}} = 7.2\text{ seconds}\).

qs.q: A turntable rotates at a constant speed of \(33\frac{1}{3}\text{ rpm}\). How many seconds does it take for the turntable to turn through \(1600^\circ\)?
qs.s: The speed of \(33\frac{1}{3}\text{ rpm} = \frac{100}{3}\text{ rpm}\) equals \(\frac{100}{3} \times \frac{360^\circ}{60\text{ s}} = 200^\circ/\text{s}\). The time required to turn through \(1600^\circ\) is \(\frac{1600^\circ}{200^\circ/\text{s}} = 8\text{ seconds}\).

qs.q: A carousel horse is positioned at a distance of \(8\text{ m}\) from the center of rotation. If the carousel makes one complete revolution every \(48\text{ seconds}\), what distance does the horse travel in \(18\text{ seconds}\)?
qs.s: In \(18\text{ seconds}\), the horse moves through \(\frac{18}{48} = \frac{3}{8}\) of a revolution, so \(\theta = \frac{3}{8}(2\pi) = \frac{3\pi}{4}\text{ radians}\). The distance traveled is \(s = r\theta = 8\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) = 6\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A Ferris wheel with a radius of \(15\text{ m}\) completes one revolution every \(60\text{ seconds}\). What distance is traversed by a passenger during a \(20\text{ second}\) ride interval?
qs.s: In \(20\text{ seconds}\), the Ferris wheel completes \(\frac{20}{60} = \frac{1}{3}\) of a revolution, which corresponds to an angle of \(\theta = \frac{1}{3}(2\pi) = \frac{2\pi}{3}\text{ radians}\). The distance traversed is \(s = r\theta = 15\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) = 10\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A satellite orbits Earth in a circular path at a distance of \(9000\text{ km}\) from the center of Earth. If the satellite completes one full orbit every \(6\text{ hours}\), what distance does it travel during a \(4\text{ hour}\) period?
qs.s: In \(4\text{ hours}\), the satellite completes \(\frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}\) of an orbit, which corresponds to \(\theta = \frac{2}{3}(2\pi) = \frac{4\pi}{3}\text{ radians}\). The distance traveled is \(s = r\theta = 9000\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right) = 12000\pi\text{ km}\).

qs.q: The minute hand of a wall clock has a length of \(10\text{ cm}\). What distance is traversed by the tip of the minute hand during a \(45\text{ minute}\) interval?
qs.s: In \(45\text{ minutes}\), the minute hand rotates through \(\frac{45}{60} = \frac{3}{4}\) of a revolution, giving \(\theta = \frac{3}{4}(2\pi) = \frac{3\pi}{2}\text{ radians}\). The distance traversed is \(s = r\theta = 10\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right) = 15\pi\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Jupiter rotates about its axis, making one full revolution every \(10\text{ hours}\). The equatorial radius of Jupiter is approximately \(70000\text{ km}\). What distance is traversed by a point on Jupiter's equator during a \(2\text{ hour}\) interval?
qs.s: In \(2\text{ hours}\), Jupiter rotates through \(\frac{2}{10} = \frac{1}{5}\) of a revolution, so the central angle is \(\theta = \frac{1}{5}(2\pi) = \frac{2\pi}{5}\text{ radians}\). The distance traversed is \(s = r\theta = 70000\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}\right) = 28000\pi\text{ km}\).

qs.q: The Moon travels around Earth in a circular orbit of radius approximately \(384000\text{ km}\), completing one full orbit every \(28\text{ days}\). What distance does the Moon travel along its orbit in \(3\text{ days and } 12\text{ hours}\)?
qs.s: The time of \(3.5\text{ days}\) is \(\frac{3.5}{28} = \frac{1}{8}\) of a complete orbit, so the central angle is \(\theta = \frac{1}{8}(2\pi) = \frac{\pi}{4}\text{ radians}\). The distance traveled is \(s = r\theta = 384000\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = 96000\pi\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A circular space station has a radius of \(150\text{ m}\) and rotates about its center to simulate gravity, completing one revolution every \(40\text{ seconds}\). What total distance is traveled by an astronaut situated on the outer rim during a \(10\text{ minute}\) shift?
qs.s: Since \(10\text{ minutes} = 600\text{ seconds}\), the station completes \(\frac{600}{40} = 15\) revolutions, giving a total central angle of \(\theta = 15(2\pi) = 30\pi\text{ radians}\). The total distance traveled is \(s = r\theta = 150(30\pi) = 4500\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: An observation wheel with a diameter of \(120\text{ m}\) rotates continuously, taking \(20\text{ minutes}\) to complete one full revolution. What total distance does a passenger travel during a ride that lasts \(45\text{ minutes}\)?
qs.s: The radius is \(r = \frac{120}{2} = 60\text{ m}\), and in \(45\text{ minutes}\) the wheel completes \(\frac{45}{20} = \frac{9}{4}\) revolutions, giving an angle of \(\theta = \frac{9}{4}(2\pi) = \frac{9\pi}{2}\text{ radians}\). The total distance traveled is \(s = 60\left(\frac{9\pi}{2}\right) = 270\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: The hour hand of a large clock tower is \(4.5\text{ m}\) long. What distance is traversed by the tip of the hour hand between 1:00 p.m. and 7:40 p.m. on the same day?
qs.s: The elapsed time is \(6\text{ hours and } 40\text{ minutes} = \frac{20}{3}\text{ hours}\). Since the hour hand makes one full revolution in \(12\text{ hours}\), it rotates through \(\theta = \frac{20/3}{12}(2\pi) = \frac{10\pi}{9}\text{ radians}\), so the distance traversed is \(s = 4.5\left(\frac{10\pi}{9}\right) = 5\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A carousel makes one complete revolution every \(45\text{ seconds}\). Child A sits on an inner horse \(3\text{ m}\) from the center, while Child B sits on an outer horse \(5\text{ m}\) from the center. How much farther does Child B travel than Child A during a ride lasting \(2\text{ minutes and } 15\text{ seconds}\)?
qs.s: In \(135\text{ seconds}\), the carousel makes \(\frac{135}{45} = 3\) complete revolutions, sweeping an angle of \(\theta = 3(2\pi) = 6\pi\text{ radians}\). The difference in distance traveled is \(\Delta s = (r_B - r_A)\theta = (5 - 3)(6\pi) = 12\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A runner jogs along a circular track with a radius of \(120\text{ m}\). If the runner starts at a mark at \(10^\circ\) and stops at a mark at \(100^\circ\), what distance does the runner cover?
qs.s: The central angle traversed is \(100^\circ - 10^\circ = 90^\circ = \frac{\pi}{2}\text{ radians}\). The distance covered is \(s = r\theta = 120 \times \frac{\pi}{2} = 60\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A ship sails due south along a meridian from \(50^\circ\text{ N}\) latitude to \(10^\circ\text{ N}\) latitude. Assuming the radius of the Earth is \(6300\text{ km}\), what distance does the ship travel?
qs.s: The change in latitude is \(50^\circ - 10^\circ = 40^\circ\), which converts to \(40^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{2\pi}{9}\text{ radians}\). The distance traveled is \(s = r\theta = 6300 \times \frac{2\pi}{9} = 1400\pi\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A Ferris wheel has a radius of \(18\text{ m}\). A passenger travels along the circular rim from an angle of \(25^\circ\) above the horizontal to \(85^\circ\) above the horizontal. What distance does the passenger travel?
qs.s: The central angle rotated through is \(85^\circ - 25^\circ = 60^\circ = \frac{\pi}{3}\text{ radians}\). Using the arc length formula, the distance is \(s = r\theta = 18 \times \frac{\pi}{3} = 6\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A satellite travels in a circular orbit of radius \(7200\text{ km}\) centered at Earth's center. What distance does the satellite travel as its angular position changes from \(35^\circ\) to \(80^\circ\)?
qs.s: The central angle swept is \(80^\circ - 35^\circ = 45^\circ\), which is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\text{ radians}\). The distance traveled is \(s = r\theta = 7200 \times \frac{\pi}{4} = 1800\pi\text{ km}\).

qs.q: An airplane flies due north along a meridian from latitude \(15^\circ\text{ N}\) to \(45^\circ\text{ N}\). Assuming Earth is a sphere with a radius of \(6000\text{ km}\), what distance does the airplane travel?
qs.s: The central angle between the two latitudes is \(45^\circ - 15^\circ = 30^\circ\), which converts to \(30^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{\pi}{6}\text{ radians}\). The distance traveled is \(s = r\theta = 6000 \times \frac{\pi}{6} = 1000\pi\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A robotic arm of length \(45\text{ cm}\) rotates about its fixed pivot through an angle of \(520^\circ\). What total distance does the tip of the arm travel?
qs.s: Converting the total angle to radians gives \(520^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \frac{26\pi}{9}\text{ radians}\). The total distance traveled by the tip is \(s = r\theta = 45 \times \frac{26\pi}{9} = 130\pi\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A motorized inspection camera travels along a circular track of radius \(14\text{ m}\). It moves clockwise through an angle of \(135^\circ\), stops briefly, and then continues clockwise through an additional angle of \(75^\circ\). What total distance does the camera travel?
qs.s: The total angle rotated through is \(135^\circ + 75^\circ = 210^\circ = \frac{7\pi}{6}\text{ radians}\). The total distance is \(s = r\theta = 14 \times \frac{7\pi}{6} = \frac{49\pi}{3}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Two cars, A and B, drive around a circular curve with a central angle of \(150^\circ\). Car A travels in the inner lane along an arc of radius \(48\text{ m}\), while Car B travels in the outer lane along an arc of radius \(60\text{ m}\). How much farther does Car B travel than Car A?
qs.s: The central angle is \(150^\circ = \frac{5\pi}{6}\text{ radians}\), and the difference in radii is \(60 - 48 = 12\text{ m}\). The difference in distance traveled is \(\Delta s = \Delta r \cdot \theta = 12 \times \frac{5\pi}{6} = 10\pi\text{ m}\).

qs.q: An aircraft flies due south along a meridian from a city at \(38^\circ\text{ N}\) latitude to a city at \(22^\circ\text{ S}\) latitude. Assuming Earth is a sphere with a radius of \(6400\text{ km}\), what distance does the aircraft travel?
qs.s: Crossing the equator from north to south means the total central angle is \(38^\circ + 22^\circ = 60^\circ = \frac{\pi}{3}\text{ radians}\). The distance traveled is \(s = r\theta = 6400 \times \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{6400\pi}{3}\text{ km}\).

qs.q: An explorer travels due south along a meridian from latitude \(50^\circ\text{ N}\) to latitude \(20^\circ\text{ S}\). Assuming Earth is a sphere of radius \(6300\text{ km}\), how much farther did the explorer travel in the Northern Hemisphere than in the Southern Hemisphere?
qs.s: The explorer covers \(50^\circ\) in the Northern Hemisphere and \(20^\circ\) in the Southern Hemisphere, giving an angular difference of \(50^\circ - 20^\circ = 30^\circ = \frac{\pi}{6}\text{ radians}\). The difference in distance is \(s = 6300 \times \frac{\pi}{6} = 1050\pi\text{ km}\).

sections.title: Trigonometric Ratios and the Unit Circle

exercises.name: Missing dimensions of a right triangle

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 8, b = 15, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{8^2 + 15^2} = \sqrt{64 + 225} = \sqrt{289} = 17\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 6, b = 8, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} = 10\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 7, b = 24, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{7^2 + 24^2} = \sqrt{49 + 576} = \sqrt{625} = 25\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 3, b = 4, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 9, b = 12, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{81 + 144} = \sqrt{225} = 15\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = \sqrt{7}, b = 3, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{(\sqrt{7})^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{7 + 9} = \sqrt{16} = 4\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = \frac{3}{2}, b = 2, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{\frac{9}{4} + \frac{16}{4}} = \sqrt{\frac{25}{4}} = \frac{5}{2}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 4, c = 8, b =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{8^2 - 4^2} = \sqrt{64 - 16} = \sqrt{48} = 4\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 2\sqrt{5}, b = 4, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{(2\sqrt{5})^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{20 + 16} = \sqrt{36} = 6\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 20, c = 29, b =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{29^2 - 20^2} = \sqrt{841 - 400} = \sqrt{441} = 21\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimensions of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 2, b = 5, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{2^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{4 + 25} = \sqrt{29}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimensions of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 4, b = 5, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{4^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{16 + 25} = \sqrt{41}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimensions of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 3, b = 5, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{3^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{9 + 25} = \sqrt{34}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimensions of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 1, b = 4, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{1^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{1 + 16} = \sqrt{17}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimensions of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 1, b = 6, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{1^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{1 + 36} = \sqrt{37}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimensions of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 8, b = 15, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{8^2 + 15^2} = \sqrt{64 + 225} = \sqrt{289} = 17\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimensions of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 7, c = 25, b =\)
qs.s: Since \(c\) is the hypotenuse, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{25^2 - 7^2} = \sqrt{625 - 49} = \sqrt{576} = 24\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimensions of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = \frac{1}{2}, b = \frac{1}{3}, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{9}} = \sqrt{\frac{13}{36}} = \frac{\sqrt{13}}{6}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimensions of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 4, c = 8, b =\)
qs.s: Since \(c\) is the hypotenuse, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{8^2 - 4^2} = \sqrt{64 - 16} = \sqrt{48} = 4\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimensions of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = \sqrt{7}, b = 3, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{(\sqrt{7})^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{7 + 9} = \sqrt{16} = 4\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 12, c = 13, b =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(12^2 + b^2 = 13^2\), which gives \(b = \sqrt{169 - 144} = \sqrt{25} = 5\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(b = 24, c = 25, a =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(a^2 + 24^2 = 25^2\), so \(a = \sqrt{625 - 576} = \sqrt{49} = 7\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 9, c = 15, b =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(9^2 + b^2 = 15^2\), so \(b = \sqrt{225 - 81} = \sqrt{144} = 12\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 2, b = 3, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{2^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{4 + 9} = \sqrt{13}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 28, c = 53, b =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{53^2 - 28^2} = \sqrt{2809 - 784} = \sqrt{2025} = 45\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 4\sqrt{2}, b = 2\sqrt{7}, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{(4\sqrt{2})^2 + (2\sqrt{7})^2} = \sqrt{32 + 28} = \sqrt{60} = 2\sqrt{15}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = \frac{1}{2}, b = \frac{2}{3}, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{4} + \frac{4}{9}} = \sqrt{\frac{25}{36}} = \frac{5}{6}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 2\sqrt{3}, c = 4\sqrt{2}, b =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{(4\sqrt{2})^2 - (2\sqrt{3})^2} = \sqrt{32 - 12} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 1.5, c = 3.9, b =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{3.9^2 - 1.5^2} = \sqrt{15.21 - 2.25} = \sqrt{12.96} = 3.6\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = \sqrt{5}, c = 3, b =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{3^2 - (\sqrt{5})^2} = \sqrt{9 - 5} = 2\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 2, c = 3, b =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{3^2 - 2^2} = \sqrt{9 - 4} = \sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 2\sqrt{3}, b = 2, c =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{(2\sqrt{3})^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{12 + 4} = 4\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = \sqrt{7}, c = 4, b =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{4^2 - (\sqrt{7})^2} = \sqrt{16 - 7} = 3\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 2, b = \sqrt{21}, c =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{2^2 + (\sqrt{21})^2} = \sqrt{4 + 21} = 5\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = \frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3}, b = \frac{1}{3}, c =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\frac{24}{9} + \frac{1}{9}} = \sqrt{\frac{25}{9}} = \frac{5}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(b = 3\sqrt{7}, c = 12, a =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(a = \sqrt{c^2 - b^2} = \sqrt{12^2 - (3\sqrt{7})^2} = \sqrt{144 - 63} = \sqrt{81} = 9\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 3\sqrt{5}, b = 5\sqrt{3}, c =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{(3\sqrt{5})^2 + (5\sqrt{3})^2} = \sqrt{45 + 75} = \sqrt{120}\). Simplifying the radical gives \(c = 2\sqrt{30}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(b = 4\sqrt{3}, c = 6\sqrt{2}, a =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(a = \sqrt{c^2 - b^2} = \sqrt{(6\sqrt{2})^2 - (4\sqrt{3})^2} = \sqrt{72 - 48} = \sqrt{24}\). Simplifying the radical gives \(a = 2\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 6\sqrt{2}, c = 2\sqrt{26}, b =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{(2\sqrt{26})^2 - (6\sqrt{2})^2} = \sqrt{104 - 72} = \sqrt{32}\). Simplifying the radical gives \(b = 4\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(c = 5\sqrt{2}, b = 5, a =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(a = \sqrt{c^2 - b^2} = \sqrt{(5\sqrt{2})^2 - 5^2} = \sqrt{50 - 25} = \sqrt{25} = 5\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(c = 2\sqrt{10}, b = 2, a =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(a = \sqrt{c^2 - b^2} = \sqrt{(2\sqrt{10})^2 - 2^2} = \sqrt{40 - 4} = \sqrt{36} = 6\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(c = 2\sqrt{13}, a = 4, b =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{(2\sqrt{13})^2 - 4^2} = \sqrt{52 - 16} = \sqrt{36} = 6\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(c = 4\sqrt{5}, a = 8, b =\)
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{(4\sqrt{5})^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{80 - 64} = \sqrt{16} = 4\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = \frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}, c = 2, b =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{2^2 - \left(\frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\right)^2} = \sqrt{4 - \frac{7}{4}} = \sqrt{\frac{9}{4}} = \frac{3}{2}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 2\sqrt{14}, b = \sqrt{70}, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{(2\sqrt{14})^2 + (\sqrt{70})^2} = \sqrt{56 + 70} = \sqrt{126} = 3\sqrt{14}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 12, c = 4\sqrt{19}, b =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{(4\sqrt{19})^2 - 12^2} = \sqrt{304 - 144} = \sqrt{160} = 4\sqrt{10}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(c = \frac{5}{6}, b = \frac{2}{3}, a =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(a = \sqrt{c^2 - b^2} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\frac{25}{36} - \frac{16}{36}} = \sqrt{\frac{9}{36}} = \frac{1}{2}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(c = 5\sqrt{6}, a = 3\sqrt{10}, b =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{(5\sqrt{6})^2 - (3\sqrt{10})^2} = \sqrt{150 - 90} = \sqrt{60} = 2\sqrt{15}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = 2\sqrt{5}, b = \sqrt{5}, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{(2\sqrt{5})^2 + (\sqrt{5})^2} = \sqrt{20 + 5} = \sqrt{25} = 5\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(c = \sqrt{34}, b = 3\sqrt{2}, a =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(a = \sqrt{c^2 - b^2} = \sqrt{(\sqrt{34})^2 - (3\sqrt{2})^2} = \sqrt{34 - 18} = \sqrt{16} = 4\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(c = 2\sqrt{3}, a = \sqrt{5}, b =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{(2\sqrt{3})^2 - (\sqrt{5})^2} = \sqrt{12 - 5} = \sqrt{7}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(c = \sqrt{22}, a = 3\sqrt{2}, b =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{(\sqrt{22})^2 - (3\sqrt{2})^2} = \sqrt{22 - 18} = \sqrt{4} = 2\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(c = \sqrt{30}, a = 2\sqrt{3}, b =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{(\sqrt{30})^2 - (2\sqrt{3})^2} = \sqrt{30 - 12} = \sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(c = \frac{7}{2}, a = \sqrt{6}, b =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{7}{2}\right)^2 - (\sqrt{6})^2} = \sqrt{\frac{49}{4} - \frac{24}{4}} = \sqrt{\frac{25}{4}} = \frac{5}{2}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(c = \frac{\sqrt{41}}{3}, a = \frac{4}{3}, b =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{\frac{41}{9} - \frac{16}{9}} = \sqrt{\frac{25}{9}} = \frac{5}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(a = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, b = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}, c =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4} + \frac{5}{4}} = \sqrt{\frac{8}{4}} = \sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Find the missing dimension of a right triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\): \(c = 3\sqrt{14}, a = 2\sqrt{21}, b =\)
qs.s: Using the Pythagorean theorem, \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2} = \sqrt{(3\sqrt{14})^2 - (2\sqrt{21})^2} = \sqrt{126 - 84} = \sqrt{42}\).

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\cos\theta < 0, \tan\theta > 0\)
qs.s: Cosine is negative in Quadrants II and III, while tangent is positive in Quadrants I and III. Therefore, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant III.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sec\theta < 0, \tan\theta < 0\)
qs.s: Secant is negative where cosine is negative (Quadrants II and III), and tangent is negative in Quadrants II and IV. Therefore, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant II.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta < 0, \cos\theta > 0\)
qs.s: Sine is negative in Quadrants III and IV, while cosine is positive in Quadrants I and IV. Therefore, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant IV.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\csc\theta > 0, \cot\theta < 0\)
qs.s: Cosecant is positive where sine is positive (Quadrants I and II), and cotangent is negative in Quadrants II and IV. Therefore, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant II.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\tan\theta > 0, \csc\theta > 0\)
qs.s: Tangent is positive in Quadrants I and III, and cosecant is positive in Quadrants I and II. Therefore, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant I.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta\tan\theta > 0, \sec\theta\cot\theta < 0\)
qs.s: The product \(\sin\theta\tan\theta > 0\) when sine and tangent have the same sign (Quadrants I and IV), while \(\sec\theta\cot\theta < 0\) when they have opposite signs (Quadrants III and IV), yielding Quadrant IV.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta\cos\theta < 0, \sec\theta > 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\sec\theta > 0\), cosine is positive (Quadrants I and IV); for the product \(\sin\theta\cos\theta < 0\), sine must be negative, placing \(\theta\) in Quadrant IV.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\cos\theta\tan\theta > 0, \cot\theta < 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta\tan\theta = \sin\theta\), we have \(\sin\theta > 0\) (Quadrants I and II). Combined with \(\cot\theta < 0\) (Quadrants II and IV), \(\theta\) must lie in Quadrant II.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta\cos\theta > 0, \csc\theta < 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\csc\theta < 0\), sine is negative (Quadrants III and IV); for \(\sin\theta\cos\theta > 0\), cosine must also be negative, which restricts \(\theta\) to Quadrant III.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\frac{\cos\theta}{\cot\theta} > 0, \frac{\sin\theta}{\tan\theta} > 0\)
qs.s: Simplifying gives \(\sin\theta > 0\) (Quadrants I and II) and \(\cos\theta > 0\) (Quadrants I and IV), so both conditions are met only in Quadrant I.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\cot\theta > 0, \sin\theta > 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\cot\theta > 0\) in Quadrants I and III, and \(\sin\theta > 0\) in Quadrants I and II, \(\theta\) must lie in Quadrant I.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\csc\theta < 0, \cos\theta > 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\csc\theta < 0\) in Quadrants III and IV, and \(\cos\theta > 0\) in Quadrants I and IV, \(\theta\) must lie in Quadrant IV.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta\tan\theta > 0, \csc\theta < 0\)
qs.s: The product \(\sin\theta\tan\theta > 0\) when \(\sin\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) share the same sign (Quadrants I and IV). Since \(\csc\theta < 0\) in Quadrants III and IV, \(\theta\) must lie in Quadrant IV.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta} < 0, \sec\theta\csc\theta > 0\)
qs.s: The quotient \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta} < 0\) when \(\sec\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) have opposite signs (Quadrants III and IV). Since \(\sec\theta\csc\theta > 0\) when both functions share the same sign (Quadrants I and III), \(\theta\) must lie in Quadrant III.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\tan\theta > 0, \cos\theta < 0\).
qs.s: Since \(\tan\theta > 0\) in Quadrants I and III, and \(\cos\theta < 0\) in Quadrants II and III, \(\theta\) must lie in Quadrant III.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\cos\theta\cot\theta < 0\) and \(\sin\theta\sec\theta > 0\).
qs.s: The product \(\cos\theta\cot\theta < 0\) in Quadrants III and IV, while \(\sin\theta\sec\theta > 0\) in Quadrants I and III. Therefore, \(\theta\) must lie in Quadrant III.

qs.s: The product \(\sec\theta\csc\theta < 0\) in Quadrants II and IV, and the quotient \(\frac{\tan\theta}{\csc\theta} > 0\) in Quadrants I and IV. Therefore, \(\theta\) must lie in Quadrant IV.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\frac{\csc\theta}{\cos\theta} < 0\) and \(\sin\theta\cot\theta < 0\).
qs.s: The quotient \(\frac{\csc\theta}{\cos\theta} < 0\) in Quadrants II and IV, while \(\sin\theta\cot\theta < 0\) in Quadrants II and III. Therefore, \(\theta\) must lie in Quadrant II.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\frac{\sin\theta}{\tan\theta} < 0\) and \(\cot\theta\sec\theta < 0\).
qs.s: The quotient \(\frac{\sin\theta}{\tan\theta} < 0\) in Quadrants II and III, while the product \(\cot\theta\sec\theta < 0\) in Quadrants III and IV. Therefore, \(\theta\) must lie in Quadrant III.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta\cos\theta > 0\) and \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\cot\theta} > 0\).
qs.s: The product \(\sin\theta\cos\theta > 0\) in Quadrants I and III, while the quotient \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\cot\theta} > 0\) in Quadrants I and II. Therefore, \(\theta\) must lie in Quadrant I.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sec\theta > 0, \cot\theta < 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\sec\theta > 0\) in Quadrants I and IV, and \(\cot\theta < 0\) in Quadrants II and IV, \(\theta\) must lie in Quadrant IV.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta < 0, \cot\theta > 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\sin\theta < 0\) in Quadrants III and IV, and \(\cot\theta > 0\) in Quadrants I and III, \(\theta\) must lie in Quadrant III.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta\cos\theta > 0, \tan\theta\sec\theta > 0\)
qs.s: The condition \(\sin\theta\cos\theta > 0\) holds when \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) have the same sign (Quadrants I and III), while \(\tan\theta\sec\theta > 0\) holds when \(\tan\theta\) and \(\sec\theta\) have the same sign (Quadrants I and II), so \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant I.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta\cos\theta < 0, \csc\theta\cot\theta > 0\)
qs.s: The condition \(\sin\theta\cos\theta < 0\) is satisfied in Quadrants II and IV, while \(\csc\theta\cot\theta > 0\) is satisfied where both have the same sign (Quadrants I and IV), so \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant IV.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta\cos\theta > 0, \tan\theta\csc\theta < 0\)
qs.s: The condition \(\sin\theta\cos\theta > 0\) requires \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) to share the same sign (Quadrants I and III), while \(\tan\theta\csc\theta < 0\) requires opposite signs (Quadrants II and III), which leaves Quadrant III.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\frac{\cos\theta}{\tan\theta} < 0, \sin\theta\cot\theta < 0\)
qs.s: The quotient \(\frac{\cos\theta}{\tan\theta} < 0\) holds where \(\cos\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) have opposite signs (Quadrants III and IV), and \(\sin\theta\cot\theta < 0\) holds where \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cot\theta\) have opposite signs (Quadrants II and III), placing \(\theta\) in Quadrant III.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\cot\theta > 0, \sec\theta > 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\cot\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant I or III, and since \(\sec\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant I or IV. Therefore, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant I.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta\cos\theta < 0, \tan\theta\cos\theta > 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\sin\theta\cos\theta < 0\), sine and cosine have opposite signs, placing \(\theta\) in Quadrant II or IV. Since \(\tan\theta\cos\theta > 0\), tangent and cosine have the same sign, placing \(\theta\) in Quadrant I or II, so \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant II.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} > 0, \sin\theta\tan\theta < 0\)
qs.s: The quotient \(\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} > 0\) when cosine and sine have the same sign (Quadrants I and III), while \(\sin\theta\tan\theta < 0\) when sine and tangent have opposite signs (Quadrants II and III). Therefore, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant III.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sec\theta\tan\theta > 0, \csc\theta\cot\theta > 0\)
qs.s: The product \(\sec\theta\tan\theta > 0\) when both functions share the same sign (Quadrants I and II), and \(\csc\theta\cot\theta > 0\) when both share the same sign (Quadrants I and IV). The common quadrant is Quadrant I.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\frac{\tan\theta}{\cos\theta} > 0, \frac{\cot\theta}{\sin\theta} < 0\)
qs.s: The quotient \(\frac{\tan\theta}{\cos\theta} > 0\) when tangent and cosine have the same sign (Quadrants I and II), and \(\frac{\cot\theta}{\sin\theta} < 0\) when cotangent and sine have opposite signs (Quadrants II and III). Therefore, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant II.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta\tan\theta > 0, \cos\theta\cot\theta < 0\)
qs.s: The product \(\sin\theta\tan\theta > 0\) in Quadrants I and IV where sine and tangent have the same sign, and \(\cos\theta\cot\theta < 0\) in Quadrants III and IV where cosine and cotangent have opposite signs. Therefore, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant IV.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\cos\theta < 0, \cot\theta < 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta < 0\) in Quadrants II and III, and \(\cot\theta < 0\) in Quadrants II and IV, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant II.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\cos\theta < 0, \csc\theta < 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta < 0\) in Quadrants II and III, and \(\csc\theta < 0\) in Quadrants III and IV, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant III.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies if \(\frac{\tan\theta}{\sin\theta} > 0\) and \(\cos\theta \csc\theta > 0\).
qs.s: The quotient \(\frac{\tan\theta}{\sin\theta} > 0\) when \(\tan\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) share the same sign (Quadrants I and IV), while \(\cos\theta \csc\theta > 0\) when \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) share the same sign (Quadrants I and III), giving Quadrant I.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies if \(\sin\theta \tan\theta > 0\) and \(\frac{\cos\theta}{\csc\theta} < 0\).
qs.s: The product \(\sin\theta \tan\theta > 0\) in Quadrants I and IV where \(\sin\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) have the same sign, and \(\frac{\cos\theta}{\csc\theta} < 0\) when \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) have opposite signs (Quadrants II and IV), placing \(\theta\) in Quadrant IV.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies if \(\cos\theta \cot\theta > 0\) and \(\sin\theta \sec\theta < 0\).
qs.s: The product \(\cos\theta \cot\theta > 0\) holds when \(\cos\theta\) and \(\cot\theta\) share the same sign (Quadrants I and II), while \(\sin\theta \sec\theta < 0\) requires opposite signs (Quadrants II and IV), so \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant II.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies if \(\sin\theta \cos\theta > 0\) and \(\sec\theta < 0\).
qs.s: Since \(\sec\theta < 0\), \(\cos\theta\) is negative (Quadrants II and III); for the product \(\sin\theta \cos\theta\) to be positive, \(\sin\theta\) must also be negative, which places \(\theta\) in Quadrant III.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies if \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta} < 0\) and \(\cot\theta > 0\).
qs.s: The quotient \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta} < 0\) when \(\sec\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) have opposite signs (Quadrants III and IV), and \(\cot\theta > 0\) in Quadrants I and III, so \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant III.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\cos^2\theta\csc\theta < 0, \tan\theta < 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\cos^2\theta > 0\), \(\csc\theta\) must be negative, meaning \(\sin\theta < 0\). With \(\sin\theta < 0\) and \(\tan\theta < 0\), \(\cos\theta\) must be positive, which places \(\theta\) in Quadrant IV.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\frac{\cos\theta}{\tan\theta} > 0, \sec\theta > 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\sec\theta > 0\), \(\cos\theta\) is positive, which requires \(\tan\theta > 0\) for the quotient \(\frac{\cos\theta}{\tan\theta}\) to be positive. Both \(\cos\theta > 0\) and \(\tan\theta > 0\) hold in Quadrant I.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\tan\theta\sin\theta < 0, \cot\theta < 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\cot\theta < 0\), \(\tan\theta\) is negative, which requires \(\sin\theta > 0\) for their product to be negative. An angle where \(\sin\theta > 0\) and \(\tan\theta < 0\) lies in Quadrant II.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\tan\theta\cos\theta < 0, \frac{\sec\theta}{\csc\theta} < 0\)
qs.s: The product \(\tan\theta\cos\theta < 0\) holds in quadrants III and IV, while \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\csc\theta} < 0\) holds in quadrants II and IV where secant and cosecant have opposite signs. Therefore, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant IV.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\cos\theta\tan\theta > 0, \sin\theta\cot\theta < 0\)
qs.s: The product \(\cos\theta\tan\theta > 0\) holds in quadrants I and II, while \(\sin\theta\cot\theta < 0\) holds in quadrants II and III. The only quadrant satisfying both conditions is Quadrant II.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\csc\theta\sec\theta > 0, \frac{\cos\theta}{\tan\theta} < 0\)
qs.s: The product \(\csc\theta\sec\theta > 0\) holds in quadrants I and III, while the quotient \(\frac{\cos\theta}{\tan\theta} < 0\) holds in quadrants III and IV where cosine and tangent have opposite signs. Therefore, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant III.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta} > 0, \csc\theta\cot\theta > 0\)
qs.s: The ratio \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta} > 0\) holds in quadrants I and II where secant and tangent have the same sign, while \(\csc\theta\cot\theta > 0\) holds in quadrants I and IV. Thus, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant I.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta > 0, \sec\theta < 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\sin\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant I or II; since \(\sec\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant II or III. Therefore, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant II.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta} < 0, \cos\theta\csc\theta > 0\)
qs.s: The quotient \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta} < 0\) when \(\sec\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) have opposite signs (Quadrants III and IV), and \(\cos\theta\csc\theta > 0\) when \(\cos\theta\) and \(\csc\theta\) have the same sign (Quadrants I and III). Thus, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant III.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta\tan\theta > 0, \frac{\cot\theta}{\sec\theta} < 0\)
qs.s: The product \(\sin\theta\tan\theta > 0\) when \(\sin\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) have the same sign (Quadrants I and IV), while \(\frac{\cot\theta}{\sec\theta} < 0\) when \(\cot\theta\) and \(\sec\theta\) have opposite signs (Quadrants III and IV). Thus, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant IV.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\cos^3\theta\sin\theta < 0, \cot\theta\csc\theta < 0\)
qs.s: Since \(\cos^3\theta\) shares the sign of \(\cos\theta\), \(\cos^3\theta\sin\theta < 0\) when \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) have opposite signs (Quadrants II and IV); meanwhile \(\cot\theta\csc\theta < 0\) in Quadrants II and III. Thus, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant II.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\cos\theta\tan\theta > 0, \sin\theta\sec\theta > 0\)
qs.s: The product \(\cos\theta\tan\theta > 0\) when \(\cos\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) have the same sign (Quadrants I and II), while \(\sin\theta\sec\theta > 0\) when \(\sin\theta\) and \(\sec\theta\) have the same sign (Quadrants I and III). Thus, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant I.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\cos\theta \cot\theta < 0, \sin\theta \sec\theta > 0\)
qs.s: Here, \(\cos\theta \cot\theta < 0\) holds where \(\cos\theta\) and \(\cot\theta\) have opposite signs (Quadrants III and IV), and \(\sin\theta \sec\theta > 0\) holds where \(\sin\theta\) and \(\sec\theta\) have the same sign (Quadrants I and III). The intersection is Quadrant III.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta \cot\theta < 0, \sec\theta \csc\theta < 0\)
qs.s: The product \(\sin\theta \cot\theta < 0\) occurs when \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cot\theta\) have opposite signs (Quadrants II and III), and \(\sec\theta \csc\theta < 0\) occurs when \(\sec\theta\) and \(\csc\theta\) have opposite signs (Quadrants II and IV). Therefore, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant II.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta \tan\theta > 0, \cos\theta \csc\theta > 0\)
qs.s: The inequality \(\sin\theta \tan\theta > 0\) holds where \(\sin\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) have the same sign (Quadrants I and IV), while \(\cos\theta \csc\theta > 0\) holds where \(\cos\theta\) and \(\csc\theta\) have the same sign (Quadrants I and III). Thus, \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant I.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\sin\theta} < 0, \cos\theta \tan\theta > 0\)
qs.s: The quotient \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\sin\theta} < 0\) when \(\sec\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) have opposite signs (Quadrants II and IV), and \(\cos\theta \tan\theta > 0\) when \(\cos\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) have the same sign (Quadrants I and II). Both conditions are satisfied in Quadrant II.

qs.q: Determine the quadrant in which \(\theta\) lies for the following: \(\sin\theta \cos\theta < 0, \cos\theta \tan\theta < 0\)
qs.s: The condition \(\sin\theta \cos\theta < 0\) requires \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) to have opposite signs (Quadrants II and IV), while \(\cos\theta \tan\theta < 0\) requires \(\cos\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) to have opposite signs (Quadrants III and IV). The common quadrant is Quadrant IV.

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cos\theta = -\frac{1}{6}, \sec\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\sec\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) are reciprocals of each other, \(\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta} = \frac{1}{-1/6} = -6\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\sec\theta = 5, \cos\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sec\theta\) are reciprocals of each other, \(\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sec\theta} = \frac{1}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cot\theta = \frac{8}{15}, \tan\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\tan\theta\) and \(\cot\theta\) are reciprocals of each other, \(\tan\theta = \frac{1}{\cot\theta} = \frac{15}{8}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\sin\theta = -\frac{7}{9}, \csc\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\csc\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) are reciprocals of each other, \(\csc\theta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta} = -\frac{9}{7}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\tan\theta = -\frac{3}{4}, \cot\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\cot\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) are reciprocals of each other, \(\cot\theta = \frac{1}{\tan\theta} = -\frac{4}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\csc\theta = \frac{5\sqrt{6}}{12}, \sin\theta =\)
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity, \(\sin\theta = \frac{1}{\csc\theta} = \frac{12}{5\sqrt{6}}\). Rationalizing and simplifying gives \(\frac{12\sqrt{6}}{30} = \frac{2\sqrt{6}}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cos\theta = -\frac{4\sqrt{14}}{21}, \sec\theta =\)
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity, \(\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta} = -\frac{21}{4\sqrt{14}}\). Rationalizing and simplifying gives \(-\frac{21\sqrt{14}}{56} = -\frac{3\sqrt{14}}{8}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cot\theta = -\frac{6\sqrt{5}}{25}, \tan\theta =\)
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity, \(\tan\theta = \frac{1}{\cot\theta} = -\frac{25}{6\sqrt{5}}\). Rationalizing and simplifying gives \(-\frac{25\sqrt{5}}{30} = -\frac{5\sqrt{5}}{6}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\sin\theta = \frac{3\sqrt{21}}{28}, \csc\theta =\)
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity, \(\csc\theta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta} = \frac{28}{3\sqrt{21}}\). Rationalizing and simplifying gives \(\frac{28\sqrt{21}}{63} = \frac{4\sqrt{21}}{9}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\sec\theta = -\frac{5\sqrt{10}}{6}, \cos\theta =\)
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity, \(\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sec\theta} = -\frac{6}{5\sqrt{10}}\). Rationalizing and simplifying gives \(-\frac{6\sqrt{10}}{50} = -\frac{3\sqrt{10}}{25}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\tan\theta = -\frac{5}{7}, \cot\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\cot\theta = \frac{1}{\tan\theta}\), taking the reciprocal of \(-\frac{5}{7}\) gives \(-\frac{7}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cot\theta = 4, \tan\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\tan\theta = \frac{1}{\cot\theta}\), the reciprocal of \(4\) is \(\frac{1}{4}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\csc\theta = -\frac{13}{12}, \sin\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\sin\theta = \frac{1}{\csc\theta}\), the reciprocal of \(-\frac{13}{12}\) is \(-\frac{12}{13}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\sec\theta = \frac{5}{2}, \cos\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sec\theta}\), the reciprocal of \(\frac{5}{2}\) is \(\frac{2}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(15\cos\theta - 4 = 5\cos\theta - 12, \sec\theta =\)
qs.s: Rearranging terms gives \(10\cos\theta = -8\), so \(\cos\theta = -\frac{4}{5}\). Taking the reciprocal gives \(\sec\theta = -\frac{5}{4}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\sin\theta = \frac{1}{4} - \frac{5}{6}, \csc\theta =\)
qs.s: Subtracting fractions gives \(\sin\theta = \frac{3}{12} - \frac{10}{12} = -\frac{7}{12}\). Then using the reciprocal identity gives \(\csc\theta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta} = -\frac{12}{7}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\csc\theta = \frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}, \sin\theta =\)
qs.s: Taking the reciprocal gives \(\sin\theta = \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}}\). Rationalizing the denominator gives \(\frac{5\sqrt{5}}{3 \times 5} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\tan\theta = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{6}, \cot\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\cot\theta = \frac{1}{\tan\theta}\), we have \(\cot\theta = -\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}\). Rationalizing the denominator gives \(-\frac{6\sqrt{3}}{3} = -2\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(7\sec\theta + 25 = 0, \cos\theta =\)
qs.s: Solving for \(\sec\theta\) yields \(\sec\theta = -\frac{25}{7}\). Using the reciprocal identity \(\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sec\theta}\), we obtain \(\cos\theta = -\frac{7}{25}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cot\theta = -\frac{8}{3}, \tan\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\cot\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) are reciprocals, \(\tan\theta = \frac{1}{\cot\theta} = \frac{1}{-8/3} = -\frac{3}{8}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\csc\theta = -6, \sin\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\csc\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) are reciprocals, \(\sin\theta = \frac{1}{\csc\theta} = \frac{1}{-6} = -\frac{1}{6}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\sin\theta = \frac{3}{10}, \csc\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\sin\theta\) and \(\csc\theta\) are reciprocals, \(\csc\theta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta} = \frac{1}{3/10} = \frac{10}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cos\theta = \frac{4}{7}, \sec\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sec\theta\) are reciprocals, \(\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta} = \frac{1}{4/7} = \frac{7}{4}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cot\theta = \frac{3\sqrt{5}}{10}, \tan\theta =\)
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity, \(\tan\theta = \frac{1}{\cot\theta} = \frac{10}{3\sqrt{5}}\). Rationalizing the denominator gives \(\frac{10\sqrt{5}}{15} = \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\sin\theta = -\frac{\sqrt{21}}{7}, \csc\theta =\)
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity, \(\csc\theta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta} = -\frac{7}{\sqrt{21}}\). Rationalizing the denominator gives \(-\frac{7\sqrt{21}}{21} = -\frac{\sqrt{21}}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\tan\theta = -\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{15}, \cot\theta =\)
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity, \(\cot\theta = \frac{1}{\tan\theta} = -\frac{15}{4\sqrt{3}}\). Rationalizing the denominator gives \(-\frac{15\sqrt{3}}{12} = -\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{4}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cos\theta = -0.375, \sec\theta =\)
qs.s: First convert the decimal to a fraction: \(-0.375 = -\frac{3}{8}\). Then apply the reciprocal identity to get \(\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta} = -\frac{8}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\sec\theta = -\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{6}, \cos\theta =\)
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity, \(\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sec\theta} = -\frac{6}{5\sqrt{2}}\). Rationalizing the denominator gives \(-\frac{6\sqrt{2}}{10} = -\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\tan\theta = -0.75\), \(\cot\theta =\)
qs.s: Write \(\tan\theta = -0.75 = -\frac{3}{4}\). Using the reciprocal identity \(\cot\theta = \frac{1}{\tan\theta}\), we obtain \(\cot\theta = -\frac{4}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\sec\theta = -1.25\), \(\cos\theta =\)
qs.s: Write \(\sec\theta = -1.25 = -\frac{5}{4}\). Using \(\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sec\theta}\), we get \(\cos\theta = -\frac{4}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cot\theta = 0.35\), \(\tan\theta =\)
qs.s: Convert \(0.35\) to \(\frac{35}{100} = \frac{7}{20}\). By the reciprocal identity \(\tan\theta = \frac{1}{\cot\theta}\), we find \(\tan\theta = \frac{20}{7}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\sin\theta = 0.32\), \(\csc\theta =\)
qs.s: Convert \(0.32\) to the fraction \(\frac{32}{100} = \frac{8}{25}\). Since \(\csc\theta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta}\), we have \(\csc\theta = \frac{25}{8}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cos\theta = -0.4\), \(\sec\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta = -0.4 = -\frac{2}{5}\) and \(\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta}\), taking the reciprocal gives \(\sec\theta = -\frac{5}{2}\).

qs.q: If \(\tan\theta = -0.375\), find the value of \(6\cot\theta + 5\).
If \(\sin\theta = 0.28\), find the value of \(7\csc\theta - 11\).
qs.s: Express \(\sin\theta = 0.28 = \frac{7}{25}\), so \(\csc\theta = \frac{25}{7}\). Substituting gives \(7\left(\frac{25}{7}\right) - 11 = 25 - 11 = 14\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cos\theta = -0.064\), \(\sec\theta =\)
