qs.s: Write \(\cos\theta = -\frac{64}{1000} = -\frac{8}{125}\). Taking the reciprocal gives \(\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta} = -\frac{125}{8}\).

qs.q: If \(14\cos\theta + 9 = 4\), find the value of \(\sec\theta\).
qs.s: Subtracting \(9\) gives \(14\cos\theta = -5\), so \(\cos\theta = -\frac{5}{14}\). Since \(\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta}\), we find \(\sec\theta = -\frac{14}{5}\).

qs.q: If \(\sec\theta = -2.25\), find the value of \(\frac{18\cos\theta - 1}{3}\).
qs.s: Write \(\sec\theta = -2.25 = -\frac{9}{4}\), which implies \(\cos\theta = -\frac{4}{9}\). Evaluating the expression gives \(\frac{18\left(-\frac{4}{9}\right) - 1}{3} = \frac{-8 - 1}{3} = -3\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cot\theta = 0.4, \tan\theta =\)
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity \(\tan\theta = \frac{1}{\cot\theta}\), we write \(0.4\) as \(\frac{2}{5}\) and invert it to obtain \(\tan\theta = \frac{5}{2}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cos\theta = 0.35, \sec\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta}\), we write \(0.35 = \frac{7}{20}\) and take the reciprocal to find \(\sec\theta = \frac{20}{7}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\tan\theta = 2.25, \cot\theta =\)
qs.s: Because \(\cot\theta = \frac{1}{\tan\theta}\), we express \(2.25\) as \(\frac{9}{4}\) and invert it to get \(\cot\theta = \frac{4}{9}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\csc\theta = 1.75, \sin\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\sin\theta = \frac{1}{\csc\theta}\), we convert \(1.75\) to \(\frac{7}{4}\) and take its reciprocal to get \(\sin\theta = \frac{4}{7}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\sec\theta = 3.5, \cos\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sec\theta}\), we write \(3.5 = \frac{7}{2}\) and take its reciprocal to get \(\cos\theta = \frac{2}{7}\).

qs.q: If \(5\cos\theta + 3 = \frac{2}{\sec\theta} + 4\), find the value of \(\sec\theta\).
qs.s: Using \(\frac{1}{\sec\theta} = \cos\theta\), the equation becomes \(5\cos\theta + 3 = 2\cos\theta + 4\), so \(3\cos\theta = 1\) and \(\cos\theta = \frac{1}{3}\). Taking the reciprocal gives \(\sec\theta = 3\).

qs.q: If \(\sin\theta = -0.375\), evaluate \(\frac{3\csc\theta + 4}{2}\).
qs.s: Converting gives \(\sin\theta = -\frac{3}{8}\), so \(\csc\theta = -\frac{8}{3}\). Substituting into the expression yields \(\frac{3(-8/3) + 4}{2} = \frac{-8 + 4}{2} = -2\).

qs.q: If \(\sec\theta = -2.5\), evaluate \(\frac{1 - \cos\theta}{1 + \cos\theta}\).
qs.s: Since \(\sec\theta = -2.5 = -\frac{5}{2}\), we have \(\cos\theta = -\frac{2}{5}\). Substituting this into the expression yields \(\frac{1 - (-2/5)}{1 + (-2/5)} = \frac{7/5}{3/5} = \frac{7}{3}\).

qs.q: If \(\tan\theta = -1.5\), evaluate \(6\cot\theta - 2\tan\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\tan\theta = -\frac{3}{2}\), its reciprocal is \(\cot\theta = -\frac{2}{3}\). Evaluating gives \(6\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) - 2\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) = -4 + 3 = -1\).

qs.q: If \(9\csc\theta - 7 = 8\), find the value of \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: Solving for cosecant gives \(9\csc\theta = 15\), so \(\csc\theta = \frac{5}{3}\). By the reciprocal identity, \(\sin\theta = \frac{1}{\csc\theta} = \frac{3}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\sec\theta = -1.6, \cos\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sec\theta}\) and \(\sec\theta = -1.6 = -\frac{8}{5}\), we have \(\cos\theta = -\frac{5}{8}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\tan\theta = 0.35, \cot\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\cot\theta = \frac{1}{\tan\theta}\) and \(\tan\theta = 0.35 = \frac{7}{20}\), we have \(\cot\theta = \frac{20}{7}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cot\theta = -1.75, \tan\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\tan\theta = \frac{1}{\cot\theta}\) and \(\cot\theta = -1.75 = -\frac{7}{4}\), we have \(\tan\theta = -\frac{4}{7}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\csc\theta = 2.25, \sin\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\sin\theta = \frac{1}{\csc\theta}\) and \(\csc\theta = 2.25 = \frac{9}{4}\), we have \(\sin\theta = \frac{4}{9}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\sin\theta = -0.625, \csc\theta =\)
qs.s: Since \(\csc\theta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta}\) and \(\sin\theta = -0.625 = -\frac{5}{8}\), we have \(\csc\theta = -\frac{8}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cot\theta = -\frac{\sqrt{15}}{6}, \tan\theta =\)
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity, \(\tan\theta = \frac{1}{\cot\theta} = -\frac{6}{\sqrt{15}}\). Rationalizing the denominator and simplifying yields \(\tan\theta = -\frac{6\sqrt{15}}{15} = -\frac{2\sqrt{15}}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\cos\theta = -\frac{\sqrt{10}}{6}, \sec\theta =\)
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity, \(\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta} = -\frac{6}{\sqrt{10}}\). Rationalizing the denominator gives \(\sec\theta = -\frac{6\sqrt{10}}{10} = -\frac{3\sqrt{10}}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\tan\theta = -\frac{\sqrt{21}}{14}, \cot\theta =\)
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity, \(\cot\theta = \frac{1}{\tan\theta} = -\frac{14}{\sqrt{21}}\). Rationalizing the denominator gives \(\cot\theta = -\frac{14\sqrt{21}}{21} = -\frac{2\sqrt{21}}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\csc\theta = \frac{7\sqrt{6}}{12}, \sin\theta =\)
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity, \(\sin\theta = \frac{1}{\csc\theta} = \frac{12}{7\sqrt{6}}\). Rationalizing the denominator gives \(\sin\theta = \frac{12\sqrt{6}}{42} = \frac{2\sqrt{6}}{7}\).

qs.q: Find the value of the indicated function: \(\sec\theta = -\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}, \cos\theta =\)
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity, \(\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sec\theta} = -\frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}}\). Rationalizing the denominator gives \(\cos\theta = -\frac{5\sqrt{5}}{15} = -\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\csc 79^\circ = \sec\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\csc x = \sec(90^\circ - x)\), we have \(\theta = 90^\circ - 79^\circ = 11^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cos 72^\circ = \sin\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\cos x = \sin(90^\circ - x)\), we have \(\theta = 90^\circ - 72^\circ = 18^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cot 54^\circ = \tan\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\cot x = \tan(90^\circ - x)\), we have \(\theta = 90^\circ - 54^\circ = 36^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sec 28^\circ = \csc\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\sec x = \csc(90^\circ - x)\), we have \(\theta = 90^\circ - 28^\circ = 62^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\tan 65^\circ = \cot\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\tan x = \cot(90^\circ - x)\), we have \(\theta = 90^\circ - 65^\circ = 25^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cot(3\theta - 5^\circ) = \tan(\theta + 15^\circ), \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity, \((3\theta - 5^\circ) + (\theta + 15^\circ) = 90^\circ\). Simplifying gives \(4\theta + 10^\circ = 90^\circ\), which leads to \(4\theta = 80^\circ\) and \(\theta = 20^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\tan(3\theta - 8^\circ) = \cot(2\theta + 18^\circ), \theta =\)
qs.s: Since tangent and cotangent are cofunctions, \((3\theta - 8^\circ) + (2\theta + 18^\circ) = 90^\circ\). This simplifies to \(5\theta + 10^\circ = 90^\circ\), which gives \(5\theta = 80^\circ\) and \(\theta = 16^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sec(4\theta - 5^\circ) = \csc(\theta + 10^\circ), \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, \((4\theta - 5^\circ) + (\theta + 10^\circ) = 90^\circ\). Combining like terms yields \(5\theta + 5^\circ = 90^\circ\), so \(5\theta = 85^\circ\) and \(\theta = 17^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cos(2\theta + 14^\circ) = \sin 46^\circ, \theta =\)
qs.s: Since the acute angles are complementary, \((2\theta + 14^\circ) + 46^\circ = 90^\circ\). Simplifying gives \(2\theta + 60^\circ = 90^\circ\), so \(2\theta = 30^\circ\) and \(\theta = 15^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sin\left(\frac{3}{2}\theta + 5^\circ\right) = \cos(\theta + 10^\circ), \theta =\)
qs.s: Set the sum of the angles equal to \(90^\circ\): \(\frac{3}{2}\theta + 5^\circ + \theta + 10^\circ = 90^\circ\). This gives \(\frac{5}{2}\theta = 75^\circ\), so \(\theta = 75^\circ \times \frac{2}{5} = 30^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\csc 37^\circ = \sec\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, \(\csc 37^\circ = \sec(90^\circ - 37^\circ)\). Therefore, \(\theta = 90^\circ - 37^\circ = 53^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cos 54^\circ = \sin\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, \(\cos 54^\circ = \sin(90^\circ - 54^\circ)\). Therefore, \(\theta = 90^\circ - 54^\circ = 36^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sec 71^\circ = \csc\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, \(\sec 71^\circ = \csc(90^\circ - 71^\circ)\). Therefore, \(\theta = 90^\circ - 71^\circ = 19^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cot 13^\circ = \tan\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, \(\cot 13^\circ = \tan(90^\circ - 13^\circ)\). Therefore, \(\theta = 90^\circ - 13^\circ = 77^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sin 28^\circ = \cos\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, \(\sin 28^\circ = \cos(90^\circ - 28^\circ)\). Therefore, \(\theta = 90^\circ - 28^\circ = 62^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2} + 12^\circ\right) = \cos 58^\circ, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity, \(\left(\frac{\theta}{2} + 12^\circ\right) + 58^\circ = 90^\circ\). Simplifying gives \(\frac{\theta}{2} + 70^\circ = 90^\circ\), so \(\frac{\theta}{2} = 20^\circ\), which yields \(\theta = 40^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cos(4\theta + 5^\circ) = \sin(\theta + 15^\circ), \theta =\)
qs.s: Since sine and cosine are cofunctions, \((4\theta + 5^\circ) + (\theta + 15^\circ) = 90^\circ\). Combining terms gives \(5\theta + 20^\circ = 90^\circ\), so \(5\theta = 70^\circ\), which yields \(\theta = 14^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\tan(3\theta - 6^\circ) = \cot 48^\circ, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity, \((3\theta - 6^\circ) + 48^\circ = 90^\circ\). Simplifying gives \(3\theta + 42^\circ = 90^\circ\), so \(3\theta = 48^\circ\), which yields \(\theta = 16^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sec(2\theta + 25^\circ) = \csc(3\theta - 10^\circ), \theta =\)
qs.s: Since secant and cosecant are cofunctions, \((2\theta + 25^\circ) + (3\theta - 10^\circ) = 90^\circ\). This gives \(5\theta + 15^\circ = 90^\circ\), so \(5\theta = 75^\circ\), which gives \(\theta = 15^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cot(5\theta - 22^\circ) = \tan(3\theta + 16^\circ), \theta =\)
qs.s: Since cotangent and tangent are cofunctions, \((5\theta - 22^\circ) + (3\theta + 16^\circ) = 90^\circ\). This simplifies to \(8\theta - 6^\circ = 90^\circ\), so \(8\theta = 96^\circ\), which gives \(\theta = 12^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cot 78^\circ = \tan\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\cot x = \tan(90^\circ - x)\), we have \(\theta = 90^\circ - 78^\circ = 12^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sin 42^\circ = \cos\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\sin x = \cos(90^\circ - x)\), we have \(\theta = 90^\circ - 42^\circ = 48^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cos 19^\circ = \sin\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\cos x = \sin(90^\circ - x)\), we have \(\theta = 90^\circ - 19^\circ = 71^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\csc 54^\circ = \sec\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\csc x = \sec(90^\circ - x)\), we have \(\theta = 90^\circ - 54^\circ = 36^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\tan 67^\circ = \cot\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\tan x = \cot(90^\circ - x)\), we have \(\theta = 90^\circ - 67^\circ = 23^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sin(4\theta - 10^\circ) = \cos(\theta + 20^\circ), \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, \((4\theta - 10^\circ) + (\theta + 20^\circ) = 90^\circ\). Simplifying gives \(5\theta + 10^\circ = 90^\circ\), which yields \(5\theta = 80^\circ\) and \(\theta = 16^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\tan(2\theta + 15^\circ) = \cot(3\theta + 5^\circ), \theta =\)
qs.s: Since tangent and cotangent are cofunctions, \((2\theta + 15^\circ) + (3\theta + 5^\circ) = 90^\circ\). Combining like terms gives \(5\theta + 20^\circ = 90^\circ\), so \(5\theta = 70^\circ\) and \(\theta = 14^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sec(2\theta + 16^\circ) = \csc 52^\circ, \theta =\)
qs.s: Since secant and cosecant are cofunctions, their acute angles sum to \(90^\circ\): \((2\theta + 16^\circ) + 52^\circ = 90^\circ\). Solving \(2\theta + 68^\circ = 90^\circ\) gives \(2\theta = 22^\circ\), so \(\theta = 11^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cos(3\theta + 24^\circ) = \sin(5\theta - 6^\circ), \theta =\)
qs.s: Since cosine and sine are cofunctions, \((3\theta + 24^\circ) + (5\theta - 6^\circ) = 90^\circ\). Simplifying gives \(8\theta + 18^\circ = 90^\circ\), which results in \(8\theta = 72^\circ\) and \(\theta = 9^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\csc(5\theta - 14^\circ) = \sec(3\theta + 8^\circ), \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity, \((5\theta - 14^\circ) + (3\theta + 8^\circ) = 90^\circ\). This simplifies to \(8\theta - 6^\circ = 90^\circ\), leading to \(8\theta = 96^\circ\), so \(\theta = 12^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sin\frac{2\pi}{5} = \cos\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\sin x = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\), we have \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{2\pi}{5} = \frac{\pi}{10}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cot\frac{\pi}{6} = \tan\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\cot x = \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\), we have \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sec\frac{\pi}{5} = \csc\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\sec x = \csc\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\), we have \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{5} = \frac{3\pi}{10}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \sin\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\cos x = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\), we have \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\pi}{6}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cos\frac{7\pi}{18} = \sin\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\cos x = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\), we have \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{7\pi}{18} = \frac{2\pi}{18} = \frac{\pi}{9}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cos\frac{\pi}{5} = \sin(2\theta), \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, \(2\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{5} = \frac{3\pi}{10}\). Dividing both sides by 2 gives \(\theta = \frac{3\pi}{20}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sec\left(2\theta - \frac{\pi}{12}\right) = \csc\frac{\pi}{3}, \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, \(2\theta - \frac{\pi}{12} = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\pi}{6}\). Adding \(\frac{\pi}{12}\) yields \(2\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}\), so \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{8}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\tan\left(2\theta - \frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \cot\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, the angles must sum to \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), giving \(\left(2\theta - \frac{\pi}{6}\right) + \theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\). Simplifying yields \(3\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}\), so \(\theta = \frac{2\pi}{9}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\tan(3\theta) = \cot(2\theta), \theta =\)
qs.s: Since tangent and cotangent are cofunctions, the sum of their acute angles is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), so \(3\theta + 2\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\). Solving \(5\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\) gives \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{10}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cos\left(\theta + \frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \sin\frac{\pi}{4}, \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, \(\theta + \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{4}\). Subtracting \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) gives \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{12}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cos\frac{3\pi}{10} = \sin\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity \(\cos x = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\), we calculate \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{3\pi}{10} = \frac{2\pi}{10} = \frac{\pi}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\tan\frac{3\pi}{8} = \cot\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\tan x = \cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\), we find \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{3\pi}{8} = \frac{\pi}{8}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \cos\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity \(\sin x = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\), we have \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\pi}{6}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\csc\frac{2\pi}{5} = \sec\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity \(\csc x = \sec\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\), we have \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{2\pi}{5} = \frac{\pi}{10}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\csc\left(4\theta - \frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \sec\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Because the angles are complementary, \(\left(4\theta - \frac{\pi}{3}\right) + \theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\), so \(5\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{5\pi}{6}\), which gives \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{6}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\tan\left(3\theta - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \cot(2\theta), \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, \(\left(3\theta - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) + 2\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\), so \(5\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{3\pi}{4}\), which yields \(\theta = \frac{3\pi}{20}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sec\left(2\theta + \frac{\pi}{5}\right) = \csc\frac{\pi}{10}, \theta =\)
qs.s: Since the acute angles of cofunctions sum to \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), we have \(\left(2\theta + \frac{\pi}{5}\right) + \frac{\pi}{10} = \frac{\pi}{2}\), which simplifies to \(2\theta + \frac{3\pi}{10} = \frac{5\pi}{10}\), so \(2\theta = \frac{\pi}{5}\) and \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{10}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cos\left(2\theta + \frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \sin\left(\theta + \frac{\pi}{12}\right), \theta =\)
qs.s: Equating the sum of the angles to \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), we have \(\left(2\theta + \frac{\pi}{6}\right) + \left(\theta + \frac{\pi}{12}\right) = \frac{\pi}{2}\), which simplifies to \(3\theta + \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2}\), giving \(3\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}\) and \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{12}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sin(3\theta) = \cos(2\theta), \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity for acute angles, \(3\theta + 2\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\), which simplifies to \(5\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\), yielding \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{10}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cot\frac{\pi}{5} = \tan\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\cot x = \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\), we obtain \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{5} = \frac{5\pi - 2\pi}{10} = \frac{3\pi}{10}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\tan\frac{\pi}{8} = \cot\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\tan x = \cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\), we have \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{8} = \frac{4\pi - \pi}{8} = \frac{3\pi}{8}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sin\frac{3\pi}{10} = \cos\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, \(\sin x = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\). Thus, \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{3\pi}{10} = \frac{5\pi - 3\pi}{10} = \frac{2\pi}{10} = \frac{\pi}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sec\frac{5\pi}{12} = \csc\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\sec x = \csc\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\), we have \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{5\pi}{12} = \frac{6\pi - 5\pi}{12} = \frac{\pi}{12}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cos\frac{2\pi}{7} = \sin\theta, \theta =\)
qs.s: Using the cofunction identity \(\cos x = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\), we find \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{2\pi}{7} = \frac{7\pi - 4\pi}{14} = \frac{3\pi}{14}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\cot\left(3\theta + \frac{\pi}{12}\right) = \tan\left(2\theta + \frac{\pi}{6}\right), \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, the angles sum to \(\frac{\pi}{2}\): \(\left(3\theta + \frac{\pi}{12}\right) + \left(2\theta + \frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{\pi}{2}\). This simplifies to \(5\theta + \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2}\), so \(5\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}\) and \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{20}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sec\left(\theta - \frac{\pi}{12}\right) = \csc\left(2\theta + \frac{\pi}{4}\right), \theta =\)
qs.s: Since secant and cosecant are cofunctions, their acute angles satisfy \(\left(\theta - \frac{\pi}{12}\right) + \left(2\theta + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{\pi}{2}\). Simplifying yields \(3\theta + \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{2}\), so \(3\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}\) and \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{9}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\sin\left(2\theta + \frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \cos\frac{\pi}{5}, \theta =\)
qs.s: Since sine and cosine are cofunctions, the angles sum to \(\frac{\pi}{2}\): \(\left(2\theta + \frac{\pi}{6}\right) + \frac{\pi}{5} = \frac{\pi}{2}\). Subtracting gives \(2\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{11\pi}{30} = \frac{4\pi}{30} = \frac{2\pi}{15}\), so \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{15}\).

qs.q: Find the acute angle \(\theta\), for the trigonometric function: \(\csc\frac{2\pi}{9} = \sec(2\theta), \theta =\)
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, the angles must sum to \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), so \(2\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{2\pi}{9} = \frac{5\pi}{18}\). Dividing by \(2\) gives \(\theta = \frac{5\pi}{36}\).

exercises.name: Trigonometric functions from a terminal point diagram

qs.q: Use the given figure showing point \(P\) on the terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position to find the exact values of \(\cot\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: The point \(P\) has coordinates \((-2, 1)\), so \(x = -2\), \(y = 1\), and \(r = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{5}\). Hence, \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y} = -2\) and \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} = -\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through point \(P\) as shown. Find the exact value of \(\sec\theta\).
qs.s: From the figure, \(P\) is located at \((2, 3)\), so \(x = 2\), \(y = 3\), and \(r = \sqrt{2^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{13}\). Therefore, \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x} = \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}\).

qs.q: The point \(P\) on the terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position is shown in the figure. Evaluate the exact value of \(\sec\theta\).
qs.s: The coordinates of \(P\) are \((3, -4)\), which gives \(x = 3\), \(y = -4\), and \(r = \sqrt{3^2 + (-4)^2} = 5\). Therefore, \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x} = \frac{5}{3}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the point \(P\) shown in the figure. Use the figure to determine the exact values of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: From the graph, point \(P\) has coordinates \((-4, 3)\), so \(x = -4\), \(y = 3\), and \(r = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + 3^2} = 5\). Thus, \(\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} = \frac{3}{5}\) and \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{4}{5}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position contains the point \(P\) shown in the figure. Find the exact values of \(\tan\theta\) and \(\csc\theta\).
qs.s: From the figure, point \(P\) is \((-3, -2)\), giving \(x = -3\), \(y = -2\), and \(r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{13}\). Consequently, \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} = \frac{2}{3}\) and \(\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y} = -\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through point \(P\) shown in the figure. Evaluate \(\frac{\sin\theta + \cos\theta}{\tan\theta}\).
qs.s: From the figure, \(P\) is \((-4, -3)\), so \(x = -4\), \(y = -3\), and \(r = 5\). Thus \(\sin\theta = -\frac{3}{5}\), \(\cos\theta = -\frac{4}{5}\), and \(\tan\theta = \frac{3}{4}\), giving \(\frac{\sin\theta + \cos\theta}{\tan\theta} = \frac{-7/5}{3/4} = -\frac{28}{15}\).

qs.q: Point \(P\) lies on the terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position as shown. Find the exact value of \(\sin\theta - \cos\theta\).
qs.s: The point is \(P(-3, 6)\), giving \(r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}\). Then \(\sin\theta = \frac{6}{3\sqrt{5}} = \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}\) and \(\cos\theta = -\frac{3}{3\sqrt{5}} = -\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\), so \(\sin\theta - \cos\theta = \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} - \left(-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\right) = \frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through point \(P\) shown in the figure. Evaluate the expression \(\csc\theta + \cot\theta\).
qs.s: Point \(P\) has coordinates \((-5, 12)\), so \(r = \sqrt{(-5)^2 + 12^2} = 13\). Then \(\csc\theta = \frac{13}{12}\) and \(\cot\theta = -\frac{5}{12}\), giving \(\csc\theta + \cot\theta = \frac{13 - 5}{12} = \frac{8}{12} = \frac{2}{3}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through point \(P\) shown in the figure. Find the exact value of \(\sin\theta\cos\theta\).
qs.s: From the figure, \(P\) is \((4, -6)\), so \(r^2 = 4^2 + (-6)^2 = 52\). Then \(\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac{y}{r}\cdot\frac{x}{r} = \frac{xy}{r^2} = \frac{4(-6)}{52} = -\frac{24}{52} = -\frac{6}{13}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position contains point \(P\) as shown in the figure. Determine the exact value of \(\sin^2\theta - \cos^2\theta\).
qs.s: Reading the graph gives \(P(5, -2)\), so \(r = \sqrt{5^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{29}\). Then \(\sin\theta = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{29}}\) and \(\cos\theta = \frac{5}{\sqrt{29}}\), so \(\sin^2\theta - \cos^2\theta = \frac{4}{29} - \frac{25}{29} = -\frac{21}{29}\).

qs.q: A point \(P\) on the terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position is shown in the figure below. Evaluate the six trigonometric functions of \(\theta\).
qs.s: From the figure, \(P = (-4, 3)\), so \(x = -4\) and \(y = 3\). The distance from the origin is \(r = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + 3^2} = 5\), giving \(\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} = \frac{3}{5}\), \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{4}{5}\), \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} = -\frac{3}{4}\), and their reciprocals \(\csc\theta = \frac{5}{3}\), \(\sec\theta = -\frac{5}{4}\), \(\cot\theta = -\frac{4}{3}\).

qs.q: A point \(P\) on the terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position is shown in the figure below. Use the trigonometric functions of \(\theta\) to find the exact value of \(\sin\theta\cos\theta - \tan\theta\).
qs.s: The coordinates are \(x = -3\) and \(y = 2\), so \(r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{13}\). Therefore, \(\sin\theta = \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\), \(\cos\theta = -\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\), and \(\tan\theta = -\frac{2}{3}\). Calculating gives \(\sin\theta\cos\theta - \tan\theta = -\frac{6}{13} - \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) = -\frac{18}{39} + \frac{26}{39} = \frac{8}{39}\).

qs.q: A point \(P\) on the terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position is shown in the figure below. Use the trigonometric functions of \(\theta\) to evaluate the exact value of \(\csc\theta + \sec\theta\).
qs.s: From the point \(P(-2, -3)\), \(x = -2\), \(y = -3\), and \(r = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (-3)^2} = \sqrt{13}\). Thus \(\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y} = -\frac{\sqrt{13}}{3}\) and \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x} = -\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}\), so \(\csc\theta + \sec\theta = -\frac{\sqrt{13}}{3} - \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2} = -\frac{5\sqrt{13}}{6}\).

qs.q: The figure shows an angle \(\theta\) in standard position whose terminal side passes through point \(P\). Use the graph to find the exact value of \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: From the graph, point \(P\) has coordinates \((-4, 3)\). The distance from the origin is \(r = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + 3^2} = 5\), so \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{4}{5}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through point \(P\), as shown in the figure. Use the graph to find the exact value of \(\csc\theta\).
qs.s: From the figure, point \(P\) is at \((3, -4)\). The distance to the origin is \(r = \sqrt{3^2 + (-4)^2} = 5\), giving \(\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y} = \frac{5}{-4} = -\frac{5}{4}\).

qs.q: An angle \(\theta\) in standard position has point \(P\) on its terminal side as shown in the figure. What is the exact value of \(\sec\theta\)?
qs.s: Reading from the graph, \(P\) is \((2, 3)\), so \(r = \sqrt{2^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{13}\). Then \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x} = \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position contains the point \(P\) shown in the figure. Use the graph to find the exact value of \(\cot\theta\).
qs.s: From the graph, the coordinates of \(P\) are \((-3, 2)\). By definition, \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y} = -\frac{3}{2}\).

qs.q: Use the given figure to find the exact value of \(\sin\theta\), where \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position with point \(P\) on its terminal side.
qs.s: From the graph, \(P\) has coordinates \((-1, -2)\), which gives \(r = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{5}\). Therefore, \(\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} = \frac{-2}{\sqrt{5}} = -\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}\).

qs.q: The figure shows an angle \(\theta\) in standard position with point \(P\) on its terminal side. Use the graph to determine the value of \(\sin\theta - \cos\theta\).
qs.s: From the graph, \(P = (-6, 8)\), so \(r = \sqrt{(-6)^2 + 8^2} = 10\). Thus \(\sin\theta = \frac{8}{10} = \frac{4}{5}\) and \(\cos\theta = \frac{-6}{10} = -\frac{3}{5}\), so \(\sin\theta - \cos\theta = \frac{4}{5} - \left(-\frac{3}{5}\right) = \frac{7}{5}\).

qs.q: An angle \(\theta\) in standard position has point \(P\) on its terminal side, as shown in the coordinate plane. Use the graph to find the exact value of \(\sin\theta\cos\theta\).
qs.s: Point \(P\) has coordinates \((-2, -4)\), so \(r = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (-4)^2} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\). Then \(\sin\theta = \frac{-4}{2\sqrt{5}} = -\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}\) and \(\cos\theta = \frac{-2}{2\sqrt{5}} = -\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\), so \(\sin\theta\cos\theta = \left(-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}\right)\left(-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\right) = \frac{2}{5}\).

qs.q: The figure shows an angle \(\theta\) in standard position whose terminal side passes through point \(P\). Use the graph to evaluate \(\frac{1 - \cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\).
qs.s: From the graph, \(P = (-3, -4)\), which gives \(r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + (-4)^2} = 5\). Then \(\cos\theta = -\frac{3}{5}\) and \(\sin\theta = -\frac{4}{5}\), so \(\frac{1 - \cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \frac{1 - (-3/5)}{-4/5} = \frac{8/5}{-4/5} = -2\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through point \(P\) as shown in the figure. Use the graph to find the exact value of \(\sec\theta + \csc\theta\).
qs.s: From the graph, \(P = (-1, 4)\), so \(r = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{17}\). Thus \(\sec\theta = \frac{\sqrt{17}}{-1} = -\sqrt{17}\) and \(\csc\theta = \frac{\sqrt{17}}{4}\), yielding \(\sec\theta + \csc\theta = -\sqrt{17} + \frac{\sqrt{17}}{4} = -\frac{3\sqrt{17}}{4}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through point \(P\) as shown in the figure. Use the graph to evaluate \(\csc\theta + \cot\theta\).
qs.s: From the graph, \(P = (8, -6)\) and \(r = \sqrt{8^2 + (-6)^2} = 10\). Then \(\csc\theta = \frac{10}{-6} = -\frac{5}{3}\) and \(\cot\theta = \frac{8}{-6} = -\frac{4}{3}\), which gives \(\csc\theta + \cot\theta = -\frac{5}{3} + \left(-\frac{4}{3}\right) = -3\).

qs.q: The terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the point \(P\) shown in the figure. Use the graph to find the exact value of \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: From the graph, point \(P\) has coordinates \((-2, 1)\), so \(x = -2\) and \(y = 1\). The distance is \(r = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{5}\), giving \(\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the point \(P\) shown in the figure. Use the graph to find the exact value of \(\sec\theta\).
qs.s: From the graph, point \(P\) has coordinates \((1, -3)\), so \(x = 1\) and \(y = -3\). The distance is \(r = \sqrt{1^2 + (-3)^2} = \sqrt{10}\), so \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x} = \frac{\sqrt{10}}{1} = \sqrt{10}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the point \(P\) shown in the figure. Use the graph to find the exact value of \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: From the graph, point \(P\) has coordinates \((-3, 4)\), so \(x = -3\) and \(y = 4\). The distance from the origin is \(r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 4^2} = 5\), giving \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{3}{5}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the point \(P\) shown in the figure. Use the graph to find the exact value of \(\cot\theta\).
qs.s: From the graph, point \(P\) has coordinates \((-4, -3)\), so \(x = -4\) and \(y = -3\). Therefore, \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y} = \frac{-4}{-3} = \frac{4}{3}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the point \(P\) shown in the figure. Use the graph to find the exact value of \(\csc\theta\).
qs.s: From the graph, point \(P\) has coordinates \((3, -4)\), so \(x = 3\) and \(y = -4\). The distance from the origin is \(r = \sqrt{3^2 + (-4)^2} = 5\), so \(\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y} = -\frac{5}{4}\).

qs.q: The figure shows the terminal sides of two angles in standard position, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), passing through points \(P\) and \(Q\) respectively. Use the graph to find the exact value of \(\cos\alpha - \sin\beta\).
qs.s: For \(\alpha\), point \(P(-3, 4)\) gives \(\cos\alpha = -\frac{3}{5}\). For \(\beta\), point \(Q(3, -4)\) gives \(\sin\beta = -\frac{4}{5}\). Thus, \(\cos\alpha - \sin\beta = -\frac{3}{5} - \left(-\frac{4}{5}\right) = \frac{1}{5}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position intersects the circle of radius \(5\) centered at the origin at point \(P\), as shown in the figure. Use the graph to find the exact value of \(\csc\theta - \cot\theta\).
qs.s: From the graph, \(P\) is \((-3, -4)\) and \(r = 5\). Thus \(\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y} = -\frac{5}{4}\) and \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y} = \frac{3}{4}\), giving \(\csc\theta - \cot\theta = -\frac{5}{4} - \frac{3}{4} = -2\).

qs.q: The terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the point \(P\) shown in the figure. Use the graph to find the exact value of \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta\).
qs.s: Point \(P\) has coordinates \((-2, 3)\), so \(x = -2\), \(y = 3\), and \(r = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{13}\). Then \(\sin\theta = \frac{3\sqrt{13}}{13}\) and \(\cos\theta = -\frac{2\sqrt{13}}{13}\), giving \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \frac{\sqrt{13}}{13}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the point \(P\) shown in the figure. Use the graph to find the exact value of \(\sec\theta + \tan\theta\).

The terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the point \(P\) shown in the figure, forming the shaded reference triangle with the \(x\)-axis. Use the graph to find the exact value of \(\sin^2\theta - \cos^2\theta\).
qs.s: From the graph, \(P\) is \((-3, 1)\), so \(x = -3\), \(y = 1\), and \(r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{10}\). Thus \(\sin^2\theta = \frac{1}{10}\) and \(\cos^2\theta = \frac{9}{10}\), giving \(\sin^2\theta - \cos^2\theta = \frac{1}{10} - \frac{9}{10} = -\frac{4}{5}\).

qs.q: The point \(P\) on the terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position is shown in the figure. Evaluate the six trigonometric functions of \(\theta\).
qs.s: From the figure, the terminal side contains \(P(-4, 3)\), so \(x = -4\) and \(y = 3\). The distance is \(r = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + 3^2} = 5\), giving \(\sin\theta = \frac{3}{5}\), \(\cos\theta = -\frac{4}{5}\), \(\tan\theta = -\frac{3}{4}\), \(\csc\theta = \frac{5}{3}\), \(\sec\theta = -\frac{5}{4}\), and \(\cot\theta = -\frac{4}{3}\).

qs.q: The point \(P\) on the terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position is shown in the figure. Evaluate \(\sin\theta\cos\theta + \tan\theta\).
qs.s: From \(P(-2, -4)\), we have \(x = -2\), \(y = -4\), and \(r = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (-4)^2} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\). Then \(\sin\theta = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\), \(\cos\theta = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\), and \(\tan\theta = 2\), so \(\sin\theta\cos\theta + \tan\theta = \left(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\right)\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right) + 2 = \frac{2}{5} + 2 = \frac{12}{5}\).

qs.q: The point \(P\) on the terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position is shown in the figure. Find the exact value of \(\sec\theta - \tan\theta\).
qs.s: The coordinates are \(x = -4\) and \(y = -3\), so \(r = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + (-3)^2} = 5\). Thus \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x} = -\frac{5}{4}\) and \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} = \frac{3}{4}\), which yields \(\sec\theta - \tan\theta = -\frac{5}{4} - \frac{3}{4} = -2\).

qs.q: The point \(P\) on the terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position is shown in the figure. Evaluate the six trigonometric functions of \(\theta\) in fully simplified form.
qs.s: From \(P(-4, 2)\), we calculate \(r = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\). Simplifying each ratio produces \(\sin\theta = \frac{2}{2\sqrt{5}} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\), \(\cos\theta = \frac{-4}{2\sqrt{5}} = -\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}\), \(\tan\theta = -\frac{1}{2}\), \(\csc\theta = \sqrt{5}\), \(\sec\theta = -\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\), and \(\cot\theta = -2\).

qs.q: A circle centered at the origin passes through point \(P\) on the terminal side of an angle \(\theta\) in standard position, as shown in the figure. Evaluate the six trigonometric functions of \(\theta\).
qs.s: From the figure, \(P(-3, 2)\) lies on the circle of radius \(r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{13}\). Evaluating each function gives \(\sin\theta = \frac{2\sqrt{13}}{13}\), \(\cos\theta = -\frac{3\sqrt{13}}{13}\), \(\tan\theta = -\frac{2}{3}\), \(\csc\theta = \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}\), \(\sec\theta = -\frac{\sqrt{13}}{3}\), and \(\cot\theta = -\frac{3}{2}\).

exercises.name: Trigonometric functions from one ratio and quadrant

qs.q: Given that \(\tan\theta = \frac{4}{3}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant I, determine the value of \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant I, \(y = 4\) and \(x = 3\), so \(r = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\). Therefore, \(\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} = \frac{4}{5}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\cos\theta = \frac{4}{5}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant I, determine the value of \(\tan\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant I, \(x = 4\) and \(r = 5\), so \(y = \sqrt{5^2 - 4^2} = 3\). Therefore, \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} = \frac{3}{4}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\tan\theta = \frac{7}{24}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant I, determine the value of \(\sec\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant I, \(y = 7\) and \(x = 24\), so \(r = \sqrt{24^2 + 7^2} = 25\). Therefore, \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x} = \frac{25}{24}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\sin\theta = \frac{8}{17}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant I, determine the value of \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant I, \(y = 8\) and \(r = 17\), so \(x = \sqrt{17^2 - 8^2} = 15\). Therefore, \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = \frac{15}{17}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\csc\theta = \frac{5}{3}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant I, determine the value of \(\cot\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant I, \(r = 5\) and \(y = 3\), so \(x = \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = 4\). Therefore, \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y} = \frac{4}{3}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\tan\theta = -\frac{3}{4}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant II, determine the value of \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant II, \(y = 3\), \(x = -4\), and \(r = 5\), which yields \(\sin\theta = \frac{3}{5}\) and \(\cos\theta = -\frac{4}{5}\). Thus, \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \frac{3}{5} + \left(-\frac{4}{5}\right) = -\frac{1}{5}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\csc\theta = -\frac{4}{3}\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\cot\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\csc\theta < 0\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in quadrant IV where \(y = -3\) and \(r = 4\), giving \(x = \sqrt{4^2 - (-3)^2} = \sqrt{7}\). Thus, \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y} = -\frac{\sqrt{7}}{3}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\sin\theta = -\frac{5}{13}\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\sec\theta - \tan\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\sin\theta < 0\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) lies in quadrant IV where \(y = -5\), \(r = 13\), and \(x = \sqrt{13^2 - (-5)^2} = 12\). Then \(\sec\theta - \tan\theta = \frac{13}{12} - \left(-\frac{5}{12}\right) = \frac{18}{12} = \frac{3}{2}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\cos\theta = -\frac{2}{5}\) and \(\tan\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta < 0\) and \(\tan\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in quadrant III where \(x = -2\) and \(r = 5\), giving \(y = -\sqrt{5^2 - (-2)^2} = -\sqrt{21}\). Therefore, \(\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} = -\frac{\sqrt{21}}{5}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\cos\theta = -\frac{15}{17}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant III, determine the value of \(\tan\theta + \sec\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant III, \(x = -15\) and \(r = 17\), which gives \(y = -\sqrt{17^2 - (-15)^2} = -8\). Therefore, \(\tan\theta + \sec\theta = \frac{-8}{-15} + \frac{17}{-15} = \frac{8 - 17}{15} = -\frac{9}{15} = -\frac{3}{5}\).

qs.q: If \(\cos\theta = -\frac{4}{5}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant II, determine the value of \(\tan\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant II, \(x = -4\) and \(y > 0\), giving \(y = \sqrt{5^2 - (-4)^2} = 3\). Thus, \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} = -\frac{3}{4}\).

qs.q: If \(\csc\theta = -\frac{5}{2}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant IV, determine the value of \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant IV, \(y = -2\) and \(r = 5\), which gives \(x = \sqrt{5^2 - (-2)^2} = \sqrt{21}\). Thus, \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = \frac{\sqrt{21}}{5}\).

qs.q: If \(\tan\theta = -\frac{7}{24}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant II, determine the value of \(\sec\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant II, \(x = -24\) and \(y = 7\), so \(r = \sqrt{(-24)^2 + 7^2} = 25\). Therefore, \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x} = -\frac{25}{24}\).

qs.q: If \(\cos\theta = -\frac{2}{3}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant III, determine the value of \(\tan\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant III, \(x = -2\) and \(y = -\sqrt{3^2 - (-2)^2} = -\sqrt{5}\). Hence, \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} = \frac{-\sqrt{5}}{-2} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\).

qs.q: If \(\sin\theta = -\frac{5}{13}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant IV, determine the value of \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant IV, \(x > 0\) and \(y = -5\), so \(x = \sqrt{13^2 - (-5)^2} = 12\). Therefore, \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = \frac{12}{13}\).

qs.q: If \(\cot\theta = -\frac{12}{5}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant II, determine the value of \(13\sin\theta - 12\tan\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant II, \(x = -12\), \(y = 5\), and \(r = \sqrt{(-12)^2 + 5^2} = 13\), so \(\sin\theta = \frac{5}{13}\) and \(\tan\theta = -\frac{5}{12}\). Thus, \(13\left(\frac{5}{13}\right) - 12\left(-\frac{5}{12}\right) = 5 - (-5) = 10\).

qs.q: If \(\tan\theta = \frac{20}{21}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant III, determine the value of \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant III, \(x = -21\) and \(y = -20\), so \(r = \sqrt{(-21)^2 + (-20)^2} = 29\). Then \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = -\frac{20}{29} + \left(-\frac{21}{29}\right) = -\frac{41}{29}\).

qs.q: If \(\tan\theta = \frac{\sqrt{7}}{3}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant III, determine the value of \(\cos\theta + \sec\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant III, \(x = -3\), \(y = -\sqrt{7}\), and \(r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + (-\sqrt{7})^2} = 4\). Then \(\cos\theta + \sec\theta = -\frac{3}{4} + \left(-\frac{4}{3}\right) = -\frac{25}{12}\).

qs.q: If \(\cos\theta = \frac{9}{41}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant IV, determine the value of \(\csc\theta + \cot\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant IV, \(x = 9\) and \(y = -\sqrt{41^2 - 9^2} = -40\). Then \(\csc\theta + \cot\theta = -\frac{41}{40} + \left(-\frac{9}{40}\right) = -\frac{50}{40} = -\frac{5}{4}\).

qs.q: If \(\sin\theta = \frac{2}{7}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant II, determine the value of \(\sec\theta - \tan\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant II, \(y = 2\) and \(x = -\sqrt{7^2 - 2^2} = -3\sqrt{5}\). Then \(\sec\theta - \tan\theta = \frac{7}{-3\sqrt{5}} - \frac{2}{-3\sqrt{5}} = \frac{-5}{3\sqrt{5}} = -\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\cot\theta = \frac{3}{2}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant III, find the value of \(\csc\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant III, \(x = -3\) and \(y = -2\), so \(r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{13}\). Therefore, \(\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y} = -\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\csc\theta = -\frac{4}{3}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant IV, find the value of \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant IV, \(x > 0\) and \(y < 0\), so with \(y = -3\) and \(r = 4\), \(x = \sqrt{4^2 - (-3)^2} = \sqrt{7}\). Thus, \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = \frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\tan\theta = -\frac{1}{3}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant II, find the value of \(\sec\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant II, \(x = -3\) and \(y = 1\), giving \(r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{10}\). Therefore, \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x} = -\frac{\sqrt{10}}{3}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\cos\theta = -\frac{2}{5}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant II, find the value of \(\tan\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant II, \(x < 0\) and \(y > 0\), so with \(x = -2\) and \(r = 5\), \(y = \sqrt{5^2 - (-2)^2} = \sqrt{21}\). Thus, \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} = -\frac{\sqrt{21}}{2}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\sin\theta = -\frac{1}{4}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant III, find the value of \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant III, both \(x\) and \(y\) are negative, so with \(y = -1\) and \(r = 4\), \(x = -\sqrt{4^2 - (-1)^2} = -\sqrt{15}\). Therefore, \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\tan\theta = -\frac{8}{15}\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), find the value of \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\tan\theta < 0\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) lies in quadrant IV where \(x = 15\), \(y = -8\), and \(r = \sqrt{15^2 + (-8)^2} = 17\). Then \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = -\frac{8}{17} + \frac{15}{17} = \frac{7}{17}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\sin\theta = -\frac{7}{25}\) and \(\theta\) is in quadrant III, find the value of \(\sec\theta - \tan\theta\).
qs.s: In quadrant III, \(x = -\sqrt{25^2 - (-7)^2} = -24\) and \(y = -7\), so \(\sec\theta = -\frac{25}{24}\) and \(\tan\theta = \frac{7}{24}\). Hence, \(\sec\theta - \tan\theta = -\frac{25}{24} - \frac{7}{24} = -\frac{32}{24} = -\frac{4}{3}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\csc\theta = -\frac{7}{3}\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), find the value of \(\cot\theta\) in simplest radical form.
qs.s: Since \(\csc\theta < 0\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in quadrant IV with \(y = -3\) and \(r = 7\), yielding \(x = \sqrt{7^2 - (-3)^2} = \sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10}\). Therefore, \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y} = -\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{3}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\cos\theta = -\frac{12}{13}\) and \(\tan\theta > 0\), find the value of \(13\sin\theta + 5\cot\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta < 0\) and \(\tan\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in quadrant III with \(x = -12\) and \(y = -\sqrt{13^2 - (-12)^2} = -5\). Then \(\sin\theta = -\frac{5}{13}\) and \(\cot\theta = \frac{12}{5}\), so \(13\left(-\frac{5}{13}\right) + 5\left(\frac{12}{5}\right) = -5 + 12 = 7\).

qs.q: Given that \(\sec\theta = -\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}\) and \(\sin\theta < 0\), find the value of \(\sin\theta\cos\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\sec\theta < 0\) and \(\sin\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) is in quadrant III with \(r = \sqrt{13}\) and \(x = -2\), so \(y = -\sqrt{13 - (-2)^2} = -3\). Thus, \(\sin\theta\cos\theta = \left(-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\right)\left(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\right) = \frac{6}{13}\).

qs.q: Given \(\sin\theta = -\frac{2}{3}\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\cot\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\sin\theta < 0\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant IV. With \(y = -2\) and \(r = 3\), \(x = \sqrt{3^2 - (-2)^2} = \sqrt{5}\), giving \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y} = -\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\).

qs.q: Given \(\cos\theta = -\frac{1}{4}\) and \(\tan\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta < 0\) and \(\tan\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant III. With \(x = -1\) and \(r = 4\), \(y = -\sqrt{4^2 - (-1)^2} = -\sqrt{15}\), giving \(\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} = -\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}\).

qs.q: Given \(\cot\theta = -\frac{5}{2}\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\csc\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\cot\theta < 0\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant IV. With \(x = 5\) and \(y = -2\), \(r = \sqrt{5^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{29}\), giving \(\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y} = -\frac{\sqrt{29}}{2}\).

qs.q: Given \(\csc\theta = -\frac{5}{3}\) and \(\cot\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\sec\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\csc\theta < 0\) and \(\cot\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant III. With \(y = -3\) and \(r = 5\), \(x = -\sqrt{5^2 - (-3)^2} = -4\), giving \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x} = -\frac{5}{4}\).

qs.q: Given \(\sec\theta = -3\) and \(\sin\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\tan\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\sec\theta < 0\) and \(\sin\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant II. With \(r = 3\) and \(x = -1\), \(y = \sqrt{3^2 - (-1)^2} = 2\sqrt{2}\), giving \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} = -2\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Given \(\tan\theta = \frac{12}{5}\) and \(\sin\theta < 0\), determine the value of \(\frac{1 - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\).
qs.s: Since \(\tan\theta > 0\) and \(\sin\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant III with \(x = -5\) and \(y = -12\), so \(r = \sqrt{(-5)^2 + (-12)^2} = 13\). Thus \(\sin\theta = -\frac{12}{13}\) and \(\cos\theta = -\frac{5}{13}\), giving \(\frac{1 - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \frac{1 - (-12/13)}{-5/13} = -5\).

qs.q: Given \(\tan\theta = -\frac{7}{24}\) and \(\sin\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\cos\theta + \sin\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\tan\theta < 0\) and \(\sin\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant II with \(y = 7\) and \(x = -24\), so \(r = \sqrt{(-24)^2 + 7^2} = 25\). Therefore, \(\cos\theta + \sin\theta = -\frac{24}{25} + \frac{7}{25} = -\frac{17}{25}\).

qs.q: Given \(\sec\theta = -4\) and \(\tan\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\sin\theta\tan\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\sec\theta < 0\) and \(\tan\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant III with \(x = -1\) and \(r = 4\), so \(y = -\sqrt{4^2 - (-1)^2} = -\sqrt{15}\). Thus, \(\sin\theta\tan\theta = \left(-\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}\right)(\sqrt{15}) = -\frac{15}{4}\).

qs.q: Given \(\csc\theta = \frac{17}{8}\) and \(\cos\theta < 0\), determine the value of \(\frac{\sin\theta}{1 + \cos\theta}\).
qs.s: Since \(\csc\theta > 0\) and \(\cos\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant II with \(y = 8\) and \(r = 17\), so \(x = -\sqrt{17^2 - 8^2} = -15\). Thus \(\sin\theta = \frac{8}{17}\) and \(\cos\theta = -\frac{15}{17}\), giving \(\frac{\sin\theta}{1 + \cos\theta} = \frac{8/17}{1 - 15/17} = 4\).

qs.q: Given \(\cos\theta = \frac{9}{41}\) and \(\sin\theta < 0\), determine the value of \(\csc\theta + \cot\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta > 0\) and \(\sin\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant IV with \(x = 9\) and \(r = 41\), so \(y = -\sqrt{41^2 - 9^2} = -40\). Then \(\csc\theta + \cot\theta = -\frac{41}{40} + \left(-\frac{9}{40}\right) = -\frac{50}{40} = -\frac{5}{4}\).

qs.q: Given \(\sin\theta = -0.6\) and \(\tan\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\sec\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\sin\theta < 0\) and \(\tan\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) terminates in Quadrant III where \(y = -3\), \(r = 5\), and \(x = -\sqrt{5^2 - (-3)^2} = -4\). Therefore, \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x} = -\frac{5}{4}\).

qs.q: Given \(\cos\theta = 0.28\) and \(\tan\theta < 0\), determine the value of \(\csc\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta > 0\) and \(\tan\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) terminates in Quadrant IV where \(x = 7\), \(r = 25\), and \(y = -\sqrt{25^2 - 7^2} = -24\). Therefore, \(\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y} = -\frac{25}{24}\).

qs.q: Given \(\cot\theta = -0.75\) and \(\sin\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\cot\theta < 0\) and \(\sin\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) terminates in Quadrant II where \(x = -3\), \(y = 4\), and \(r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 4^2} = 5\). Therefore, \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{3}{5}\).

qs.q: Given \(\tan\theta = \frac{15}{8}\) and \(\cos\theta < 0\), determine the value of \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\tan\theta > 0\) and \(\cos\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant III where \(x = -8\), \(y = -15\), and \(r = \sqrt{(-8)^2 + (-15)^2} = 17\). Therefore, \(\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} = -\frac{15}{17}\).

qs.q: Given \(\sec\theta = -2.6\) and \(\sin\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\cot\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\sec\theta < 0\) and \(\sin\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) terminates in Quadrant II where \(r = 13\), \(x = -5\), and \(y = \sqrt{13^2 - (-5)^2} = 12\). Therefore, \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y} = -\frac{5}{12}\).

qs.q: Given \(\sec\theta = -\frac{25}{7}\) and \(\sin\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\frac{1 - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\).
qs.s: In Quadrant II, \(r = 25\) and \(x = -7\), so \(y = \sqrt{25^2 - (-7)^2} = 24\), giving \(\sin\theta = \frac{24}{25}\) and \(\cos\theta = -\frac{7}{25}\). Thus, \(\frac{1 - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \frac{1 - 24/25}{-7/25} = -\frac{1}{7}\).

qs.q: Given \(\cot\theta = \frac{8}{15}\) and \(\sin\theta < 0\), determine the value of \(\csc\theta + \sec\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\cot\theta > 0\) and \(\sin\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant III with \(x = -8\), \(y = -15\), and \(r = 17\). Then \(\csc\theta + \sec\theta = -\frac{17}{15} + \left(-\frac{17}{8}\right) = -\frac{391}{120}\).

qs.q: Given \(\cos\theta = \frac{5}{6}\) and \(\tan\theta < 0\), determine the value of \(\sin\theta \cdot \tan\theta\).
qs.s: In Quadrant IV, \(x = 5\) and \(r = 6\), giving \(y = -\sqrt{6^2 - 5^2} = -\sqrt{11}\). Thus, \(\sin\theta \cdot \tan\theta = \left(-\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6}\right)\left(-\frac{\sqrt{11}}{5}\right) = \frac{11}{30}\).

qs.q: Given \(\tan\theta = -\frac{7}{24}\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\sin\theta - \cos\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\tan\theta < 0\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant IV with \(x = 24\), \(y = -7\), and \(r = 25\). Then \(\sin\theta = -\frac{7}{25}\) and \(\cos\theta = \frac{24}{25}\), so \(\sin\theta - \cos\theta = -\frac{7}{25} - \frac{24}{25} = -\frac{31}{25}\).

qs.q: Given \(\sin\theta = -0.8\) and \(\cos\theta < 0\), determine the value of \(\frac{\tan\theta - \sec\theta}{\csc\theta}\).
qs.s: In Quadrant III, \(y = -4\) and \(r = 5\), giving \(x = -3\), which yields \(\tan\theta = \frac{4}{3}\), \(\sec\theta = -\frac{5}{3}\), and \(\csc\theta = -\frac{5}{4}\). Therefore, \(\frac{\tan\theta - \sec\theta}{\csc\theta} = \frac{4/3 - (-5/3)}{-5/4} = \frac{3}{-5/4} = -\frac{12}{5}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\cos\theta = -\frac{1}{4}\) and \(\tan\theta < 0\), determine the value of \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta < 0\) and \(\tan\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant II where \(y\) is positive. With \(x = -1\) and \(r = 4\), \(y = \sqrt{4^2 - (-1)^2} = \sqrt{15}\), which gives \(\sin\theta = \frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\tan\theta = -\frac{3}{4}\) and \(\sin\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\tan\theta < 0\) and \(\sin\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant II, giving \(y = 3\), \(x = -4\), and \(r = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + 3^2} = 5\). Thus, \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{4}{5}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\sec\theta = -\frac{3}{2}\) and \(\sin\theta < 0\), determine the value of \(\tan\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\sec\theta < 0\) and \(\sin\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant III with \(x = -2\), \(r = 3\), and \(y = -\sqrt{3^2 - (-2)^2} = -\sqrt{5}\). Hence, \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} = \frac{-\sqrt{5}}{-2} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\cos\theta = -0.6\) and \(\tan\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta < 0\) and \(\tan\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant III where sine is negative. Thus, \(\sin\theta = -\sqrt{1 - (-0.6)^2} = -\sqrt{0.64} = -0.8\).

qs.q: Given that \(\sin\theta = \frac{5}{13}\) and \(\cos\theta < 0\), determine the value of \(\tan\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\sin\theta > 0\) and \(\cos\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant II, so \(y = 5\), \(r = 13\), and \(x = -\sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = -12\). Therefore, \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} = -\frac{5}{12}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\cos\theta = -\frac{7}{25}\) and \(\sin\theta < 0\), determine the value of \(\csc\theta + \cot\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta < 0\) and \(\sin\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant III, so \(x = -7\), \(r = 25\), and \(y = -\sqrt{25^2 - (-7)^2} = -24\). Thus, \(\csc\theta + \cot\theta = -\frac{25}{24} + \frac{7}{24} = -\frac{18}{24} = -\frac{3}{4}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\sin\theta = -\frac{8}{17}\) and \(\tan\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\sec\theta - \tan\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\sin\theta < 0\) and \(\tan\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant III, so \(y = -8\), \(r = 17\), and \(x = -\sqrt{17^2 - (-8)^2} = -15\). Then \(\sec\theta - \tan\theta = -\frac{17}{15} - \frac{8}{15} = -\frac{25}{15} = -\frac{5}{3}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\tan\theta = 2\) and \(\sin\theta < 0\), determine the value of \(\sin\theta\cos\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\tan\theta > 0\) and \(\sin\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant III with \(x = -1\), \(y = -2\), and \(r = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{5}\). Hence, \(\sin\theta\cos\theta = \left(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\right)\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right) = \frac{2}{5}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\cos\theta = -\frac{20}{29}\) and \(\tan\theta < 0\), determine the value of \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta\).
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta < 0\) and \(\tan\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant II, giving \(x = -20\), \(r = 29\), and \(y = \sqrt{29^2 - (-20)^2} = 21\). Therefore, \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \frac{21}{29} + \left(-\frac{20}{29}\right) = \frac{1}{29}\).

qs.q: Given that \(\cot\theta = -\frac{12}{5}\) and \(\sin\theta > 0\), determine the value of \(\frac{1 - \cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\).
qs.s: Since \(\cot\theta < 0\) and \(\sin\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in Quadrant II with \(x = -12\), \(y = 5\), and \(r = \sqrt{(-12)^2 + 5^2} = 13\). Substituting \(\cos\theta = -\frac{12}{13}\) and \(\sin\theta = \frac{5}{13}\) gives \(\frac{1 - (-12/13)}{5/13} = \frac{25/13}{5/13} = 5\).

exercises.name: Trigonometric functions from terminal ray equation

qs.q: Find \(\cos\theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(x - 3y = 0, x \leq 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(x = -3\) yields \(y = -1\), giving \(r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{10}\). Hence, \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\).

qs.q: Find \(\sin\theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(5x - 2y = 0, x \leq 0\).
qs.s: A point on the terminal ray is \((-2, -5)\), giving \(r = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (-5)^2} = \sqrt{29}\). Therefore, \(\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} = -\frac{5}{\sqrt{29}}\).

qs.q: Find \(\cos\theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(2x + 3y = 0, x \geq 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(x = 3\) gives \(y = -2\), so \(r = \sqrt{3^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{13}\). Thus, \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\).

qs.q: Find \(\sec\theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(3x - 4y = 0, x \geq 0\).
qs.s: A point on the terminal ray is \((4, 3)\), which gives \(r = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5\). Therefore, \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x} = \frac{5}{4}\).

qs.q: Find \(\csc\theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(x + 4y = 0, x \leq 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(x = -4\) gives \(y = 1\), which gives \(r = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{17}\). Thus, \(\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y} = \frac{\sqrt{17}}{1} = \sqrt{17}\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(\csc\theta + \cot\theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(21x - 20y = 0, y \leq 0\).
Find the value of \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(5x + 12y = 0, y \geq 0\).
qs.s: For \(y \geq 0\), choosing \(y = 5\) gives \(x = -12\) and \(r = \sqrt{(-12)^2 + 5^2} = 13\). Therefore, \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \frac{5}{13} + \left(-\frac{12}{13}\right) = -\frac{7}{13}\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(\sin\theta - \cos\theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(7x + 24y = 0, x \leq 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(x = -24\) gives \(y = 7\) and \(r = \sqrt{(-24)^2 + 7^2} = 25\). Therefore, \(\sin\theta - \cos\theta = \frac{7}{25} - \left(-\frac{24}{25}\right) = \frac{31}{25}\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(\sec\theta - \tan\theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(8x - 15y = 0, x \leq 0\).
Find the value of \(\sqrt{34}(\sin\theta + \cos\theta)\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(2(x - 3y) = 5x - y, x \leq 0\).
qs.s: Simplifying gives \(3x + 5y = 0\); with \(x \leq 0\), a point on the ray is \((-5, 3)\) with \(r = \sqrt{34}\). Thus, \(\sqrt{34}(\sin\theta + \cos\theta) = \sqrt{34}\left(\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}} - \frac{5}{\sqrt{34}}\right) = -2\).

qs.q: Find \(\cos \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the relation \(3x - 2y = 0, y \leq 0\).
qs.s: Selecting \(y = -3\) gives \(x = -2\), so \(r = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (-3)^2} = \sqrt{13}\). Thus, \(\cos \theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\).

qs.q: Find \(\sin \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the relation \(3x + y = 0, x \leq 0\).
qs.s: A point on the terminal side with \(x \leq 0\) is \((-1, 3)\), which gives \(r = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{10}\). Therefore, \(\sin \theta = \frac{y}{r} = \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\).

qs.q: Find \(\csc \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the relation \(5x - 2y = 0, y \leq 0\).
qs.s: Setting \(y = -5\) yields \(x = -2\) and \(r = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (-5)^2} = \sqrt{29}\). Therefore, \(\csc \theta = \frac{r}{y} = -\frac{\sqrt{29}}{5}\).

qs.q: Find \(\sec \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the relation \(x + 2y = 0, x \geq 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(x = 2\) gives \(y = -1\) and \(r = \sqrt{2^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{5}\). Thus, \(\sec \theta = \frac{r}{x} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\).

qs.q: Find \(\cot \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the relation \(3x + 5y = 0, y \leq 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(y = -3\) gives \(x = 5\), placing the point at \((5, -3)\). Therefore, \(\cot \theta = \frac{x}{y} = -\frac{5}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(\sec \theta + \tan \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the relation \(7x - 24y = 0, y \leq 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(y = -7\) gives \(x = -24\) and \(r = \sqrt{(-24)^2 + (-7)^2} = 25\). Thus, \(\sec \theta = -\frac{25}{24}\) and \(\tan \theta = \frac{7}{24}\), which yields \(\sec \theta + \tan \theta = -\frac{25}{24} + \frac{7}{24} = -\frac{18}{24} = -\frac{3}{4}\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(2\sin \theta + 3\cos \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the relation \(2(7x - y) = 2x + 3y, x \leq 0\).
qs.s: Simplifying the equation gives \(12x - 5y = 0\), so a point with \(x \leq 0\) is \((-5, -12)\), which gives \(r = \sqrt{(-5)^2 + (-12)^2} = 13\). Then \(2\sin \theta + 3\cos \theta = 2\left(-\frac{12}{13}\right) + 3\left(-\frac{5}{13}\right) = -\frac{39}{13} = -3\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(\sin \theta - \cos \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the relation \(8x + 15y = 0, x \geq 0\).
qs.s: A point on the terminal side with \(x \geq 0\) is \((15, -8)\), which gives \(r = \sqrt{15^2 + (-8)^2} = 17\). Then \(\sin \theta = -\frac{8}{17}\) and \(\cos \theta = \frac{15}{17}\), so \(\sin \theta - \cos \theta = -\frac{8}{17} - \frac{15}{17} = -\frac{23}{17}\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(\frac{\sin \theta}{1 + \cos \theta}\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the relation \(20x - 21y = 0, x \leq 0\).
qs.s: A point on the terminal side is \((-21, -20)\), giving \(r = \sqrt{(-21)^2 + (-20)^2} = 29\). Therefore, \(\sin \theta = -\frac{20}{29}\) and \(\cos \theta = -\frac{21}{29}\), so \(\frac{\sin \theta}{1 + \cos \theta} = \frac{-20/29}{1 - 21/29} = \frac{-20/29}{8/29} = -\frac{5}{2}\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(\sin \theta + \cos \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the relation \(9x + 40y = 0, y \geq 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(y = 9\) gives \(x = -40\) and \(r = \sqrt{(-40)^2 + 9^2} = 41\). Then \(\sin \theta = \frac{9}{41}\) and \(\cos \theta = -\frac{40}{41}\), so \(\sin \theta + \cos \theta = \frac{9}{41} - \frac{40}{41} = -\frac{31}{41}\).

qs.q: Find \(\sin \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(x + \sqrt{3}y = 0, y \ge 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(y = 1\) yields \(x = -\sqrt{3}\), so \(r = \sqrt{(-\sqrt{3})^2 + 1^2} = 2\). Thus, \(\sin \theta = \frac{y}{r} = \frac{1}{2}\).

qs.q: Find \(\cot \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(3x + 4y = 0, x \ge 0\).
qs.s: A point on the ray with \(x \ge 0\) is \((4, -3)\), which lies in Quadrant IV. Therefore, \(\cot \theta = \frac{x}{y} = -\frac{4}{3}\).

qs.q: Find \(\cos \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(\sqrt{7}x - 3y = 0, x \le 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(x = -3\) gives \(y = -\sqrt{7}\), which lies in Quadrant III. Then \(r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + (-\sqrt{7})^2} = 4\), so \(\cos \theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{3}{4}\).

qs.q: Find \(\csc \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(x - 2\sqrt{2}y = 0, x \le 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(y = -1\) gives \(x = -2\sqrt{2}\), which has distance \(r = \sqrt{(-2\sqrt{2})^2 + (-1)^2} = 3\) from the origin. Thus, \(\csc \theta = \frac{r}{y} = \frac{3}{-1} = -3\).

qs.q: Find \(\sec \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(\sqrt{21}x + 2y = 0, y \ge 0\).
qs.s: Since \(y \ge 0\), choosing \(x = -2\) gives \(y = \sqrt{21}\) and \(r = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (\sqrt{21})^2} = 5\). Thus, \(\sec \theta = \frac{r}{x} = -\frac{5}{2}\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(\frac{\cos \theta}{1 - \sin \theta}\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(8x + 15y = 0, y \le 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(y = -8\) gives \(x = 15\) and \(r = \sqrt{15^2 + (-8)^2} = 17\), so \(\cos \theta = \frac{15}{17}\) and \(\sin \theta = -\frac{8}{17}\). Evaluating the expression gives \(\frac{15/17}{1 - (-8/17)} = \frac{15/17}{25/17} = \frac{3}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(\cos \theta - \sin \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the relation \(3(x + 2y) = x + y, y \ge 0\).
qs.s: Simplifying yields \(2x + 5y = 0\), so with \(y = 2\) we have \(x = -5\) and \(r = \sqrt{(-5)^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{29}\). Then \(\cos \theta - \sin \theta = -\frac{5}{\sqrt{29}} - \frac{2}{\sqrt{29}} = -\frac{7\sqrt{29}}{29}\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(\sin \theta - \cos \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(5x + 12y = 0, x \le 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(x = -12\) gives \(y = 5\), so \(r = \sqrt{(-12)^2 + 5^2} = 13\). Then \(\sin \theta = \frac{5}{13}\) and \(\cos \theta = -\frac{12}{13}\), so \(\sin \theta - \cos \theta = \frac{5}{13} - \left(-\frac{12}{13}\right) = \frac{17}{13}\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(\sqrt{7}\cos \theta - \sqrt{2}\sin \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(\sqrt{2}x + \sqrt{7}y = 0, x \le 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(x = -\sqrt{7}\) gives \(y = \sqrt{2}\) and \(r = \sqrt{(-\sqrt{7})^2 + (\sqrt{2})^2} = 3\). Then \(\sqrt{7}\cos \theta - \sqrt{2}\sin \theta = \sqrt{7}\left(-\frac{\sqrt{7}}{3}\right) - \sqrt{2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\right) = -\frac{7}{3} - \frac{2}{3} = -3\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(\sec \theta - \tan \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(24x - 7y = 0, x \le 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(x = -7\) gives \(y = -24\) in Quadrant III, with \(r = \sqrt{(-7)^2 + (-24)^2} = 25\). Then \(\sec \theta = -\frac{25}{7}\) and \(\tan \theta = \frac{24}{7}\), so \(\sec \theta - \tan \theta = -\frac{25}{7} - \frac{24}{7} = -7\).

qs.q: Find \(\cos \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(4x + 3y = 0, x \le 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(x = -3\) yields \(y = 4\), which gives \(r = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 4^2} = 5\). Thus, \(\cos \theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{3}{5}\).

qs.q: Find \(\cos \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(y = 0, x \le 0\).
qs.s: A point on the ray is \((-1, 0)\), giving \(r = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + 0^2} = 1\). Thus, \(\cos \theta = \frac{x}{r} = \frac{-1}{1} = -1\).

qs.q: Find \(\sin \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(3x - 4y = 0, x \ge 0\).
qs.s: Setting \(x = 4\) yields \(y = 3\), giving the point \((4, 3)\) with \(r = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5\). Thus, \(\sin \theta = \frac{y}{r} = \frac{3}{5}\).

qs.q: Find \(\sin \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(x = 0, y \ge 0\).
qs.s: A point on the ray is \((0, 1)\), giving \(r = \sqrt{0^2 + 1^2} = 1\). Thus, \(\sin \theta = \frac{y}{r} = \frac{1}{1} = 1\).

qs.q: Find \(\tan \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(y = -2x, x \ge 0\).
qs.s: Choosing \(x = 1\) gives \(y = -2(1) = -2\), so a point on the ray is \((1, -2)\). Thus, \(\tan \theta = \frac{y}{x} = \frac{-2}{1} = -2\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(\sin^2 \theta - \cos^2 \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(3x + 2y = 0, x \le 0\).
qs.s: A point on the ray is \((-2, 3)\), which gives \(r = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{13}\). Then \(\sin^2 \theta - \cos^2 \theta = \left(\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\right)^2 - \left(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\right)^2 = \frac{9}{13} - \frac{4}{13} = \frac{5}{13}\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(\frac{1 - \cos \theta}{\sin \theta}\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(4x - 3y = 0, x \le 0\).
qs.s: A point on the ray is \((-3, -4)\), giving \(r = 5\), \(\cos \theta = -\frac{3}{5}\), and \(\sin \theta = -\frac{4}{5}\). Then \(\frac{1 - (-3/5)}{-4/5} = \frac{8/5}{-4/5} = -2\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(\sec \theta - \tan \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(8x - 15y = 0, x \le 0\).
qs.s: A point on the ray is \((-15, -8)\), yielding \(r = \sqrt{(-15)^2 + (-8)^2} = 17\). Then \(\sec \theta - \tan \theta = \frac{17}{-15} - \frac{-8}{-15} = -\frac{25}{15} = -\frac{5}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the value of \(25\sin \theta + 24\tan \theta\) if \(\theta\) is an angle in standard position whose terminal side is the graph of the given relation: \(7x + 24y = 0, x \ge 0\).
qs.s: A point on the ray is \((24, -7)\), giving \(r = \sqrt{24^2 + (-7)^2} = 25\). Then \(25\sin \theta + 24\tan \theta = 25\left(-\frac{7}{25}\right) + 24\left(-\frac{7}{24}\right) = -7 - 7 = -14\).

exercises.name: Coordinates of a point from distance and trigonometric ratio

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 25; II; \(\cos\theta = -\frac{7}{25}\)
qs.s: In quadrant II, \(x < 0\) and \(y > 0\). With \(r = 25\), \(x = 25\left(-\frac{7}{25}\right) = -7\) and \(y = \sqrt{25^2 - (-7)^2} = 24\), giving the coordinates \((-7, 24)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 15; IV; \(\cos\theta = \frac{4}{5}\)
qs.s: In quadrant IV, \(x > 0\) and \(y < 0\). Using \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = \frac{4}{5}\) with \(r = 15\), we get \(x = 15\left(\frac{4}{5}\right) = 12\) and \(y = -\sqrt{15^2 - 12^2} = -9\), giving the coordinates \((12, -9)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 34; IV; \(\tan\theta = -\frac{8}{15}\)
qs.s: In quadrant IV, \(x > 0\) and \(y < 0\). The reference hypotenuse is \(\sqrt{15^2 + (-8)^2} = 17\), so scaling by \(\frac{34}{17} = 2\) gives \(x = 2(15) = 30\) and \(y = 2(-8) = -16\), resulting in \((30, -16)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 26; III; \(\sin\theta = -\frac{5}{13}\)
qs.s: In quadrant III, both \(x\) and \(y\) are negative. With \(r = 26\) and \(y = 26\left(-\frac{5}{13}\right) = -10\), we find \(x = -\sqrt{26^2 - (-10)^2} = -24\), so the coordinates are \((-24, -10)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 20; I; \(\tan\theta = \frac{3}{4}\)
qs.s: In quadrant I, \(x > 0\) and \(y > 0\). The reference ratio has base hypotenuse \(\sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5\), so scaling by \(\frac{20}{5} = 4\) yields \(x = 4(4) = 16\) and \(y = 4(3) = 12\), giving \((16, 12)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 15; III; \(\cos\theta = -\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\)
qs.s: In quadrant III, \(x < 0\) and \(y < 0\). With \(r = 15\), \(x = 15\left(-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\right) = -3\sqrt{5}\) and \(y = -\sqrt{15^2 - (-3\sqrt{5})^2} = -\sqrt{180} = -6\sqrt{5}\), giving \((-3\sqrt{5}, -6\sqrt{5})\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 6; IV; \(\sec\theta = \frac{3}{2}\)
qs.s: Since \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x} = \frac{3}{2}\) and \(r = 6\), we find \(x = 4\). In quadrant IV, \(y < 0\), giving \(y = -\sqrt{6^2 - 4^2} = -\sqrt{20} = -2\sqrt{5}\), which yields \((4, -2\sqrt{5})\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 14; I; \(\csc\theta = \frac{7}{3}\)
qs.s: Since \(\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y} = \frac{7}{3}\) and \(r = 14\), solving gives \(y = 6\). In quadrant I, \(x > 0\), so \(x = \sqrt{14^2 - 6^2} = \sqrt{160} = 4\sqrt{10}\), giving the coordinates \((4\sqrt{10}, 6)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 10; III; \(\sin\theta = -\frac{1}{3}\)
qs.s: In quadrant III, both coordinates are negative. With \(r = 10\), \(y = 10\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) = -\frac{10}{3}\) and \(x = -\sqrt{10^2 - \left(-\frac{10}{3}\right)^2} = -\sqrt{\frac{800}{9}} = -\frac{20\sqrt{2}}{3}\), giving \(\left(-\frac{20\sqrt{2}}{3}, -\frac{10}{3}\right)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 12; II; \(\tan\theta = -\frac{5}{12}\)
qs.s: In quadrant II, \(x < 0\) and \(y > 0\). The reference right triangle has hypotenuse \(\sqrt{(-12)^2 + 5^2} = 13\), so by proportion \(x = 12\left(-\frac{12}{13}\right) = -\frac{144}{13}\) and \(y = 12\left(\frac{5}{13}\right) = \frac{60}{13}\), giving \(\left(-\frac{144}{13}, \frac{60}{13}\right)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 7; I; \(\tan\theta = 1\)
qs.s: In quadrant I, both \(x\) and \(y\) are positive, so \(\tan\theta = 1\) gives a reference point \((1, 1)\) with distance \(r_0 = \sqrt{2}\). Multiplying by the ratio \(\frac{7}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{7\sqrt{2}}{2}\) gives \(\left(\frac{7\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{7\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 4; IV; \(\tan\theta = -1\)
qs.s: In quadrant IV, \(x > 0\) and \(y < 0\), so \(\tan\theta = -1\) gives a reference point \((1, -1)\) with distance \(r_0 = \sqrt{2}\). Scaling by \(\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} = 2\sqrt{2}\) gives the coordinates \((2\sqrt{2}, -2\sqrt{2})\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 2; II; \(\tan\theta = -1\)
qs.s: In quadrant II, \(x < 0\) and \(y > 0\), so \(\tan\theta = -1\) gives reference point \((-1, 1)\) with distance \(r_0 = \sqrt{2}\). Scaling by \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}\) gives \((-\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2})\).
