qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 5; II; \(\tan\theta = -1\)
qs.s: In quadrant II, \(x < 0\) and \(y > 0\), so \(\tan\theta = -1\) corresponds to a reference point \((-1, 1)\) with distance \(r_0 = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{2}\). Scaling by \(\frac{r}{r_0} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}\) gives the coordinates \(\left(-\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 6; III; \(\tan\theta = 1\)
qs.s: In quadrant III, both \(x\) and \(y\) are negative, so \(\tan\theta = 1\) corresponds to reference point \((-1, -1)\) with distance \(r_0 = \sqrt{2}\). Scaling by \(\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} = 3\sqrt{2}\) gives \((-3\sqrt{2}, -3\sqrt{2})\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 10; II; \(\cot\theta = -\frac{12}{5}\)
qs.s: In quadrant II, \(x < 0\) and \(y > 0\), so \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y} = -\frac{12}{5}\) gives reference point \((-12, 5)\) with distance \(r_0 = \sqrt{(-12)^2 + 5^2} = 13\). Scaling by \(\frac{10}{13}\) gives \(\left(-\frac{120}{13}, \frac{50}{13}\right)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 15; II; \(\cos\theta = -\frac{2}{3}\)
qs.s: Using \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r}\), we find \(x = 15\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) = -10\). Since \(y > 0\) in quadrant II, \(y = \sqrt{15^2 - (-10)^2} = \sqrt{125} = 5\sqrt{5}\), giving \((-10, 5\sqrt{5})\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: \(2\sqrt{10}\); III; \(\csc\theta = -\sqrt{10}\)
qs.s: From \(\csc\theta = \frac{r_0}{y} = -\sqrt{10}\), in quadrant III we have \(y_0 = -1\) and \(x_0 = -\sqrt{(\sqrt{10})^2 - (-1)^2} = -3\). Scaling by \(\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{\sqrt{10}} = 2\) yields \((-6, -2)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 12; III; \(\tan\theta = \frac{\sqrt{7}}{3}\)
qs.s: In quadrant III, \(x < 0\) and \(y < 0\), giving reference point \((-3, -\sqrt{7})\) with distance \(r_0 = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + (-\sqrt{7})^2} = \sqrt{16} = 4\). Scaling by \(\frac{12}{4} = 3\) gives the coordinates \((-9, -3\sqrt{7})\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 6; I; \(\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2}\)
qs.s: With \(r = 6\), \(y = r\sin\theta = 6\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = 3\). In quadrant I, \(x = \sqrt{6^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{27} = 3\sqrt{3}\), so the point is \((3\sqrt{3}, 3)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 10; II; \(\cos\theta = -\frac{3}{5}\)
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{3}{5}\), \(x = 10\left(-\frac{3}{5}\right) = -6\). In quadrant II, \(y > 0\), so \(y = \sqrt{10^2 - (-6)^2} = 8\), giving \((-6, 8)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 5; IV; \(\tan\theta = -\frac{4}{3}\)
qs.s: In quadrant IV, \(x > 0\) and \(y < 0\), so \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} = -\frac{4}{3}\) gives reference radius \(r = \sqrt{3^2 + (-4)^2} = 5\). Since the given distance is 5, \((x, y) = (3, -4)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 4; III; \(\csc\theta = -2\)
qs.s: Since \(\csc\theta = -2\), \(\sin\theta = -\frac{1}{2}\), so \(y = 4\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = -2\). In quadrant III, \(x = -\sqrt{4^2 - (-2)^2} = -\sqrt{12} = -2\sqrt{3}\), giving \((-2\sqrt{3}, -2)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 6; III; \(\cot\theta = 1\)
qs.s: In quadrant III, \(x < 0\), \(y < 0\), and \(\cot\theta = 1\) means \(x = y\). From \(x^2 + y^2 = 6^2\), we have \(2x^2 = 36 \implies x = y = -\sqrt{18} = -3\sqrt{2}\), giving \((-3\sqrt{2}, -3\sqrt{2})\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 15; II; \(\tan\theta = -\frac{5}{12}\)
qs.s: In quadrant II, \(x < 0\) and \(y > 0\), so \(\cos\theta = -\frac{12}{13}\) and \(\sin\theta = \frac{5}{13}\). Multiplying each by \(r = 15\) gives \(x = -\frac{180}{13}\) and \(y = \frac{75}{13}\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 14; IV; \(\csc\theta = -\frac{7}{3}\)
qs.s: Since \(\sin\theta = -\frac{3}{7}\), \(y = 14\left(-\frac{3}{7}\right) = -6\). In quadrant IV, \(x = \sqrt{14^2 - (-6)^2} = \sqrt{160} = 4\sqrt{10}\), yielding \((4\sqrt{10}, -6)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: \(\sqrt{39}\); III; \(\sec\theta = -\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}\)
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\), \(x = \sqrt{39}\left(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\right) = -2\sqrt{3}\). In quadrant III, \(y = -\sqrt{(\sqrt{39})^2 - (-2\sqrt{3})^2} = -\sqrt{27} = -3\sqrt{3}\), giving \((-2\sqrt{3}, -3\sqrt{3})\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 7; III; \(\sin\theta = -\frac{2}{3}\)
qs.s: Here \(y = 7\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) = -\frac{14}{3}\). In quadrant III, \(x = -\sqrt{7^2 - \left(-\frac{14}{3}\right)^2} = -\sqrt{\frac{245}{9}} = -\frac{7\sqrt{5}}{3}\), giving \(\left(-\frac{7\sqrt{5}}{3}, -\frac{14}{3}\right)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 12; I; \(\cot\theta = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\)
qs.s: With \(x_{\text{ref}} = \sqrt{5}\) and \(y_{\text{ref}} = 2\), the reference hypotenuse is \(\sqrt{5+4} = 3\). Scaling by \(\frac{12}{3} = 4\) yields \(x = 4\sqrt{5}\) and \(y = 8\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 7; III; \(\sec\theta = -\frac{5}{4}\)
qs.s: In quadrant III, \(x < 0\) and \(y < 0\). With \(\sec\theta = \frac{r_0}{x_0} = -\frac{5}{4}\), choose \(x_0 = -4\) and \(r_0 = 5\), giving \(y_0 = -\sqrt{5^2 - (-4)^2} = -3\). Scaling to distance \(r = 7\) yields \((x, y) = \left(7\cdot\left(-\frac{4}{5}\right), 7\cdot\left(-\frac{3}{5}\right)\right) = \left(-\frac{28}{5}, -\frac{21}{5}\right)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 6; IV; \(\tan\theta = -\frac{3}{4}\)
qs.s: In quadrant IV, \(x > 0\) and \(y < 0\). With \(\tan\theta = -\frac{3}{4}\), choose \(x_0 = 4\) and \(y_0 = -3\), yielding \(r_0 = \sqrt{4^2 + (-3)^2} = 5\). Scaling by \(r = 6\) gives \(x = 6\left(\frac{4}{5}\right) = \frac{24}{5}\) and \(y = 6\left(-\frac{3}{5}\right) = -\frac{18}{5}\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 9; III; \(\cos\theta = -\frac{5}{13}\)
qs.s: In quadrant III, \(x < 0\) and \(y < 0\). Since \(\cos\theta = \frac{x_0}{r_0} = -\frac{5}{13}\), set \(x_0 = -5\) and \(r_0 = 13\), which gives \(y_0 = -\sqrt{13^2 - (-5)^2} = -12\). Scaling to distance \(r = 9\) gives \((x, y) = \left(9\cdot\left(-\frac{5}{13}\right), 9\cdot\left(-\frac{12}{13}\right)\right) = \left(-\frac{45}{13}, -\frac{108}{13}\right)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 4; I; \(\csc\theta = \frac{13}{12}\)
qs.s: In quadrant I, both \(x\) and \(y\) are positive. Since \(\csc\theta = \frac{r_0}{y_0} = \frac{13}{12}\), set \(r_0 = 13\) and \(y_0 = 12\), giving \(x_0 = \sqrt{13^2 - 12^2} = 5\). Scaling to distance \(r = 4\) gives \((x, y) = \left(4\cdot\frac{5}{13}, 4\cdot\frac{12}{13}\right) = \left(\frac{20}{13}, \frac{48}{13}\right)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 8; IV; \(\cos\theta = \frac{3}{7}\)
qs.s: In quadrant IV, \(x > 0\) and \(y < 0\). With \(\cos\theta = \frac{x_0}{r_0} = \frac{3}{7}\), set \(x_0 = 3\) and \(r_0 = 7\), giving \(y_0 = -\sqrt{7^2 - 3^2} = -\sqrt{40} = -2\sqrt{10}\). Scaling to distance \(r = 8\) gives \((x, y) = \left(8\cdot\frac{3}{7}, 8\cdot\left(-\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}\right)\right) = \left(\frac{24}{7}, -\frac{16\sqrt{10}}{7}\right)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 15; III; \(\csc\theta = -\frac{5}{2}\)
qs.s: In quadrant III, \(x < 0\) and \(y < 0\). With \(\csc\theta = \frac{r_0}{y_0} = -\frac{5}{2}\), we have \(y_0 = -2\) and \(r_0 = 5\), giving \(x_0 = -\sqrt{5^2 - (-2)^2} = -\sqrt{21}\). Scaling to distance \(r = 15\) gives \((x, y) = \left(15\cdot\left(-\frac{\sqrt{21}}{5}\right), 15\cdot\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right)\right) = (-3\sqrt{21}, -6)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 6; III; \(\cot\theta = \frac{40}{9}\)
qs.s: In quadrant III, \(x < 0\) and \(y < 0\). With \(\cot\theta = \frac{x_0}{y_0} = \frac{40}{9}\), set \(x_0 = -40\) and \(y_0 = -9\), so \(r_0 = \sqrt{(-40)^2 + (-9)^2} = \sqrt{1681} = 41\). Scaling to distance \(r = 6\) yields \((x, y) = \left(6\cdot\left(-\frac{40}{41}\right), 6\cdot\left(-\frac{9}{41}\right)\right) = \left(-\frac{240}{41}, -\frac{54}{41}\right)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 11; II; \(\sec\theta = -\frac{17}{15}\)
qs.s: In quadrant II, \(x < 0\) and \(y > 0\). With \(\sec\theta = \frac{r_0}{x_0} = -\frac{17}{15}\), we have \(x_0 = -15\) and \(r_0 = 17\), so \(y_0 = \sqrt{17^2 - (-15)^2} = 8\). Scaling by \(r = 11\) gives \((x, y) = \left(11\cdot\left(-\frac{15}{17}\right), 11\cdot\frac{8}{17}\right) = \left(-\frac{165}{17}, \frac{88}{17}\right)\).

qs.q: Determine the coordinates of the point at the given distance from the origin in the stated quadrant, if \(\theta\) is its position angle: 15; IV; \(\tan\theta = -\frac{24}{7}\)
qs.s: In quadrant IV, \(x > 0\) and \(y < 0\). With \(\tan\theta = -\frac{24}{7}\), set \(x_0 = 7\) and \(y_0 = -24\), giving \(r_0 = \sqrt{7^2 + (-24)^2} = 25\). Scaling to distance \(r = 15\) yields \((x, y) = \left(15\cdot\frac{7}{25}, 15\cdot\left(-\frac{24}{25}\right)\right) = \left(\frac{21}{5}, -\frac{72}{5}\right)\).

exercises.name: Reciprocal and cofunction values in terms of a variable

qs.q: Let \(A\) be an acute angle with \(\cos A = m\). Find \(\sin(90^\circ - A)\) in terms of \(m\).
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, \(\sin(90^\circ - A) = \cos A\). Therefore, \(\sin(90^\circ - A) = m\).

qs.q: Let \(B\) be an acute angle with \(\tan B = k\). Find \(\cot(90^\circ - B)\) in terms of \(k\).
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, \(\cot(90^\circ - B) = \tan B\). Since \(\tan B = k\), \(\cot(90^\circ - B) = k\).

qs.q: Let \(\alpha\) be an acute angle with \(\cot \alpha = p\). Find \(\tan \alpha\) in terms of \(p\).
qs.s: Tangent and cotangent are reciprocals, so \(\tan \alpha = \frac{1}{\cot \alpha} = \frac{1}{p}\).

qs.q: Let \(\theta\) be an acute angle with \(\cos \theta = c\). Find \(\sec \theta\) in terms of \(c\).
qs.s: Secant is the reciprocal of cosine, so \(\sec \theta = \frac{1}{\cos \theta}\). Since \(\cos \theta = c\), we obtain \(\sec \theta = \frac{1}{c}\).

qs.q: Let \(\beta\) be an acute angle with \(\sec \beta = u\). Find \(\csc(90^\circ - \beta)\) in terms of \(u\).
qs.s: By the cofunction identity, \(\csc(90^\circ - \beta) = \sec \beta\). Since \(\sec \beta = u\), we have \(\csc(90^\circ - \beta) = u\).

qs.q: Let \(B\) be an acute angle with \(\sin B = \frac{x}{3}\). Express \(\csc B + \cos(90^\circ - B)\) in terms of \(x\) as a single simplified fraction.
qs.s: Since \(\csc B = \frac{1}{\sin B} = \frac{3}{x}\) and \(\cos(90^\circ - B) = \sin B = \frac{x}{3}\), their sum is \(\frac{3}{x} + \frac{x}{3} = \frac{9 + x^2}{3x}\).

qs.q: Let \(\beta\) be an acute angle with \(\sin \beta = \frac{3}{w}\). Express \(\frac{\csc \beta}{\cos(90^\circ - \beta) + 1}\) in terms of \(w\) as a single simplified fraction.
qs.s: We have \(\csc \beta = \frac{w}{3}\) and \(\cos(90^\circ - \beta) = \frac{3}{w}\), making the denominator \(\frac{3}{w} + 1 = \frac{w + 3}{w}\). Dividing gives \(\frac{w/3}{(w+3)/w} = \frac{w^2}{3(w + 3)} = \frac{w^2}{3w + 9}\).

qs.q: Let \(\alpha\) be an acute angle with \(\sec \alpha = \frac{3a}{2}\). Express \(\csc(90^\circ - \alpha) + 6\cos \alpha\) in terms of \(a\) as a single simplified fraction.
qs.s: Since \(\csc(90^\circ - \alpha) = \sec \alpha = \frac{3a}{2}\) and \(\cos \alpha = \frac{1}{\sec \alpha} = \frac{2}{3a}\), the expression equals \(\frac{3a}{2} + 6\left(\frac{2}{3a}\right) = \frac{3a}{2} + \frac{4}{a} = \frac{3a^2 + 8}{2a}\).

qs.q: Let \(\theta\) be an acute angle with \(\cos \theta = \frac{2}{y}\). Express \(\sec \theta - 4\sin(90^\circ - \theta)\) in terms of \(y\) as a single simplified fraction.
qs.s: We have \(\sec \theta = \frac{1}{\cos \theta} = \frac{y}{2}\) and \(\sin(90^\circ - \theta) = \cos \theta = \frac{2}{y}\), so \(\sec \theta - 4\sin(90^\circ - \theta) = \frac{y}{2} - \frac{8}{y} = \frac{y^2 - 16}{2y}\).

qs.q: Let \(A\) be an acute angle with \(\tan A = \frac{k}{5}\). Express \(\frac{\cot(90^\circ - A)}{\cot A}\) in terms of \(k\) in simplest form.
qs.s: Using cofunction and reciprocal identities, \(\cot(90^\circ - A) = \tan A = \frac{k}{5}\) and \(\cot A = \frac{1}{\tan A} = \frac{5}{k}\). Dividing these yields \(\frac{k/5}{5/k} = \frac{k^2}{25}\).

exercises.name: Reciprocal and cofunction values in terms of a variable

qs.q: Let \(\phi\) be an acute angle with \(\cos \phi = c\). Express \(\sec \phi - \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \phi\right)\) in terms of \(c\).
qs.s: Since \(\sec \phi = \frac{1}{c}\) and \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \phi\right) = \cos \phi = c\), the difference is \(\frac{1}{c} - c = \frac{1 - c^2}{c}\).

qs.q: Let \(\theta\) be an acute angle with \(\tan \theta = k\). Express \(\cot \theta + \cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)\) in terms of \(k\).
qs.s: Using the reciprocal identity, \(\cot \theta = \frac{1}{k}\), and using the cofunction identity, \(\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \tan \theta = k\). Thus, \(\frac{1}{k} + k = \frac{k^2 + 1}{k}\).

qs.q: Let \(\theta\) be an acute angle with \(\sin \theta = a\). Express \(\csc \theta + \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)\) in terms of \(a\).
qs.s: By the reciprocal identity, \(\csc \theta = \frac{1}{a}\), and by the cofunction identity, \(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \sin \theta = a\). Adding these gives \(\frac{1}{a} + a = \frac{a^2 + 1}{a}\).

qs.q: Let \(\beta\) be an acute angle with \(\cos \beta = p\). Express \(\frac{\sec \beta}{\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \beta\right)}\) in terms of \(p\).
qs.s: We know \(\sec \beta = \frac{1}{p}\) and \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \beta\right) = \cos \beta = p\). Dividing gives \(\frac{1/p}{p} = \frac{1}{p^2}\).

qs.q: Let \(\alpha\) be an acute angle with \(\sin \alpha = m\). Express \(\csc \alpha - \cos(90^\circ - \alpha)\) in terms of \(m\).
qs.s: We have \(\csc \alpha = \frac{1}{m}\) and \(\cos(90^\circ - \alpha) = \sin \alpha = m\). Subtracting yields \(\frac{1}{m} - m = \frac{1 - m^2}{m}\).

qs.q: Let \(\theta\) be an acute angle with \(\sin \theta = \frac{a}{3}\). Express \(2\csc \theta + 3\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)\) in terms of \(a\).
qs.s: Here \(\csc \theta = \frac{3}{a}\) and \(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \frac{a}{3}\), so \(2\left(\frac{3}{a}\right) + 3\left(\frac{a}{3}\right) = \frac{6}{a} + a = \frac{a^2 + 6}{a}\).

qs.q: Let \(\theta\) be an acute angle with \(\cos \theta = \frac{2}{x}\). Express \(\sec^2 \theta - \sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)\) in terms of \(x\).
qs.s: We have \(\sec \theta = \frac{x}{2}\) and \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \frac{2}{x}\). Squaring and subtracting gives \(\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{2}{x}\right)^2 = \frac{x^2}{4} - \frac{4}{x^2} = \frac{x^4 - 16}{4x^2}\).

qs.q: Let \(\beta\) be an acute angle with \(\sec \beta = \frac{3u}{2}\). Express \(\frac{2\cos \beta + \csc\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \beta\right)}{\csc\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \beta\right) - \cos \beta}\) in terms of \(u\).
qs.s: Since \(\cos \beta = \frac{2}{3u}\) and \(\csc\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \beta\right) = \sec \beta = \frac{3u}{2}\), the numerator is \(\frac{4}{3u} + \frac{3u}{2} = \frac{8 + 9u^2}{6u}\) and the denominator is \(\frac{3u}{2} - \frac{2}{3u} = \frac{9u^2 - 4}{6u}\), giving \(\frac{9u^2 + 8}{9u^2 - 4}\).

qs.q: Let \(\theta\) be an acute angle with \(\tan \theta = \frac{k}{2}\). Express \(\cot \theta + 4\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) - \cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)\) in terms of \(k\).
qs.s: Since \(\cot \theta = \frac{2}{k}\), \(\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \cot \theta = \frac{2}{k}\), and \(\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \tan \theta = \frac{k}{2}\), the expression evaluates to \(\frac{2}{k} + 4\left(\frac{2}{k}\right) - \frac{k}{2} = \frac{10}{k} - \frac{k}{2} = \frac{20 - k^2}{2k}\).

qs.q: Let \(\theta\) be an acute angle with \(\cos \theta = \frac{m}{4}\). Express \(\frac{\sec \theta - \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)}\) in terms of \(m\).
qs.s: Substitute \(\sec \theta = \frac{4}{m}\) and \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \frac{m}{4}\) to get \(\frac{\frac{4}{m} - \frac{m}{4}}{\frac{m}{4}} = \frac{\frac{16 - m^2}{4m}}{\frac{m}{4}} = \frac{16 - m^2}{m^2}\).

exercises.name: Trigonometric ratios from curve intersection point

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the lines \(x + y = -7\) and \(3x - y = 39\). Find \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: Adding the equations gives \(4x = 32\), which gives \(x = 8\) and \(y = -15\). With \(r = \sqrt{8^2 + (-15)^2} = 17\), we find \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = \frac{8}{17}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the lines \(x - y = 7\) and \(2x + y = -22\). Find \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: Adding the equations yields \(3x = -15\), so \(x = -5\) and \(y = -12\). The distance from the origin is \(r = \sqrt{(-5)^2 + (-12)^2} = 13\), giving \(\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} = -\frac{12}{13}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the lines \(2x - 3y = -1\) and \(3x + y = 15\). Find \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: Solving the system gives \(x = 4\) and \(y = 3\), giving \(r = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5\). Hence, \(\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} = \frac{3}{5}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the lines \(x + 2y = 2\) and \(2x - y = -11\). Find \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: Solving the system gives the intersection point \((-4, 3)\), with distance \(r = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + 3^2} = 5\). Therefore, \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{4}{5}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the lines \(x + 3y = 3\) and \(2x + y = -19\). Find \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: Solving the system yields the point \((-12, 5)\). The distance to the origin is \(r = \sqrt{(-12)^2 + 5^2} = 13\), so \(\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} = \frac{5}{13}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the lines \(2(x + 3) - 3(y - 2) = 6\) and \(3(x - 1) + 2(y + 4) = -56\). Find \(\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta\).
qs.s: Simplifying the equations gives \(2x - 3y = -6\) and \(3x + 2y = -61\), yielding the intersection point \((-15, -8)\) and \(r = 17\). Therefore, \(\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta = -\frac{8}{17} + 2\left(-\frac{15}{17}\right) = -\frac{38}{17}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the lines \(\frac{x}{4} + \frac{y}{3} = 0\) and \(\frac{x}{2} - \frac{y}{6} = 5\). Find \(\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta\).
qs.s: Clearing fractions yields \(3x + 4y = 0\) and \(3x - y = 30\), whose intersection is \((8, -6)\) with \(r = 10\). Thus, \(\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta = \left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^2 - \left(-\frac{3}{5}\right)^2 = \frac{7}{25}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the lines \(2x - y = -19\) and \(3x - 2y = -18\). Find \(\cos\theta - \sin\theta\).
qs.s: Solving the system gives the intersection point \((-20, -21)\) and \(r = \sqrt{(-20)^2 + (-21)^2} = 29\). Then \(\cos\theta - \sin\theta = -\frac{20}{29} - \left(-\frac{21}{29}\right) = \frac{1}{29}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the lines \(2(x + 3) + (y - 2) = 6\) and \((x - 1) + 2(y + 2) = 22\). Find \(\sin\theta\cos\theta\).
qs.s: Expanding and simplifying yields the system \(2x + y = 2\) and \(x + 2y = 19\), with solution \((-5, 12)\) and \(r = 13\). Therefore, \(\sin\theta\cos\theta = \left(\frac{12}{13}\right)\left(-\frac{5}{13}\right) = -\frac{60}{169}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the lines \(3x + y = 3\) and \(5x + 2y = 13\). Find \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta\).
qs.s: Solving the system gives the intersection point \((-7, 24)\), so \(r = \sqrt{(-7)^2 + 24^2} = 25\). Thus, \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \frac{24}{25} + \left(-\frac{7}{25}\right) = \frac{17}{25}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the curves \(y = x^2 - 2x + 1\) and \(y = 4x - 8\). Find \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: Setting \(x^2 - 2x + 1 = 4x - 8\) yields \((x - 3)^2 = 0\), giving the intersection point \((3, 4)\). With \(r = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\), we have \(\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} = \frac{4}{5}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the curves \(y = x^2 - 4x - 1\) and \(y = 2x - 10\). Find \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: Equating \(x^2 - 4x - 1 = 2x - 10\) yields \((x - 3)^2 = 0\), giving the intersection point \((3, -4)\). With \(r = \sqrt{3^2 + (-4)^2} = 5\), we obtain \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = \frac{3}{5}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the curves \(y = x^2 + 6x + 10\) and \(y = 2x + 6\). Find \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: Setting \(x^2 + 6x + 10 = 2x + 6\) gives \((x + 2)^2 = 0\), so the intersection point is \((-2, 2)\). With \(r = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + 2^2} = 2\sqrt{2}\), we have \(\sin\theta = \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the curves \(y = x^2 + 6x + 5\) and \(y = -2x - 11\). Find \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: Equating \(x^2 + 6x + 5 = -2x - 11\) gives \((x + 4)^2 = 0\), so the intersection point is \((-4, -3)\). With \(r = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + (-3)^2} = 5\), we find \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{4}{5}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the curves \(y = x^2 + 4x + 5\) and \(y = 2x + 4\). Find \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: Setting \(x^2 + 4x + 5 = 2x + 4\) yields \((x + 1)^2 = 0\), which gives the intersection point \((-1, 2)\). With \(r = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{5}\), we get \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the curves \(y = x^2 - 8x - 15\) and \(y = -x - 7\) in Quadrant IV. Find \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: Solving \(x^2 - 8x - 15 = -x - 7\) gives \(x = 8\) or \(x = -1\), which identifies the Quadrant IV intersection point as \((8, -15)\). With \(r = \sqrt{8^2 + (-15)^2} = 17\), we have \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r} = \frac{8}{17}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the curves \(y = x^2 + x - 8\) and \(y = -2x + 2\) in Quadrant II. Find \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: Solving \(x^2 + x - 8 = -2x + 2\) yields \(x = -5\) or \(x = 2\), so the Quadrant II intersection point is \((-5, 12)\). With \(r = \sqrt{(-5)^2 + 12^2} = 13\), we find \(\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} = \frac{12}{13}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the curves \(y = 2x^2 + 19x - 55\) and \(y = x^2 + 9x - 31\) in Quadrant II. Find \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta\).
qs.s: Equating the two curves yields \(x^2 + 10x - 24 = 0\), giving the Quadrant II intersection point \((-12, 5)\). With \(r = \sqrt{(-12)^2 + 5^2} = 13\), \(\sin\theta = \frac{5}{13}\) and \(\cos\theta = -\frac{12}{13}\), so \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = -\frac{7}{13}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the curves \(y = 2x^2 + 5x - 7\) and \(y = x^2 + 3x - 4\) in Quadrant III. Find \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta\).
qs.s: Equating the equations gives \(x^2 + 2x - 3 = 0\), yielding the Quadrant III point \((-3, -4)\). With \(r = 5\), \(\sin\theta = -\frac{4}{5}\) and \(\cos\theta = -\frac{3}{5}\), so \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = -\frac{7}{5}\).

qs.q: The terminal side of angle \(\theta\) in standard position passes through the intersection point of the curves \(y = x^2 - 7x - 24\) and \(y = -2x - 10\) in Quadrant IV. Find \(\cos\theta - \sin\theta\).
qs.s: Solving \(x^2 - 7x - 24 = -2x - 10\) gives \(x = 7\) or \(x = -2\), so the Quadrant IV point is \((7, -24)\). With \(r = 25\), \(\cos\theta = \frac{7}{25}\) and \(\sin\theta = -\frac{24}{25}\), so \(\cos\theta - \sin\theta = \frac{7}{25} - \left(-\frac{24}{25}\right) = \frac{31}{25}\).

qs.q: Find the largest angle \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ\), for which \(\tan\theta = 1\).
qs.s: Since \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} = 1\), we have \(y = x\), which occurs in Quadrants I and III with a reference angle of \(45^\circ\). The solutions are \(45^\circ\) and \(180^\circ + 45^\circ = 225^\circ\), so the largest angle is \(225^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the largest angle \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ\), for which \(\cot\theta = -1\).
qs.s: The ratio \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y} = -1\) requires \(x = -y\), which occurs in Quadrants II and IV with reference angle \(45^\circ\). The solutions are \(135^\circ\) and \(315^\circ\), so the largest angle is \(315^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the sum of all angles \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ\), for which \(\sin\theta = -\cos\theta\).
qs.s: The equation \(\sin\theta = -\cos\theta\) means \(y = -x\), which occurs in Quadrants II and IV with a reference angle of \(45^\circ\). The solutions are \(135^\circ\) and \(315^\circ\), giving a sum of \(135^\circ + 315^\circ = 450^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the sum of all angles \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ\), for which \(\sec\theta = \csc\theta\).
qs.s: By definition, \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x}\) and \(\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y}\), so \(\sec\theta = \csc\theta\) requires \(x = y\) with \(x, y \ne 0\). This occurs in Quadrants I and III at \(\theta = 45^\circ\) and \(\theta = 225^\circ\), giving a sum of \(45^\circ + 225^\circ = 270^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the smallest positive angle \(\theta\), \(0^\circ < \theta \le 360^\circ\), for which \(\tan\theta = -1\).
qs.s: Since \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} = -1\), we have \(y = -x\), which lies in Quadrants II and IV with a reference angle of \(45^\circ\). The solutions are \(180^\circ - 45^\circ = 135^\circ\) and \(360^\circ - 45^\circ = 315^\circ\), so the smallest positive angle is \(135^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the sum of all angles \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ\), for which \(\sin\theta\cos\theta + \cos^2\theta = 0\).
qs.s: Factoring gives \(\cos\theta(\sin\theta + \cos\theta) = 0\), so \(\cos\theta = 0\) or \(\sin\theta = -\cos\theta\). In the given interval, \(\cos\theta = 0\) yields \(90^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\), while \(\sin\theta = -\cos\theta\) yields \(135^\circ\) and \(315^\circ\), giving a sum of \(90^\circ + 135^\circ + 270^\circ + 315^\circ = 810^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the sum of all angles \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ\), for which \(\tan^2\theta + \tan\theta = 0\).
qs.s: Factoring gives \(\tan\theta(\tan\theta + 1) = 0\), so \(\tan\theta = 0\) or \(\tan\theta = -1\). The solutions in the interval are \(0^\circ, 180^\circ, 360^\circ\) (where \(\tan\theta = 0\)) and \(135^\circ, 315^\circ\) (where \(\tan\theta = -1\)), giving a sum of \(0^\circ + 135^\circ + 180^\circ + 315^\circ + 360^\circ = 990^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the sum of all angles \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ\), for which \(\sin^2\theta = \cos^2\theta\).
qs.s: Taking the square root gives \(|\sin\theta| = |\cos\theta|\), which means \(|y| = |x|\) and yields a reference angle of \(45^\circ\) in all four quadrants. The solutions are \(45^\circ, 135^\circ, 225^\circ,\) and \(315^\circ\), and their sum is \(45^\circ + 135^\circ + 225^\circ + 315^\circ = 720^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the sum of all angles \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \le \theta \le 720^\circ\), for which \(\sin\theta = \cos\theta\).
qs.s: In the first revolution (\(0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ\)), \(\sin\theta = \cos\theta\) yields \(45^\circ\) and \(225^\circ\). In the second revolution (\(360^\circ < \theta \le 720^\circ\)), the coterminal solutions are \(405^\circ\) and \(585^\circ\), giving a total sum of \(45^\circ + 225^\circ + 405^\circ + 585^\circ = 1260^\circ\).

exercises.name: Evaluating trigonometric function from a linear trigonometric equation

qs.q: If \(1 + 4\cos\theta = \cos\theta - 1\) and \(\sin\theta > 0\), find \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: Solving the equation gives \(3\cos\theta = -2\), so \(\cos\theta = -\frac{2}{3}\). Since \(\cos\theta < 0\) and \(\sin\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in quadrant II, where \(y = \sqrt{3^2 - (-2)^2} = \sqrt{5}\), giving \(\sin\theta = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\).

qs.q: If \(5\tan\theta - 2 = 2\tan\theta + 1\) and \(\cos\theta < 0\), find \(\sec\theta\).
qs.s: Solving the equation gives \(3\tan\theta = 3\), so \(\tan\theta = 1\). Since \(\tan\theta > 0\) and \(\cos\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) lies in quadrant III with \(x = -1\) and \(y = -1\), yielding \(r = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{2}\) and \(\sec\theta = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{-1} = -\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: If \(3 - 2\sin\theta = 4\sin\theta + 1\) and \(\cos\theta < 0\), find \(\cot\theta\).
qs.s: Solving gives \(6\sin\theta = 2\), so \(\sin\theta = \frac{1}{3}\). In quadrant II (where \(\sin\theta > 0\) and \(\cos\theta < 0\)), \(x = -\sqrt{3^2 - 1^2} = -2\sqrt{2}\), so \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y} = -2\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: If \(3 + 2\sin\theta = 7\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta < 0\), find \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: Solving the equation yields \(5\sin\theta = 3\), so \(\sin\theta = \frac{3}{5}\). Since \(\sin\theta > 0\) and \(\cos\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) is in quadrant II, which gives \(x = -\sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = -4\) and \(\cos\theta = -\frac{4}{5}\).

qs.q: If \(2 - \cos\theta = 3\cos\theta\) and \(\tan\theta < 0\), find \(\sin\theta\).
qs.s: Solving gives \(4\cos\theta = 2\), so \(\cos\theta = \frac{1}{2}\). Since \(\cos\theta > 0\) and \(\tan\theta < 0\), \(\theta\) is in quadrant IV, where \(y = -\sqrt{2^2 - 1^2} = -\sqrt{3}\), so \(\sin\theta = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

qs.q: If \(2(2\tan\theta + 1) = \tan\theta - 2\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), find \(\csc\theta - \cos\theta\).
qs.s: Simplifying gives \(3\tan\theta = -4\), so \(\tan\theta = -\frac{4}{3}\). In quadrant IV, \(x = 3, y = -4, r = 5\), which gives \(\csc\theta = -\frac{5}{4}\) and \(\cos\theta = \frac{3}{5}\), so \(\csc\theta - \cos\theta = -\frac{5}{4} - \frac{3}{5} = -\frac{37}{20}\).

qs.q: If \(\frac{5\sin\theta + 1}{4} - \sin\theta = \frac{1}{6}\) and \(\cos\theta < 0\), find \(\cos\theta\).
qs.s: Multiplying by 12 gives \(3(5\sin\theta + 1) - 12\sin\theta = 2\), which simplifies to \(3\sin\theta = -1\), so \(\sin\theta = -\frac{1}{3}\). In quadrant III, \(x = -\sqrt{3^2 - (-1)^2} = -2\sqrt{2}\), so \(\cos\theta = -\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}\).

qs.q: If \(5(3\cos\theta + 2) = 2\cos\theta + 5\) and \(\sin\theta < 0\), find \(\sin\theta + \tan\theta\).
qs.s: Simplifying gives \(13\cos\theta = -5\), so \(\cos\theta = -\frac{5}{13}\). In quadrant III, \(y = -\sqrt{13^2 - (-5)^2} = -12\), so \(\sin\theta = -\frac{12}{13}\) and \(\tan\theta = \frac{12}{5}\); their sum is \(-\frac{12}{13} + \frac{12}{5} = \frac{96}{65}\).

qs.q: If \(3(3\cos\theta - 2) = 2 - 8\cos\theta\) and \(\tan\theta < 0\), find \(\csc\theta + \cot\theta\).
qs.s: Expanding gives \(17\cos\theta = 8\), so \(\cos\theta = \frac{8}{17}\). In quadrant IV, \(y = -\sqrt{17^2 - 8^2} = -15\), giving \(\csc\theta = -\frac{17}{15}\) and \(\cot\theta = -\frac{8}{15}\), so \(\csc\theta + \cot\theta = -\frac{25}{15} = -\frac{5}{3}\).

qs.q: If \(2(9\sin\theta + 4) = 1 - 7\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), find \(\cot\theta\).
qs.s: Expanding and simplifying gives \(25\sin\theta = -7\), so \(\sin\theta = -\frac{7}{25}\). With \(\sin\theta < 0\) and \(\cos\theta > 0\), \(\theta\) is in quadrant IV, so \(x = \sqrt{25^2 - (-7)^2} = 24\), giving \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y} = -\frac{24}{7}\).

qs.q: From point \(P\) on level ground the angle of elevation to the top of a tower is \(\alpha=30^\circ\). From point \(Q\), which is \(d=8\) m closer to the tower on the same line, the angle of elevation is \(\beta=60^\circ\). Use the figure and \(h=\frac{d}{\cot\alpha-\cot\beta}\) to find the height \(h\) of the tower.
qs.s: \(h=\frac{8}{\sqrt3-\frac1{\sqrt3}}=\frac{8}{2/\sqrt3}=4\sqrt3\) m.

qs.q: Find the reference angle \(\theta'\) for the angle \(\theta = 120^\circ\).
qs.s: Since \(120^\circ\) lies in Quadrant II, the reference angle is \(\theta' = 180^\circ - \theta = 180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the reference angle \(\theta'\) for the angle \(\theta = 315^\circ\).
qs.s: Since \(315^\circ\) lies in Quadrant IV, the reference angle is \(\theta' = 360^\circ - \theta = 360^\circ - 315^\circ = 45^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the reference angle \(\theta'\) for the angle \(\theta = 210^\circ\).
qs.s: Since \(210^\circ\) lies in Quadrant III, the reference angle is \(\theta' = \theta - 180^\circ = 210^\circ - 180^\circ = 30^\circ\).

qs.s: Since \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\) lies in Quadrant II, the reference angle is \(\theta' = \pi - \theta = \pi - \frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{6}\).

qs.s: Subtracting \(8\pi = \frac{40\pi}{5}\) gives the coterminal angle \(\frac{3\pi}{5}\), which lies in Quadrant II since \(\frac{\pi}{2} < \frac{3\pi}{5} < \pi\). The reference angle is \(\theta' = \pi - \frac{3\pi}{5} = \frac{2\pi}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the reference angle \(\theta'\) for \(\theta = \frac{23\pi}{2} - \frac{17\pi}{3}\).
qs.s: Combining terms gives \(\theta = \frac{69\pi - 34\pi}{6} = \frac{35\pi}{6}\), which is coterminal with \(\frac{11\pi}{6}\) in Quadrant IV after subtracting \(4\pi\). The reference angle is \(\theta' = 2\pi - \frac{11\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{6}\).

qs.q: Find the reference angle \(\theta'\) for \(\theta = -\frac{149\pi}{6}\).
qs.s: Adding \(26\pi = \frac{156\pi}{6}\) gives the coterminal angle \(\frac{7\pi}{6}\), which lies in Quadrant III. The reference angle is \(\theta' = \frac{7\pi}{6} - \pi = \frac{\pi}{6}\).

qs.q: Find the reference angle \(\theta'\) for \(\theta = -\frac{176\pi}{3}\).
qs.s: Adding \(60\pi = \frac{180\pi}{3}\) gives the coterminal angle \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\), which lies in Quadrant III. The reference angle is \(\theta' = \frac{4\pi}{3} - \pi = \frac{\pi}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the reference angle \(\theta'\) for the angle \(\theta = \frac{19\pi}{5}\).
qs.s: Subtract \(2\pi\) to find the coterminal angle \(\frac{19\pi}{5} - 2\pi = \frac{9\pi}{5}\), which lies in Quadrant IV. The reference angle is \(\theta' = 2\pi - \frac{9\pi}{5} = \frac{\pi}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the reference angle \(\theta'\) for the angle \(\theta = \frac{13\pi}{4}\).
qs.s: Subtract \(2\pi\) to find the coterminal angle \(\frac{13\pi}{4} - 2\pi = \frac{5\pi}{4}\), which lies in Quadrant III. The reference angle is \(\theta' = \frac{5\pi}{4} - \pi = \frac{\pi}{4}\).

qs.q: Find the reference angle \(\theta'\) for the angle \(\theta = \frac{23\pi}{7}\).
qs.s: Subtract \(2\pi\) to obtain the coterminal angle \(\frac{23\pi}{7} - 2\pi = \frac{9\pi}{7}\), which lies in Quadrant III. The reference angle is \(\theta' = \frac{9\pi}{7} - \pi = \frac{2\pi}{7}\).

qs.q: Find the reference angle \(\theta'\) for the angle \(\theta = -\frac{46\pi}{7}\).
qs.s: Add \(8\pi\) (4 full revolutions) to find the coterminal angle \(-\frac{46\pi}{7} + 8\pi = \frac{10\pi}{7}\), which lies in Quadrant III. The reference angle is \(\theta' = \frac{10\pi}{7} - \pi = \frac{3\pi}{7}\).

qs.q: Find the reference angle \(\theta'\) for the angle \(\theta = -\frac{53\pi}{8}\).
qs.s: Add \(8\pi\) (4 full revolutions) to obtain the coterminal angle \(-\frac{53\pi}{8} + 8\pi = \frac{11\pi}{8}\), which lies in Quadrant III. The reference angle is \(\theta' = \frac{11\pi}{8} - \pi = \frac{3\pi}{8}\).

qs.q: Find the reference angle \(\theta'\) for the angle \(\theta = \frac{19\pi}{6} + \frac{9\pi}{4}\).
qs.s: Combine the terms to get \(\theta = \frac{65\pi}{12}\), then subtract \(4\pi\) to find the coterminal angle \(\frac{17\pi}{12}\) in Quadrant III. The reference angle is \(\theta' = \frac{17\pi}{12} - \pi = \frac{5\pi}{12}\).

qs.q: Find the reference angle \(\theta'\) for the angle \(\theta = -\frac{79\pi}{9}\).
qs.s: Add \(10\pi\) (5 full revolutions) to find the coterminal angle \(-\frac{79\pi}{9} + 10\pi = \frac{11\pi}{9}\), which lies in Quadrant III. The reference angle is \(\theta' = \frac{11\pi}{9} - \pi = \frac{2\pi}{9}\).

qs.q: Find the reference angle \(\theta'\) for the angle \(\theta = \frac{44\pi}{3}\).
qs.s: Subtract \(14\pi\) (7 full revolutions) to find the coterminal angle \(\frac{44\pi}{3} - 14\pi = \frac{2\pi}{3}\), which lies in Quadrant II. The reference angle is \(\theta' = \pi - \frac{2\pi}{3} = \frac{\pi}{3}\).

exercises.name: Evaluate trigonometric function of an angle

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sin 315^\circ\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The reference angle for \(315^\circ\) is \(360^\circ - 315^\circ = 45^\circ\). Since \(315^\circ\) lies in Quadrant IV where sine is negative, \(\sin 315^\circ = -\sin 45^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\cos 300^\circ\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The reference angle for \(300^\circ\) is \(360^\circ - 300^\circ = 60^\circ\). Since \(300^\circ\) lies in Quadrant IV where cosine is positive, \(\cos 300^\circ = \cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\cos 150^\circ\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The reference angle for \(150^\circ\) is \(180^\circ - 150^\circ = 30^\circ\). Since \(150^\circ\) lies in Quadrant II where cosine is negative, \(\cos 150^\circ = -\cos 30^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\tan 240^\circ\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The reference angle for \(240^\circ\) is \(240^\circ - 180^\circ = 60^\circ\). Since \(240^\circ\) lies in Quadrant III where tangent is positive, \(\tan 240^\circ = \tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sin 210^\circ\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The reference angle for \(210^\circ\) is \(210^\circ - 180^\circ = 30^\circ\). Since \(210^\circ\) lies in Quadrant III where sine is negative, \(\sin 210^\circ = -\sin 30^\circ = -\frac{1}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\cos\left(-\frac{17\pi}{6}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(4\pi\) gives the coterminal angle \(\frac{7\pi}{6}\) in Quadrant III, which has reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). Since cosine is negative in Quadrant III, \(\cos\left(-\frac{17\pi}{6}\right) = -\cos\frac{\pi}{6} = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sin^2 135^\circ + \cos^2 240^\circ\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: We have \(\sin 135^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\) and \(\cos 240^\circ = -\frac{1}{2}\). Squaring and adding gives \(\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)^2 + \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(4\sin 150^\circ - 2\cos 180^\circ + \tan 315^\circ\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Evaluating each term yields \(\sin 150^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\), \(\cos 180^\circ = -1\), and \(\tan 315^\circ = -1\). Substituting these values gives \(4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) - 2(-1) + (-1) = 2 + 2 - 1 = 3\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\tan\left(-\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(2\pi\) gives the coterminal angle \(\frac{7\pi}{6}\) in Quadrant III, with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). Since tangent is positive in Quadrant III, \(\tan\left(-\frac{5\pi}{6}\right) = \tan\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\csc 480^\circ\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: A coterminal angle is \(480^\circ - 360^\circ = 120^\circ\), which lies in Quadrant II with reference angle \(60^\circ\). Since sine is positive in Quadrant II, \(\csc 480^\circ = \frac{1}{\sin 60^\circ} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\tan 225^\circ\) without using a calculator.
qs.s: The angle \(225^\circ\) lies in Quadrant III with a reference angle of \(225^\circ - 180^\circ = 45^\circ\). Since tangent is positive in Quadrant III, \(\tan 225^\circ = \tan 45^\circ = 1\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sin 330^\circ\) without using a calculator.
qs.s: The angle \(330^\circ\) lies in Quadrant IV with a reference angle of \(360^\circ - 330^\circ = 30^\circ\). Since sine is negative in Quadrant IV, \(\sin 330^\circ = -\sin 30^\circ = -\frac{1}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sec 315^\circ\) without using a calculator.
qs.s: The angle \(315^\circ\) lies in Quadrant IV with a reference angle of \(360^\circ - 315^\circ = 45^\circ\). Since secant is positive in Quadrant IV, \(\sec 315^\circ = \sec 45^\circ = \sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\cot 300^\circ\) without using a calculator.
qs.s: The angle \(300^\circ\) lies in Quadrant IV with a reference angle of \(360^\circ - 300^\circ = 60^\circ\). Since cotangent is negative in Quadrant IV, \(\cot 300^\circ = -\cot 60^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sec 120^\circ\) without using a calculator.
qs.s: The angle \(120^\circ\) lies in Quadrant II with a reference angle of \(180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ\). Since secant is negative in Quadrant II, \(\sec 120^\circ = -\sec 60^\circ = -2\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(4\sin(420^\circ)\tan(-240^\circ)\) without using a calculator.
qs.s: Since \(420^\circ\) is coterminal with \(60^\circ\), \(\sin 420^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), and since \(-240^\circ\) is coterminal with \(120^\circ\) in Quadrant II, \(\tan(-240^\circ) = -\sqrt{3}\). Evaluating the product yields \(4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)(-\sqrt{3}) = -6\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\csc(-495^\circ)\) without using a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(720^\circ\) yields the coterminal angle \(225^\circ\), which lies in Quadrant III with a reference angle of \(45^\circ\). Since cosecant is negative in Quadrant III, \(\csc(-495^\circ) = -\csc 45^\circ = -\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sec\left(\frac{7\pi}{4}\right)\csc\left(\frac{5\pi}{4}\right) + \tan^2\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\) without using a calculator.
qs.s: Using reference angles, \(\sec\left(\frac{7\pi}{4}\right) = \sqrt{2}\), \(\csc\left(\frac{5\pi}{4}\right) = -\sqrt{2}\), and \(\tan\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) = -\sqrt{3}\). Substituting these values gives \((\sqrt{2})(-\sqrt{2}) + (-\sqrt{3})^2 = -2 + 3 = 1\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\tan\left(-\frac{13\pi}{6}\right)\) without using a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(4\pi\) gives the coterminal angle \(\frac{11\pi}{6}\), which is in Quadrant IV with a reference angle of \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). Because tangent is negative in Quadrant IV, \(\tan\left(-\frac{13\pi}{6}\right) = -\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sec(-300^\circ) - \csc(210^\circ)\) without using a calculator.
qs.s: The angle \(-300^\circ\) is coterminal with \(60^\circ\), giving \(\sec(-300^\circ) = \sec 60^\circ = 2\). In Quadrant III, \(\csc 210^\circ = -\csc 30^\circ = -2\), so \(2 - (-2) = 4\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sin 225^\circ\).
qs.s: The angle \(225^\circ\) lies in Quadrant III with a reference angle of \(225^\circ - 180^\circ = 45^\circ\). Since sine is negative in Quadrant III, \(\sin 225^\circ = -\sin 45^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\cos 210^\circ\).
qs.s: The angle \(210^\circ\) lies in Quadrant III with a reference angle of \(210^\circ - 180^\circ = 30^\circ\). Since cosine is negative in Quadrant III, \(\cos 210^\circ = -\cos 30^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sec 300^\circ\).
qs.s: The angle \(300^\circ\) lies in Quadrant IV with a reference angle of \(360^\circ - 300^\circ = 60^\circ\). Since secant is positive in Quadrant IV, \(\sec 300^\circ = \sec 60^\circ = 2\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\csc 135^\circ\).
qs.s: The angle \(135^\circ\) lies in Quadrant II with a reference angle of \(180^\circ - 135^\circ = 45^\circ\). Since cosecant is positive in Quadrant II, \(\csc 135^\circ = \csc 45^\circ = \sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\tan 150^\circ\).
qs.s: The angle \(150^\circ\) lies in Quadrant II with a reference angle of \(180^\circ - 150^\circ = 30^\circ\). Since tangent is negative in Quadrant II, \(\tan 150^\circ = -\tan 30^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sec 780^\circ + \tan(-405^\circ)\).
qs.s: Find coterminal angles: \(780^\circ - 720^\circ = 60^\circ\) and \(-405^\circ + 720^\circ = 315^\circ\). Evaluating gives \(\sec 60^\circ + \tan 315^\circ = 2 + (-1) = 1\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sin^2 240^\circ + \cos^2 330^\circ\).
qs.s: Evaluate each function using reference angles: \(\sin 240^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(\cos 330^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). Squaring and adding gives \(\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{3}{4} + \frac{3}{4} = \frac{3}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\csc\left(-\frac{13\pi}{6}\right)\).
qs.s: Add \(4\pi\) to find the coterminal angle: \(-\frac{13\pi}{6} + 4\pi = \frac{11\pi}{6}\), which lies in Quadrant IV with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). Since cosecant is negative in Quadrant IV, \(\csc\left(-\frac{13\pi}{6}\right) = -\csc\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -2\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\tan 315^\circ \sin 210^\circ + \cos 180^\circ\).
qs.s: Evaluating the special and quadrantal values yields \(\tan 315^\circ = -1\), \(\sin 210^\circ = -\frac{1}{2}\), and \(\cos 180^\circ = -1\). Substituting these gives \((-1)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) + (-1) = \frac{1}{2} - 1 = -\frac{1}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\cos(-570^\circ)\).
qs.s: Add \(2(360^\circ) = 720^\circ\) to find a coterminal angle: \(-570^\circ + 720^\circ = 150^\circ\). The angle \(150^\circ\) is in Quadrant II with reference angle \(30^\circ\), so \(\cos(-570^\circ) = -\cos 30^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sin 480^\circ\).
qs.s: Subtract \(360^\circ\) to find the coterminal angle \(120^\circ\), which lies in Quadrant II with reference angle \(60^\circ\). Since sine is positive in Quadrant II, \(\sin 480^\circ = \sin 60^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sec 675^\circ\).
qs.s: The angle \(675^\circ\) is coterminal with \(675^\circ - 360^\circ = 315^\circ\), which lies in Quadrant IV with reference angle \(45^\circ\). Since secant is positive in Quadrant IV, \(\sec 675^\circ = \sec 45^\circ = \sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\cot 495^\circ\).
qs.s: The angle \(495^\circ\) is coterminal with \(495^\circ - 360^\circ = 135^\circ\), located in Quadrant II with reference angle \(45^\circ\). Since cotangent is negative in Quadrant II, \(\cot 495^\circ = -\cot 45^\circ = -1\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\cos 420^\circ\).
qs.s: The angle \(420^\circ\) is coterminal with \(420^\circ - 360^\circ = 60^\circ\) in Quadrant I. Thus, \(\cos 420^\circ = \cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\csc 570^\circ\).
qs.s: Subtract \(360^\circ\) to find the coterminal angle \(210^\circ\), which is in Quadrant III with reference angle \(30^\circ\). Since cosecant is negative in Quadrant III, \(\csc 570^\circ = -\csc 30^\circ = -2\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\frac{\tan 585^\circ + \sqrt{3}\csc 480^\circ}{\sec 780^\circ}\).
qs.s: Evaluating each component using coterminal angles gives \(\tan 585^\circ = 1\), \(\csc 480^\circ = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\), and \(\sec 780^\circ = 2\). Substituting these values yields \(\frac{1 + \sqrt{3}(2/\sqrt{3})}{2} = \frac{1 + 2}{2} = \frac{3}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\csc(-1110^\circ)\).
qs.s: Add \(4 \times 360^\circ = 1440^\circ\) to find the coterminal angle \(330^\circ\), which lies in Quadrant IV with reference angle \(30^\circ\). Because cosecant is negative in Quadrant IV, \(\csc(-1110^\circ) = -\csc 30^\circ = -2\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sin 420^\circ \cos 750^\circ + \cos 420^\circ \sin 750^\circ\).
qs.s: Evaluating each term using coterminal angles gives \(\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) + \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\). This simplifies to \(\frac{3}{4} + \frac{1}{4} = 1\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\tan(-840^\circ) \sec 480^\circ\).
qs.s: Since \(-840^\circ\) is coterminal with \(240^\circ\), \(\tan(-840^\circ) = \tan 240^\circ = \sqrt{3}\), and since \(480^\circ\) is coterminal with \(120^\circ\), \(\sec 480^\circ = \sec 120^\circ = -2\). Their product is \(\sqrt{3} \times (-2) = -2\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\cos(-930^\circ)\).
qs.s: Add \(3 \times 360^\circ = 1080^\circ\) to get the coterminal angle \(150^\circ\), which lies in Quadrant II with reference angle \(30^\circ\). Since cosine is negative in Quadrant II, \(\cos(-930^\circ) = -\cos 30^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\cot 1215^\circ\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The angle \(1215^\circ\) is coterminal to \(1215^\circ - 3(360^\circ) = 135^\circ\), which is in Quadrant II with reference angle \(45^\circ\). Since cotangent is negative in Quadrant II, \(\cot 1215^\circ = -\cot 45^\circ = -1\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sec 1110^\circ\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The angle \(1110^\circ\) is coterminal to \(1110^\circ - 3(360^\circ) = 30^\circ\) in Quadrant I. Therefore, \(\sec 1110^\circ = \sec 30^\circ = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\tan 840^\circ\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The angle \(840^\circ\) is coterminal to \(840^\circ - 2(360^\circ) = 120^\circ\), which is in Quadrant II with reference angle \(60^\circ\). Since tangent is negative in Quadrant II, \(\tan 840^\circ = -\tan 60^\circ = -\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\csc 930^\circ\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The angle \(930^\circ\) is coterminal to \(930^\circ - 2(360^\circ) = 210^\circ\), which lies in Quadrant III with reference angle \(30^\circ\). Since cosecant is negative in Quadrant III, \(\csc 930^\circ = -\csc 30^\circ = -2\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sin 750^\circ\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The angle \(750^\circ\) is coterminal to \(750^\circ - 2(360^\circ) = 30^\circ\) in Quadrant I. Thus, \(\sin 750^\circ = \sin 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sec 1500^\circ - \tan 1125^\circ\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Since \(1500^\circ\) is coterminal to \(60^\circ\), \(\sec 1500^\circ = \sec 60^\circ = 2\), and since \(1125^\circ\) is coterminal to \(45^\circ\), \(\tan 1125^\circ = \tan 45^\circ = 1\). Subtracting gives \(2 - 1 = 1\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sin 1230^\circ \cos 1560^\circ + \tan 1575^\circ\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The angles reduce to \(\sin 150^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\), \(\cos 120^\circ = -\frac{1}{2}\), and \(\tan 135^\circ = -1\). Evaluating the expression yields \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) + (-1) = -\frac{1}{4} - 1 = -\frac{5}{4}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\csc(-1290^\circ)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(4(360^\circ) = 1440^\circ\) gives the coterminal angle \(-1290^\circ + 1440^\circ = 150^\circ\) in Quadrant II with reference angle \(30^\circ\). Since cosecant is positive in Quadrant II, \(\csc(-1290^\circ) = \csc 30^\circ = 2\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\frac{\cos 1260^\circ - \sin 1590^\circ}{\csc 990^\circ}\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The coterminal angles are \(180^\circ\), \(150^\circ\), and \(270^\circ\), giving \(\cos 1260^\circ = -1\), \(\sin 1590^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\), and \(\csc 990^\circ = -1\). The quotient evaluates to \(\frac{-1 - 1/2}{-1} = \frac{-3/2}{-1} = \frac{3}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\cot(-1110^\circ) + \sec(-1470^\circ)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Both angles are coterminal to \(330^\circ\) in Quadrant IV, where \(\cot(-1110^\circ) = -\cot 30^\circ = -\sqrt{3}\) and \(\sec(-1470^\circ) = \sec 30^\circ = \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\). Their sum is \(-\sqrt{3} + \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3} = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

qs.q:
Determine the exact value of the trigonometric function. Do not use a calculator.

\(\displaystyle \cot \frac{\pi}{6}\)
qs.s: Since \(\tan \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\), we have \(\cot \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{\tan(\pi/6)} = \sqrt{3}\).

qs.q:
Determine the exact value of the trigonometric function. Do not use a calculator.

\(\displaystyle \sec \frac{\pi}{4}\)
qs.s: Since \(\cos \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), we have \(\sec \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{1}{\cos(\pi/4)} = \sqrt{2}\).

qs.q:
Determine the exact value of the trigonometric function. Do not use a calculator.

\(\displaystyle \cot \frac{\pi}{3}\)
qs.s: Since \(\tan \frac{\pi}{3} = \sqrt{3}\), we have \(\cot \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{\tan(\pi/3)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

qs.q:
Determine the exact value of the trigonometric function. Do not use a calculator.

\(\displaystyle \csc \frac{\pi}{3}\)
qs.s: Since \(\sin \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), we have \(\csc \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{\sin(\pi/3)} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

qs.q:
Determine the exact value of the trigonometric function. Do not use a calculator.

\(\displaystyle \csc \frac{\pi}{6}\)
qs.s: Since \(\sin \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}\), we have \(\csc \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{\sin(\pi/6)} = 2\).

qs.q:
Determine the exact value of the trigonometric function. Do not use a calculator.

\(\displaystyle \cot \frac{17\pi}{6}\)
qs.s: Subtracting \(2\pi\) gives the coterminal angle \(\frac{17\pi}{6} - 2\pi = \frac{5\pi}{6}\) in Quadrant II, where cotangent is negative with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). Therefore, \(\cot \frac{17\pi}{6} = -\cot \frac{\pi}{6} = -\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q:
Determine the exact value of the trigonometric function. Do not use a calculator.

\(\displaystyle \cot\left(-\frac{16\pi}{3}\right)\)
qs.s: Adding \(6\pi\) gives the coterminal angle \(-\frac{16\pi}{3} + 6\pi = \frac{2\pi}{3}\) in Quadrant II, with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Since cotangent is negative in Quadrant II, \(\cot\left(-\frac{16\pi}{3}\right) = -\cot \frac{\pi}{3} = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

qs.q:
Determine the exact value of the trigonometric function. Do not use a calculator.

\(\displaystyle \sec\left(-\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\)
qs.s: A coterminal angle is \(-\frac{4\pi}{3} + 2\pi = \frac{2\pi}{3}\), which lies in Quadrant II with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Since secant is negative in Quadrant II, \(\sec\left(-\frac{4\pi}{3}\right) = -\sec \frac{\pi}{3} = -2\).

qs.q:
Determine the exact value of the trigonometric function. Do not use a calculator.

\(\displaystyle \sec \frac{3\pi}{4}\)
qs.s: The angle \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\) lies in Quadrant II where secant is negative, with reference angle \(\pi - \frac{3\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{4}\). Thus, \(\sec \frac{3\pi}{4} = -\sec \frac{\pi}{4} = -\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q:

qs.s: The angle \(-\frac{\pi}{6}\) is in Quadrant IV with a reference angle of \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). Because cosecant is negative in Quadrant IV, \(\csc\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\csc\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -2\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\tan\left(-\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The coterminal angle is \(-\frac{4\pi}{3} + 2\pi = \frac{2\pi}{3}\), which lies in Quadrant II with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Because tangent is negative in Quadrant II, \(\tan\left(-\frac{4\pi}{3}\right) = -\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = -\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sec\left(-\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(2\pi\) gives the coterminal angle \(\frac{5\pi}{4}\) in Quadrant III, where the reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\). Since secant is negative in Quadrant III, \(\sec\left(-\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) = -\sec\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = -\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\cot\left(-\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The coterminal angle is \(-\frac{5\pi}{4} + 2\pi = \frac{3\pi}{4}\), located in Quadrant II with a reference angle of \(\frac{\pi}{4}\). Since cotangent is negative in Quadrant II, \(\cot\left(-\frac{5\pi}{4}\right) = -\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = -1\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sin\left(-\frac{17\pi}{4}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(3(2\pi) = \frac{24\pi}{4}\) gives the coterminal angle \(\frac{7\pi}{4}\), which lies in Quadrant IV with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{4}\). Since sine is negative in Quadrant IV, \(\sin\left(-\frac{17\pi}{4}\right) = -\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\frac{\sec\left(-\frac{7\pi}{3}\right)}{\tan\left(-\frac{11\pi}{6}\right)}\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The coterminal angle for \(-\frac{7\pi}{3}\) is \(\frac{5\pi}{3}\) (Quadrant IV) giving \(\sec\left(\frac{5\pi}{3}\right) = 2\), and for \(-\frac{11\pi}{6}\) is \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) (Quadrant I) giving \(\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\). Dividing gives \(\frac{2}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}} = \frac{6}{\sqrt{3}} = 2\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(4\cos\left(-\frac{13\pi}{3}\right) - \tan\left(-\frac{17\pi}{4}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(6\pi\) yields coterminal angles \(\frac{5\pi}{3}\) (Quadrant IV) with \(\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\), and \(\frac{7\pi}{4}\) (Quadrant IV) with \(\tan\left(\frac{7\pi}{4}\right) = -1\). Evaluating gives \(4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) - (-1) = 2 + 1 = 3\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\tan\left(-\frac{7\pi}{6}\right) + \cot\left(-\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The coterminal angles are \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\) and \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\), both in Quadrant II where tangent and cotangent are negative. Thus, \(\tan\left(-\frac{7\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\) and \(\cot\left(-\frac{4\pi}{3}\right) = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\), yielding a sum of \(-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\cos\left(-\frac{7\pi}{4}\right)\sin\left(-\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Evaluating each term using reference angles gives \(\cos\left(-\frac{7\pi}{4}\right) = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\) and \(\sin\left(-\frac{4\pi}{3}\right) = \sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). Multiplying the results gives \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sec\left(-\frac{19\pi}{3}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(8\pi\) gives the coterminal angle \(\frac{5\pi}{3}\) in Quadrant IV, with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Since secant is positive in Quadrant IV, \(\sec\left(-\frac{19\pi}{3}\right) = \sec\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = 2\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sin\left(-\frac{25\pi}{6}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(6\pi\) gives the coterminal angle \(\frac{11\pi}{6}\) in Quadrant IV, which has a reference angle of \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). Since sine is negative in Quadrant IV, \(\sin\left(-\frac{25\pi}{6}\right) = -\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{1}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\cot\left(-\frac{23\pi}{4}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(6\pi\) gives the coterminal angle \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) in Quadrant I. Therefore, \(\cot\left(-\frac{23\pi}{4}\right) = \cot\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = 1\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\cos\left(-\frac{17\pi}{4}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(6\pi\) gives the coterminal angle \(\frac{7\pi}{4}\) in Quadrant IV, which has a reference angle of \(\frac{\pi}{4}\). Since cosine is positive in Quadrant IV, \(\cos\left(-\frac{17\pi}{4}\right) = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\csc\left(-\frac{22\pi}{3}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(8\pi\) yields the coterminal angle \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\) in Quadrant II, which has a reference angle of \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Since cosecant is positive in Quadrant II, \(\csc\left(-\frac{22\pi}{3}\right) = \csc\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sin\left(-\frac{71\pi}{6}\right) + \cos\left(-\frac{43\pi}{3}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(12\pi\) to \(-\frac{71\pi}{6}\) gives \(\frac{\pi}{6}\), so \(\sin\left(-\frac{71\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\). Adding \(16\pi\) to \(-\frac{43\pi}{3}\) gives \(\frac{5\pi}{3}\) in Quadrant IV, so \(\cos\left(-\frac{43\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\). Summing the two values gives \(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\csc\left(-\frac{85\pi}{3}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(30\pi\) gives the coterminal angle \(\frac{5\pi}{3}\) in Quadrant IV, which has a reference angle of \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Since cosecant is negative in Quadrant IV, \(\csc\left(-\frac{85\pi}{3}\right) = -\csc\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = -\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\tan\left(-\frac{49\pi}{4}\right) + \cot\left(-\frac{31\pi}{6}\right) \tan\left(-\frac{26\pi}{3}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The coterminal angles in \([0, 2\pi)\) are \(\frac{7\pi}{4}\), \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\), and \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\), which evaluate to \(\tan\left(\frac{7\pi}{4}\right) = -1\), \(\cot\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right) = -\sqrt{3}\), and \(\tan\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right) = \sqrt{3}\). Evaluating gives \(-1 + (-\sqrt{3})(\sqrt{3}) = -1 - 3 = -4\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sec\left(-\frac{41\pi}{6}\right) \sin\left(-\frac{31\pi}{3}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(8\pi\) to \(-\frac{41\pi}{6}\) gives \(\frac{7\pi}{6}\) in Quadrant III, so \(\sec\left(-\frac{41\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\). Adding \(12\pi\) to \(-\frac{31\pi}{3}\) gives \(\frac{5\pi}{3}\) in Quadrant IV, so \(\sin\left(-\frac{31\pi}{3}\right) = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). Multiplying them yields \(\left(-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 1\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\frac{\sin\left(-\frac{31\pi}{4}\right)}{\cos\left(-\frac{25\pi}{3}\right)}\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(8\pi\) to \(-\frac{31\pi}{4}\) gives \(\frac{\pi}{4}\), so \(\sin\left(-\frac{31\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\), and adding \(10\pi\) to \(-\frac{25\pi}{3}\) gives \(\frac{5\pi}{3}\), so \(\cos\left(-\frac{25\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\). Dividing the two values yields \(\frac{\sqrt{2}/2}{1/2} = \sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\csc\left(-\frac{19\pi}{4}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(6\pi\) yields the coterminal angle \(-\frac{19\pi}{4} + \frac{24\pi}{4} = \frac{5\pi}{4}\) in Quadrant III with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{4}\). Since sine is negative in Quadrant III, \(\csc\left(-\frac{19\pi}{4}\right) = -\csc\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = -\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\tan\left(-\frac{25\pi}{6}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(6\pi\) gives the coterminal angle \(-\frac{25\pi}{6} + \frac{36\pi}{6} = \frac{11\pi}{6}\), which lies in Quadrant IV with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). Since tangent is negative in Quadrant IV, \(\tan\left(-\frac{25\pi}{6}\right) = -\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sin\left(-\frac{29\pi}{6}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(6\pi\) gives the coterminal angle \(-\frac{29\pi}{6} + \frac{36\pi}{6} = \frac{7\pi}{6}\), which lies in Quadrant III with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). Since sine is negative in Quadrant III, \(\sin\left(-\frac{29\pi}{6}\right) = -\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{1}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sec\left(-\frac{11\pi}{3}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Adding \(4\pi\) gives the coterminal angle \(-\frac{11\pi}{3} + \frac{12\pi}{3} = \frac{\pi}{3}\) in Quadrant I. Thus, \(\sec\left(-\frac{11\pi}{3}\right) = \sec\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{\cos(\pi/3)} = 2\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(4\cos\left(-\frac{49\pi}{3}\right) - 2\sqrt{3}\sin\left(-\frac{44\pi}{3}\right) + \tan\left(-\frac{37\pi}{4}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Coterminal angles yield \(\cos\left(-\frac{49\pi}{3}\right) = \cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\), \(\sin\left(-\frac{44\pi}{3}\right) = \sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right) = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), and \(\tan\left(-\frac{37\pi}{4}\right) = \tan\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) = -1\). Substituting these values gives \(4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) - 2\sqrt{3}\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) + (-1) = 2 + 3 - 1 = 4\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of the expression \(\cos\left(-\frac{31\pi}{6}\right)\tan\left(-\frac{20\pi}{3}\right) + \sin\left(\frac{25\pi}{4}\right)\csc\left(-\frac{15\pi}{4}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Finding coterminal angles gives \(\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), \(\tan\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right) = \sqrt{3}\), \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\), and \(\csc\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \sqrt{2}\). Evaluating yields \(\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)(\sqrt{3}) + \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)(\sqrt{2}) = -\frac{3}{2} + 1 = -\frac{1}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sec^2\left(-\frac{35\pi}{4}\right) - \tan^2\left(-\frac{41\pi}{6}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: The coterminal angle for \(-\frac{35\pi}{4}\) is \(\frac{5\pi}{4}\), giving \(\sec\left(\frac{5\pi}{4}\right) = -\sqrt{2}\), and for \(-\frac{41\pi}{6}\) is \(\frac{7\pi}{6}\), giving \(\tan\left(\frac{7\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\). Evaluating yields \((-\sqrt{2})^2 - \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)^2 = 2 - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{5}{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\frac{\sin\left(-\frac{17\pi}{3}\right) - \cos\left(-\frac{19\pi}{6}\right)}{\tan\left(-\frac{29\pi}{4}\right)}\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Finding coterminal angles gives \(\sin\left(-\frac{17\pi}{3}\right) = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), \(\cos\left(-\frac{19\pi}{6}\right) = \cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), and \(\tan\left(-\frac{29\pi}{4}\right) = \tan\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) = -1\). Evaluating gives \(\frac{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}{-1} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{-1} = -\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sin\left(-\frac{37\pi}{2}\right) + \cos\left(-\frac{26\pi}{3}\right) - \cot\left(-\frac{27\pi}{4}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: Coterminal angles give \(\sin\left(-\frac{37\pi}{2}\right) = \sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right) = -1\), \(\cos\left(-\frac{26\pi}{3}\right) = \cos\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right) = -\frac{1}{2}\), and \(\cot\left(-\frac{27\pi}{4}\right) = \cot\left(\frac{5\pi}{4}\right) = 1\). The sum is \(-1 + \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) - 1 = -\frac{5}{2}\).

qs.q: Determine the exact value of \(\sec\left(-\frac{25\pi}{3}\right)\). Do not use a calculator.
qs.s: A coterminal angle is \(-\frac{25\pi}{3} + 5(2\pi) = \frac{5\pi}{3}\), which lies in Quadrant IV with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Since cosine is positive in Quadrant IV, \(\sec\left(-\frac{25\pi}{3}\right) = \sec\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = 2\).

exercises.name: Identify angles where trigonometric function is undefined

qs.q: Find the largest angle \(\theta\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\) for which \(\sec\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The secant function \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x}\) is undefined when \(x = 0\). In the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\), this occurs at \(\theta = 90^\circ\) and \(\theta = 270^\circ\), so the largest angle is \(270^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the smallest angle \(\theta\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\) for which \(\csc\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The cosecant function \(\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y}\) is undefined when \(y = 0\). In the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\), \(y = 0\) occurs at \(\theta = 0^\circ\) and \(\theta = 180^\circ\), so the smallest angle is \(0^\circ\).

qs.q: For which angle \(\theta\) in the interval \(0^\circ < \theta < 360^\circ\) is \(\cot\theta\) undefined?
qs.s: The cotangent function \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y}\) is undefined when \(y = 0\). In the open interval \(0^\circ < \theta < 360^\circ\), \(y = 0\) occurs only at \(\theta = 180^\circ\).

qs.q: How many values of \(\theta\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\) make \(\cos\theta\) undefined?
qs.s: Since \(\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r}\) and the radius \(r > 0\) is never zero, \(\cos\theta\) is defined for all values of \(\theta\). Therefore, there are 0 values in the interval where it is undefined.

qs.q: Find the smallest angle \(\theta\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\) for which \(\tan\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The tangent function \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}\) is undefined when \(x = 0\). In the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\), this occurs at \(\theta = 90^\circ\) and \(\theta = 270^\circ\), so the smallest angle is \(90^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the sum of all values of \(\theta\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\) for which \(\tan\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The tangent function is undefined when \(x = 0\), which occurs at \(\theta = 90^\circ\) and \(\theta = 270^\circ\) in the given interval. Their sum is \(90^\circ + 270^\circ = 360^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the sum of all values of \(\theta\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\) for which the expression \(\sec\theta + \csc\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The expression is undefined whenever \(\sec\theta\) is undefined (\(\theta = 90^\circ, 270^\circ\)) or \(\csc\theta\) is undefined (\(\theta = 0^\circ, 180^\circ\)). The sum of all these distinct angles is \(0^\circ + 90^\circ + 180^\circ + 270^\circ = 540^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the largest angle \(\theta\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 720^\circ\) for which \(\sec\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The secant function is undefined when \(x = 0\), which occurs at \(90^\circ, 270^\circ, 450^\circ,\) and \(630^\circ\) within the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 720^\circ\). The largest of these angles is \(630^\circ\).

qs.q: How many values of \(\theta\) in the interval \(0 \leq \theta \leq 4\pi\) make \(\csc\theta\) undefined?
qs.s: The cosecant function is undefined when \(\sin\theta = 0\). On the closed interval \([0, 4\pi]\), \(\sin\theta = 0\) at \(\theta = 0, \pi, 2\pi, 3\pi,\) and \(4\pi\), which is a total of 5 values.

qs.q: For which value of \(\theta\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\) is the expression \(\frac{1}{\sin\theta + 1}\) undefined?
qs.s: The expression is undefined when the denominator is zero, meaning \(\sin\theta + 1 = 0\), so \(\sin\theta = -1\). In the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\), this occurs only at \(\theta = 270^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the smallest angle \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\), for which \(\cot\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The cotangent function \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y}\) is undefined when \(y = 0\), which occurs at \(0^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\). The smallest angle in the interval is \(0^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the smallest angle \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\), for which \(\tan\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The tangent function \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}\) is undefined when \(x = 0\), which occurs at \(90^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\). The smallest angle in the given interval is \(90^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the largest angle \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\), for which \(\csc\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The cosecant function \(\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y}\) is undefined when \(y = 0\), which occurs at \(0^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\) for \(\theta < 360^\circ\). The largest angle in this interval is \(180^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the largest angle \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\), for which \(\sec\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The secant function \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x}\) is undefined when \(x = 0\), which occurs at \(90^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\). The largest angle in the interval is \(270^\circ\).

qs.q: How many values of \(\theta\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\) make \(\sin\theta\) undefined?
qs.s: Since \(\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r}\) and \(r > 0\) for all points on the terminal side, \(\sin\theta\) is defined for all values of \(\theta\). Therefore, there are 0 values where \(\sin\theta\) is undefined.

qs.q: What is the largest negative angle \(\theta\) (in degrees) for which \(\tan\theta\) is undefined?
qs.s: The tangent function is undefined when its terminal side lies along the y-axis, where \(x = 0\). The negative angles on the y-axis are \(-90^\circ, -270^\circ, -450^\circ, \dots\), so the largest (closest to zero) is \(-90^\circ\).

qs.q: What is the sum of all angles \(\theta\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\) for which \(\tan\theta\) is undefined?
qs.s: The function \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}\) is undefined when \(x = 0\), which occurs at \(\theta = 90^\circ\) and \(\theta = 270^\circ\). The sum of these angles is \(90^\circ + 270^\circ = 360^\circ\).

qs.q: How many values of \(\theta\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 720^\circ\) make the function \(\sec\theta\) undefined?
qs.s: The secant function is undefined when \(x = 0\), which happens twice per revolution (at \(90^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\)). Over two full revolutions (\(0^\circ \leq \theta < 720^\circ\)), it is undefined at \(90^\circ, 270^\circ, 450^\circ\), and \(630^\circ\), for a total of 4 values.

qs.q: How many values of \(\theta\) in the interval \(-180^\circ \leq \theta \leq 180^\circ\) make \(\cot\theta\) undefined?
qs.s: The function \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y}\) is undefined when \(y = 0\), which occurs on the x-axis. In the interval \(-180^\circ \leq \theta \leq 180^\circ\), this happens at \(\theta = -180^\circ\), \(\theta = 0^\circ\), and \(\theta = 180^\circ\), giving 3 values.

qs.q: Find the sum of all angles \(\theta\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\) for which the expression \(\sec\theta + \csc\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The expression is undefined when either \(\sec\theta\) is undefined (\(90^\circ, 270^\circ\)) or \(\csc\theta\) is undefined (\(0^\circ, 180^\circ\)). Summing these four angles gives \(0^\circ + 90^\circ + 180^\circ + 270^\circ = 540^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the largest value of \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\), for which \(\cot\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The function \(\cot\theta\) is undefined when \(\sin\theta = 0\), which occurs at \(\theta = 0^\circ\) and \(\theta = 180^\circ\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\). Therefore, the largest value is \(180^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the largest value of \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\), for which \(\csc\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The function \(\csc\theta = \frac{r}{y}\) is undefined when \(y = 0\), which occurs at \(\theta = 0^\circ\) and \(\theta = 180^\circ\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\). Thus, the largest value is \(180^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the smallest value of \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\), for which \(\sec\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The function \(\sec\theta = \frac{r}{x}\) is undefined when \(x = 0\), which corresponds to \(\cos\theta = 0\). In the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\), this occurs at \(\theta = 90^\circ\) and \(\theta = 270^\circ\), so the smallest value is \(90^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the smallest value of \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\), for which \(\cot\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The function \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y}\) is undefined when \(y = 0\), which corresponds to \(\sin\theta = 0\). In the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\), this occurs at \(\theta = 0^\circ\) and \(\theta = 180^\circ\), so the smallest value is \(0^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the largest value of \(\theta\), \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\), for which \(\sec\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The function \(\sec\theta\) is undefined when \(\cos\theta = 0\), which occurs at \(\theta = 90^\circ\) and \(\theta = 270^\circ\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\). Therefore, the largest value is \(270^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the largest angle \(\theta\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 720^\circ\) for which \(\cot\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The function \(\cot\theta\) is undefined when \(\sin\theta = 0\), which occurs at integer multiples of \(180^\circ\). In the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 720^\circ\), the values are \(0^\circ, 180^\circ, 360^\circ\), and \(540^\circ\), so the largest is \(540^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the sum of all values of \(\theta\) in the interval \(0 \leq \theta < 2\pi\) for which \(\tan\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The function \(\tan\theta\) is undefined when \(\cos\theta = 0\), which occurs at \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\theta = \frac{3\pi}{2}\) in the interval \(0 \leq \theta < 2\pi\). Their sum is \(\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{3\pi}{2} = 2\pi\).

qs.q: Find the sum of all values of \(\theta\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\) for which \(\sec\theta\) is undefined.
qs.s: The function \(\sec\theta\) is undefined when \(\cos\theta = 0\), which occurs at \(\theta = 90^\circ\) and \(\theta = 270^\circ\) in the interval \(0^\circ \leq \theta < 360^\circ\). The sum of these values is \(90^\circ + 270^\circ = 360^\circ\).

qs.q: Find the sum of all values of \(\theta\) in the interval \(0 \leq \theta < 2\pi\) for which \(\cot\theta\) is undefined.
